Model Output:
# Brainstorming **The prompt: "Gods wore sneakers."** Four words, past tense, a flat declarative that suggests either (a) a world where gods are present and mundane, or (b) a narrator recounting a time when gods were among us — past tense implying they're gone now, or changed. The past tense is interesting. It hints at nostalgia, a lost era, or an aftermath. ## Possible directions **1. Urban pantheon, contemporary.** Gods live in a city, taking odd jobs, wearing Air Force 1s, running bodegas. A mortal protagonist stumbles into their world. Familiar territory (American Gods, Percy Jackson, Good Omens), risk of feeling derivative. Would need a sharp angle. **2. The marathon / footrace.** Sneakers = running. Hermes, Atalanta, Mercury, the Norse Hermod, Yoruba Eshu (messenger/trickster of the crossroads). A story built around an actual race — a mythic footrace where gods compete in mortal disguise. The sneakers are literal equipment. Could be funny and kinetic. **3. The cobbler / shoemaker.** A mortal who makes shoes for gods. Hephaestus is the divine craftsman, but what if a human sneaker designer (a Tinker Hatfield type) gets commissioned by the gods? The gods need new footwear because their old sandals don't work anymore — the world has changed and they need to walk on asphalt. The shoemaker becomes the point-of-view character, observing the gods through their feet. Intimate, odd, specific. **4. Post-divine aftermath.** "Gods wore sneakers" as an elegy. The gods have left/died/faded, and what remains are their shoes. A found-object story. Someone inherits a shoebox. Melancholy, quiet. **5. The gods as a running crew.** A group of runners in a city — a run club — turns out to be diminished deities who keep themselves alive through motion. Faith is gone; they survive on the endorphins of the last thing humans still do religiously: exercise. The sneakers are their new vestments. Running is the new liturgy. **6. Child's-eye view.** A kid in a housing project notices the neighbors are gods. The god upstairs in the Jordans is Thor. Whimsical, could go sentimental. **7. Mythological blending.** Rather than one pantheon, a mix — Hermes, Eshu, Anansi, Hermod, Ninshubur (Sumerian messenger goddess), Iris. Messengers specifically. A story about messengers who have no messages to carry anymore because of phones. They still run. The sneakers are their identity. **8. Sneakerhead culture as religious practice.** Drops, queues, worship of the object. A pair of sneakers is literally divine — the last artifact. A sneakerhead protagonist who treats shoes with the reverence once given to relics, and discovers the reverence is warranted. ## Characters that surface - **A mortal shoemaker/repair person.** Older, hands ruined, runs a shop in a dying neighborhood. Not a designer — a cobbler. Fixes soles. The gods come to her because they wear through shoes faster than anyone; they walk more than anyone. - **Hermes** — obvious but rich. The messenger, thief, god of boundaries and travelers. Restless. Could be a bike courier or just someone who never sits down. - **Eshu/Elegba** — Yoruba orisha of crossroads and messages. Would pair interestingly with Hermes; both tricksters, both liminal. Pairing them risks flattening distinct traditions, so handle with care and specificity. - **Atalanta** — not a god, but a hero-runner. Refused marriage, got tricked by golden apples. A diminished figure. - **A young person** — apprentice, grandchild, someone who sees the gods with fresh eyes. - **A god who can't run anymore.** Hephaestus, lame. He makes the shoes. Or an aged Hermes with a bad knee. ## Tone options - Comic-melancholy (Good Omens register) - Elegiac, quiet, literary - Kinetic, propulsive, race-structured - Deadpan realism ## Structural ideas for 8 chapters **Structure A — The commission.** A cobbler is asked to make/repair shoes for a series of gods, one per chapter. Episodic. Ends with her making shoes for herself. Risk: repetitive, no throughline. **Structure B — The race.** One night, one footrace across a city. Gods compete. Eight legs of the race, eight chapters. Kinetic but could feel gimmicky and shallow on character. **Structure C — The last messenger.** Hermes (or a composite messenger figure) has one last message to deliver and has forgotten what it is. He runs the city over one night trying to remember, encountering other diminished gods. The cobbler is where he starts and ends. **Structure D — Mortal POV, slow revelation.** A cobbler's apprentice slowly realizes who her customers are. Chapter 4 midpoint: revelation. Second half: she has to decide what to do with the knowledge. Risk: "slow reveal of gods" is very well-trodden. **Structure E — The elegy, framed.** An older narrator remembers when gods wore sneakers — a specific summer, a specific neighborhood, a specific pair of shoes. The gods are gone by the time of narration. We learn why across the chapters. ## Key images - A god standing in line at a sneaker drop, anonymous. - Wings on the heels — literal Talaria — reimagined as the swoosh, the wing logo. Hermes looking at a Nike logo with something between amusement and grief: they named it after her. - Worn-through soles. Gods walk so much they destroy shoes in weeks. - A cobbler who can tell everything about a person from how their shoe wore down. Gods wear down shoes in impossible patterns — no heel strike, as if they float and only occasionally touch. - A shoebox as reliquary. - Laces. Tying a god's laces. - Nike herself, the actual goddess of victory, in a world where her name is on everyone's feet. Does she get royalties? Does she feel honored or erased? This is potentially the richest single idea. ## Nike as a character Nike — winged goddess of victory, daughter of Pallas and Styx, attendant of Zeus and Athena. In the modern world her name is the most recognizable brand on earth. She is everywhere and nowhere. Everyone says her name; no one prays to her. She might be the most "successful" god and the most hollowed out. What does she want? Not victory — she IS victory. Maybe she wants to lose something, once. Maybe she wants to be a person. Contrast: Hermes, whose name is on nothing (well — Hermès scarves, ha). Hermes, the actual patron of runners and travelers, gets no sneaker. Nike gets everything. A story about two gods — Nike and Hermes — and the mortal who repairs their shoes. Nike is famous-but-erased; Hermes is forgotten-but-intact. ## Possible plot: "Sole" Wren (or similar), a cobbler in her sixties, runs a shoe repair shop. A regular customer — a wiry woman who calls herself Vic — brings in sneakers that are destroyed in ways that make no sense. Another regular, a courier called Herm or Manny or Mercury (too cute?) — brings in shoes worn only at the toe. Over the story Wren comes to understand what they are. The plot engine: Nike/Vic wants Wren to make her a pair of shoes with no brand on them — she wants to run in something that doesn't say her own name. Hermes wants... something else. Maybe he wants his job back. There's a race, or a delivery, or simply a death — Wren's, perhaps, or the shop's. Ending options: - Wren dies and Hermes (psychopompos — he guides souls to the underworld!) is the one who walks her down. He's the only messenger left with a route that still matters. She goes barefoot; or in shoes she made. - The shop closes and Nike buys it, anonymously, with money she doesn't understand having. - Wren makes one pair of shoes with wings on the heels — actual Talaria — and gives them to a mortal kid. Hermes as psychopomp is the key mythological hinge. The messenger god also conducts the dead. His sneakers aren't for racing — they're for the long walk down. That gives the past tense of the prompt a reason: the narrator could be the one he walked down. # Reflection The slow-reveal "my neighbors are secretly gods" structure is the biggest trap here — it's been done extensively and readers are ahead of it from page one. Better to have the gods known, or known quickly, and put the story's energy elsewhere: into relationship, into want, into a specific ending. The Nike idea is the strongest single conceit because it's *specific to the prompt*. "Gods wore sneakers" — and one of them has her name on the sneakers. That irony isn't decoration; it's a whole emotional situation. Fame as erasure. Being invoked millions of times a day and never once addressed. It also gives the story a natural mortal-god axis that isn't about power but about attention and name, which is a more interesting thing for a god to lack. Hermes as psychopomp is the second-strongest idea because it supplies an ending with weight and turns the "sneakers" from gag into meaning: the shoes are for walking someone home. It also justifies the past tense — a narrator who has already been walked down, or a narrator recounting from just before. It gives the story stakes that don't require a villain or a quest, which at 8,000 words is the right scale. A cosmic plot would feel rushed; a death in a shoe shop won't. The cobbler POV works better than an apprentice or kid because she has a craft that reads people through their shoes — that's a way to *show* divinity without exposition, through wear patterns, through what the soles say. It's also sensory and grounded, keeping the piece from floating off into whimsy. An older mortal facing the end gives the story a clock without an artificial one. Risks to manage: it could become precious or sentimental — dying cobbler, kindly gods. The gods must have edges. Nike should be difficult, maybe cold, maybe faintly contemptuous of losing. Hermes should be a thief and a liar who still steals small things from the shop. The mortal shouldn't be wise; she should be prickly and a bit greedy for the work. Humor should come from deadpan, not quirk. The race structure is fun but wrong for this — it would prioritize kinetics over the quieter payoff. Multi-pantheon blending is tempting but at this length would spread thin and risk tokenism; two Greek figures with a real mythological relationship (Nike and Hermes both attend Zeus, both are winged, both are about swiftness) is enough. The dying-neighborhood/closing-shop element is useful as texture but shouldn't become the plot — gentrification stories have their own gravity and would pull focus. Pacing across eight chapters: establish the shop and the impossible shoes fast (1), introduce both gods as customers with distinct wear patterns (2–3), let the reveal be quiet and almost incidental rather than a twist (3–4), midpoint should turn on Nike's request — shoes with no name (4), the making of those shoes and what it costs (5–6), the mortal's decline arriving without melodrama (6–7), the final walk with Hermes (8). The last line should land the prompt's past tense. What I'd want the reader to feel: that the ordinary is the disguise, and that the most sacred thing in the story is a repaired sole — that gods wore sneakers because they had far to walk, and someone had to keep the shoes together.

Model Output:
# Intention The story is a quiet, deadpan, faintly comic elegy told in the first person by **Ruth Adair**, a 67-year-old cobbler who runs a shoe-repair shop, narrated retrospectively from a point she does not specify until the end. She is prickly, exact, and a little greedy for good work. Her craft — reading a person from how their soles wear — is the story's method: divinity is shown through wear patterns, laces, and heel drop, never through exposition or spectacle. There is no slow reveal and no twist. The two gods are known to the reader almost at once and known to Ruth soon after; she simply doesn't make a fuss, because fussing isn't her register. The story's energy goes instead into **want**. **Nike** (calling herself Vic) is the most-spoken name on earth and never once addressed; she wants a pair of shoes that don't say her name, and beneath that, she wants to know what losing is. **Hermes** (who gives his name plainly and is assumed to be joking) is forgotten but intact; he still steals laces, still lies, and still has one job that matters, which is not delivery but conduction — he walks the dead down. That job supplies the ending and justifies the prompt's past tense. Stylistic aims: short declarative sentences; sensory specificity about leather, glue, awls, rubber; humor by understatement; mythology worn lightly and accurately (Talaria, Styx, psychopompos, the swoosh as an unpaid wing). Gods have edges — Nike is cold and competitive, Hermes is a thief. Ruth is not wise; she is competent, which is different. I will avoid: sentimentality about the dying cobbler, a gentrification subplot, multi-pantheon sprawl, a race-as-structure, villains, and any scene where someone explains what a god is. The last line lands the prompt. Each chapter runs roughly 1,000 words and is anchored on a single pair of shoes. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Heel Drop.** Ruth introduces the shop and her creed: a shoe tells the truth its wearer won't. A wiry woman called Vic brings in a pair of running shoes destroyed in three weeks — outsole ground to the midsole across the forefoot, heel untouched, as if she's never landed. The swoosh has been scraped off with a blade. Ruth quotes a price too high; Vic pays without looking. Ruth notes the woman has never, in two years, said thank you. **Chapter 2 — Laces.** The courier who calls himself Hermes. Bike, satchel, talks constantly, says nothing. His shoes come in with uppers shredded and soles pristine — the wear pattern of someone who moves through things rather than over them. Every visit, laces go missing from the shop's rack. Ruth confronts him; he returns a pair, wrong color, and says he was a thief before he was anything else. Ruth decides the name isn't a joke and finds she doesn't much care. **Chapter 3 — Wings.** Both customers in the shop at once. They know each other; the air goes tight. Vic and Hermes talk over Ruth's head in the shorthand of siblings, and it comes out plainly: he had wings on his heels once, she had them on her back, and now his are gone and hers are on the side of every foot in the city, printed, unpaid. Hermes finds this very funny. Vic does not. Ruth learns Vic is Nike by hearing her name said as an insult. **Chapter 4 — The Commission.** Nike returns alone and asks Ruth to make — not repair — a pair of shoes with no name on them, no logo, nothing. Ruth is a cobbler, not a maker; she hasn't built from a last in forty years. She says no. Nike says she has never asked anyone for anything. Ruth, who has a letter from a hospital in her apron she's been ignoring, says yes for reasons she doesn't examine. Midpoint: the work begins. **Chapter 5 — Last.** The making. Ruth pulls her old lasts from the cellar, measures a goddess's foot (high arch, no callus, a heel that has never taken weight). Hermes drops in daily, steals a thimble, brings coffee, asks what she's building and why. She asks him what he still delivers. He says "people, mostly" and changes the subject. Her hands hurt in a new way. She works through it. **Chapter 6 — Unmarked.** The shoes are finished: plain, dark, nameless. Nike laces them in the shop and stands in them, and for a moment looks unsteady — the first time she has ever felt her heel touch ground. She says she is going to run the Saturday 5K in the park and try to come second. Ruth doesn't understand this as the gift it is until later. Nike leaves. Hermes, watching from the doorway, says quietly that she'll fail at it, and that that's the point. **Chapter 7 — Walking Shoes.** Ruth's decline arrives without drama: a fall in the shop, a week she doesn't remember. Hermes visits and finally stops joking. He tells her about the one route that still runs, the long walk down, and that he's the only one left who knows it. Nike comes too, in the unmarked shoes, scuffed now — she came second by a stride and has not stopped thinking about it. She says thank you. It is the first time. Ruth chooses what she'll wear. **Chapter 8 — Gods Wore Sneakers.** The walk. Ruth in a pair she resoled herself, Hermes beside her in the shredded uppers she never managed to fix. The city empties toward a river she half recognizes. He talks the whole way, tells her three lies and one truth, and steals her laces at the water's edge because, he says, she won't need them and he's never once crossed with a full pair. She looks back once at the shop lights. The narration's vantage clarifies — where she has been telling this from. Last line lands the prompt in past tense: what she remembers of them is not their faces but their feet, and that they had far to walk.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This A human writer given "Gods wore sneakers" would probably not start with a plan at all. They'd start with an irritation or an image — a pair of shoes they actually owned, a cobbler they actually knew, a memory of a name on a shoe. They'd write toward something they didn't fully understand yet and let the prompt be a launching pad rather than a thesis to prove. The story would end up lopsided in some way that reflected what they cared about: maybe 3,000 words on the smell of contact cement and 200 on the god. A human writer would also, crucially, resist the *obvious cleverness* of the prompt. "Gods wore sneakers" invites a wink — ha, gods, but casual! — and a good human writer would feel that wink as a trap and either lean into it hard and stupid (make it really a comedy) or refuse it entirely and write something that barely acknowledges the joke. What they wouldn't do is sit at the exact midpoint: "deadpan, faintly comic elegy." That midpoint is where LLM writing lives, because it's the safest place — a little funny, a little sad, nothing risked in either direction. A human would let the story have a *problem*. Not a plot problem — a real problem in the writing, something unresolved or ugly or too long. Humans leave hair in the soup. They have opinions about cobblers, or about Nike the corporation, or about dying, and those opinions leak in unevenly. # Telltale LLM Approaches (Generally) **The balanced register.** Every LLM story is "quiet, wry, melancholy with moments of humor." It's the literary equivalent of beige. Real stories have a dominant temperature. **The bow.** Threads get tied. The gift is received. The thank-you arrives. The last line rhymes with the first. Nothing is left on the table because the model can't tolerate loose ends — it reads them as errors. **Symmetry and echo.** Chapter 1's detail returns in Chapter 8. Every image pays off. This is craft when done once; it's mechanical when done everywhere. Humans forget their own setups. **The wise mortal, the humbled god.** LLMs love reversals of status that feel egalitarian. The cobbler teaches the goddess about losing. Gods learn from humans. It's flattering to the reader and totally predictable. **Explaining the metaphor.** The story tells you what the sneakers mean. "The shoes were for walking someone home." The model can't resist naming the theme because naming it is how it knows the theme is there. **Prose that performs.** Short declarative sentences announced as a style. "Sensory specificity" as a checkbox — leather, glue, awls. The model lists textures rather than being interested in one. Every paragraph has a quotable line. Nobody talks the way LLM characters talk — they speak in aphorisms. **Risk aversion in content.** No one is cruel. No one is boring. No sex, no real money trouble, no politics, no body horror, no long digression. Death is tasteful. Illness is "a letter from a hospital." **The tidy chapter.** Each chapter is a unit with a title, a single anchor image, an ending beat. Real chapters are uneven — some are all dialogue, some are 300 words, some wander. **Over-signposting significance.** "It is the first time." "She doesn't understand this as the gift it is until later." The narrator keeps telling you which moments matter. **Research-flavored detail.** Mythology "worn lightly and accurately" — Talaria, psychopompos, daughter of Styx. It reads like the writer checked Wikipedia and wants credit. A human who actually knew the myths would misremember them or hold a grudge about one. # Deep Dive: Critiquing the Intention & Plan **The register is the safe midpoint.** "Deadpan, faintly comic elegy" — this is exactly the LLM sweet spot. It hedges. Is this story funny or is it about dying? A human would pick. If it's about dying, the humor should be the kind that's actually inappropriate, that a reader might find in poor taste. If it's funny, Ruth's death should be funny too, or not happen. **"No twist, no slow reveal" is good — but the plan still stages reveals.** Chapter 3 "Ruth learns Vic is Nike by hearing her name said as an insult." That's a reveal, just a soft one, and it's the kind LLMs love: information delivered obliquely so it feels earned. Would a human just have Ruth know from the start? Or never confirm it? The plan claims to reject the trope while performing a polite version of it. **The wise-mortal/humbled-god reversal is fully present.** Nike wants to know what losing is; the cobbler provides. Nike says thank you for the first time. This is the egalitarian-reversal trope in its purest form. It's *nice*. A human writer might find it cloying. What if Nike never says thank you? What if the shoes don't work — she wins anyway, easily, and is bored, and the whole commission was a waste of Ruth's last good months? What if the goddess is simply not changed, because gods don't change, and the story is about Ruth wanting her to be? **Hermes is too lovable.** "Steals laces, brings coffee, steals a thimble." This is the LLM's idea of a rogue — a scamp. Petty theft as charm. A real thief is unsettling. A real trickster ruins something. What does Hermes cost Ruth? The plan gives him no teeth. Also: "tells her three lies and one truth" is a very LLM move — a numerical pattern that sounds mythic and means nothing specific. **The illness is euphemized to death.** "A letter from a hospital in her apron she's been ignoring." "Her decline arrives without drama." "A week she doesn't remember." The plan is congratulating itself on restraint, but this restraint is avoidance. A human writing about a 67-year-old dying would know what she's dying *of*, would have a scene where she can't grip the hammer, would have her be angry or cheap about it, would mention the cost of the scan. The plan uses "without melodrama" as cover for "without specificity." **Every chapter is anchored on a shoe. Every chapter has a one-word title.** This is the tidy-chapter problem. It will read as a structure imposed from above. Humans don't build eight equal rooms. **The ending is the biggest bow in the story.** Psychopomp walk, river, looking back at the shop lights, laces stolen at the water's edge, vantage clarified, last line lands the prompt. This is *four* endings stacked. It's also the Orpheus look-back gesture, the Styx crossing, the shoes-for-the-dead — a full mythology-payoff sequence. And "what she remembers is not their faces but their feet" is a line the plan is already proud of, which is a bad sign. The last line being the prompt in past tense is the model closing the loop for the grader. **"Ruth is not wise; she is competent, which is different."** This is the plan pre-writing its own good line. It's also a dodge — competence as a virtue that lets her be the moral center without the story admitting it. **The swoosh-as-unpaid-wing is the single strongest idea and the plan underuses it by making it clever rather than *felt*.** Hermes finds it funny, Nike doesn't. That's a stated reaction, not a scene. What does it actually feel like to be Nike walking past a Foot Locker? The plan doesn't know because it hasn't imagined it — it's noted it. **No one has a body except through wear patterns.** Nike has a "high arch, no callus." Ruth has hands that hurt "in a new way." Hermes has a bike. Nobody sweats, eats, smells, pisses, has a bad back. Nobody is attractive or unattractive. The gods are ideas with feet. **The story has no money.** A cobbler in a dying neighborhood in 2020-something has rent. Nike "pays without looking" — of course she does. But what does Ruth charge for a bespoke pair? Does she undercharge because she wants the work? Does the commission cost her the shop? Money is the most human thing and the plan skips it because it's unglamorous. **Dialogue will be aphoristic.** "He says 'people, mostly' and changes the subject." "He was a thief before he was anything else." Every quoted line in the plan is a mic drop. Nobody in the story is going to say "hang on, where'd I put the—" or talk about the weather for real. # Brainstorm: Making It More Human **Pick a temperature.** Either go fully deadpan-comic (Ruth is annoyed by the gods, finds them tedious customers, her dying is inconvenient mainly because of the backlog) or go fully elegiac and drop the whimsy. Don't blend. **Let Nike be unchanged.** She gets the shoes. She runs. She wins by a mile because she is victory and shoes don't change that. She's irritated. She never comes back. Ruth's last real work was for someone who didn't need it. That's a truer story about gods. **Or: let Nike lose and hate it.** Not "learn from it." Hate it. Throw the shoes in the shop's bin. Ruth fishes them out and resoles them for a kid. **Give Hermes a real theft.** He takes something that matters — Ruth's late husband's awl, a photograph, the deposit money. He doesn't return it. He is the god of thieves and the story lets him be one. **Name the illness. Show a body.** Pancreatic, or a heart, or just the kind of stroke that takes the left hand. Have Ruth drop things. Have her be vain about her hands. Have her wet herself once in the shop and clean it up before opening. **Cut the river.** Or cut the shop-lights look-back. Or cut the laces. Pick one gesture at the end, and maybe make it a wrong one — Hermes gets them lost, or has to check his phone, or the walk is boring and long and she's bored on it. **Break the chapter symmetry.** One chapter that's 400 words. One that's all dialogue. One that's a list of repair tickets. One where nothing happens and Ruth just fixes a stranger's boots and thinks about her sister. **Let the narration have a bias.** Ruth should be *wrong* about something. She should misjudge Hermes, or be unfair to a customer, or have a petty grudge she never resolves. The retrospective vantage should not make her serene. **Real talk.** Have the gods discuss something dull — parking, the weather, a TV show they don't understand. Have Ruth explain shoe glue for two paragraphs because she cares about it and the story lets her. **Don't confirm the gods.** Consider never stating it. Ruth knows. The reader knows. Nobody says "Nike." The insult in Chapter 3 is just an insult. **Lose the last-line landing.** The prompt is a prompt, not a contract. If "gods wore sneakers" appears anywhere, let it be a throwaway in the middle, from Ruth, dismissive — "The gods wore sneakers. Everybody wore sneakers. It's not a personality." **Let something be unresolved.** Who Ruth is telling this to. Whether the shop closed. Whether the shoes she made were any good. What happened to the kid who got them. Leave a door open and don't look through it. **Money.** A price. An argument about it. Ruth charging Nike four hundred dollars and feeling both cheap and thrilled. **Let the mythology be misremembered.** Ruth thinks Nike was the goddess of shoes. Hermes doesn't correct her. Or he does, pedantically, and it's the most human he seems. **One ugly scene.** Someone cruel. Nike sneering at a fat runner. Hermes taking a cut from a delivery. Ruth refusing to fix a poor man's boots because she's saving her hands for the goddess's commission. Let the story cost someone something it doesn't repay.

# Intention The story is a first-person account by **Ruth Adair**, 67, a cobbler, told after the fact to no one she names. The dominant temperature is **deadpan-annoyed comedy**. Ruth finds the gods tedious as customers. Her dying is an inconvenience mainly because of the backlog. Grief is never stated; it leaks through what she won't discuss and what she over-explains (contact cement, heel drop, why nobody knows how to resole a Blundstone anymore). Whimsy is refused. If a line sounds quotable, it gets cut or undercut. **Choices made explicit:** - Ruth has already had a stroke before the story opens. Left hand doesn't close. A cobbler needs the left hand to hold the shoe. This is named in Chapter 1 and never softened. - The gods are never confirmed. Nobody says "you're a god." Ruth knows; the reader knows; the story doesn't stop for it. Ruth misremembers mythology (thinks Nike was goddess of shoes) and is corrected, pedantically, by Hermes — the most human he gets. - **Nike is not changed.** She commissions nameless shoes, runs in them, wins by a mile, is bored, drops them on the counter, and never comes back. The last real work of Ruth's life was for someone it did nothing for. No thank-you. Ever. - **Hermes steals something that matters**: the $400 cash Nike paid. He doesn't return it. He still walks Ruth down. She is still angry about the money the entire way and never forgives him. - **Money is present.** Ruth undercharges and knows it. Rent is mentioned. The scan cost is mentioned. - **One ugly scene**: Ruth refuses to fix a man's work boots because she's saving her hand for the goddess's shoes. He needs them Monday. She doesn't repair this in the narrative. - The phrase "gods wore sneakers" appears once, in Chapter 2, from Ruth, dismissively. It is not the last line. - Chapters are **uneven**. No matching titles. One is mostly a list of repair tickets. One is nearly all dialogue. Lengths flex toward the 1,000 target but two run short and one runs long. - The ending: the walk is long and dull. Hermes checks his phone. They take a wrong turn. No river, no look-back, no laces, no clarified vantage. It ends mid-annoyance on an unfixed shoe. - Loose ends left open: who Ruth is telling this to; whether the shop closed; whether the nameless shoes were any good; what became of the boots man. **Avoid:** aphoristic dialogue, sensory checklists, symmetry between opening and close, signposted significance ("it was the first time"), any moment where a god learns from a mortal, tasteful illness, the last line landing the prompt. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1.** Ruth on the shop, the rent ($1,850, up in March), and the hand — six weeks since the stroke, left fingers won't close past a half-fist, she's been holding shoes against her hip. Vic comes in with running shoes destroyed in three weeks: forefoot ground to the midsole, heel factory-fresh, swoosh scraped off with a blade. Ruth explains what heel drop is for two paragraphs because she'd rather do that than talk about the hand. She quotes $65 for a job she'd have done for $40 before. Vic pays, doesn't say thank you, hasn't in two years. Ruth notes she's the kind of customer you dread and can't afford to lose. **Chapter 2.** The courier. Says his name is Hermes and Ruth says "sure," because everyone in this neighborhood is called something. Uppers shredded, soles pristine — he moves through things. Laces disappear from the rack every visit; she's stopped stocking the good ones. He talks the whole time about a parking ticket. Ruth mentions her mother used to say Nike was the goddess of shoes; Hermes, irritated, corrects her at length — victory, daughter of Styx, nothing to do with feet, the shoe people just took it. Ruth doesn't care. "The gods wore sneakers. Everyone wore sneakers. It's not a personality." She notices he never once looks at her bad hand, which is either kind or not noticing, and she can't tell which. **Chapter 3.** *(Short, ~650 words.)* Mostly the ticket book — a week of repairs in Ruth's shorthand: heel/heel/zipper/no/heel/Blundstone (why does nobody make these serviceable)/patent shoe, no, tell them no. Interrupted by a man with work boots, sole separated, needs them Monday. Ruth looks at the boots, looks at her hand, thinks about how many good hours it has left this week. She says she's backed up. He says he'll pay extra. She says no. He leaves. She writes nothing in the book for him. Vic comes in that afternoon. **Chapter 4.** *(Runs long, ~1,200.)* Vic wants a pair made — not fixed, made, from nothing, with no name on them, no mark, nothing anyone could read. Ruth hasn't built from a last in forty years and has one working hand and says so. Vic says she has never asked anyone for anything and doesn't intend to start twice. They argue about money because Ruth can't say what a bespoke pair costs anymore. She says $400, knows it's a third of what it's worth, hates herself. Vic puts four hundred cash on the counter, in a rubber band, and leaves without arranging a fitting. Ruth puts the money in the tin under the register. The plan is to take the scan bill out of it. **Chapter 5.** The making. Old lasts from the cellar, a foot measured off Vic's destroyed shoes because Vic won't come sit. Ruth works one-handed with the shoe clamped against her thigh and the hip bruises. Hermes comes by daily, brings coffee she didn't ask for, talks about the parking ticket appeal. Day four the tin is $400 lighter. She knows. He knows she knows. Neither says anything and he keeps coming. She does not report him, does not confront him, does not forgive him, and puts the scan on a card. She finishes the shoes anyway: dark, plain, ugly in the way things are ugly before they're worn in. **Chapter 6.** *(Nearly all dialogue.)* Vic in the shop trying them on. Standing. Walking to the door and back. She says the heel feels wrong. Ruth says that's a heel, that's what they feel like. Vic says she's running the park 5K Saturday. Ruth asks what she's trying to do. Vic says she's going to see what happens. Hermes is there, off to the side, eating something. He says, not to anyone, that she'll win by a mile and she knows it. Vic says shut up. Nobody discusses the money. Vic leaves in the shoes and Ruth realizes she never made her sign a ticket, so technically there's no record the shoes exist. **Chapter 7.** Tuesday. Vic comes in, puts the shoes on the counter — one lace undone, mud on the heel, that's all. She won by a mile. It was the same. She says the shoes are fine, they didn't do anything, and leaves. Ruth never sees her again. She puts the shoes in the window with a tag that says $400 because she doesn't know what else to write. Later that week the second stroke; she's on the shop floor a while before Hermes finds her, and he sits on the stool and waits with her rather than calling anyone, and she's too tired to ask why. She thinks about the boots man and whether he found someone. **Chapter 8.** The walk. Ruth in her own resoled clogs, Hermes in the shredded uppers she never got around to — the one ticket she left open, and it bothers her. He talks about the parking ticket the whole way; he lost the appeal. She brings up the $400 twice; he changes the subject twice. The city thins out but not into anything grand — bus shelters, a closed Payless, a stretch of nothing. He checks his phone. They take a wrong turn and have to double back. She's tired and says so. He says it's not much farther and she knows what that's worth from a courier. The last thing she notices, before whatever comes next, is that the left upper is coming away from the sole again and someone should really see to that.

Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc

# Ruth Adair **Background.** Sixty-seven. Born in the neighborhood when it was a different neighborhood — Portuguese bakeries, a shoe factory two blocks over that closed in '81. Her father worked the factory floor; she learned lasting at fifteen from a man named Sal who smelled of naphtha and had no eyebrows. Married Dennis Adair at twenty-two; he ran the front of the shop for thirty-one years and died of a heart attack in the stockroom in 2016, sitting down, with a receipt book in his lap. She hasn't rearranged the stockroom. Not for sentiment — she knows where things are. The shop is Adair's Shoe Repair, though the sign has said ADAIR SHOE REPAI since 2019 and she's decided the R is a test of who's paying attention. Rent is $1,850 and going to $2,100 in March. She has a sister, Carol, in Sarasota, who calls on Sundays and wants her to sell. Ruth lets it ring twice before picking up so Carol knows she was doing something. Stroke six weeks before the story opens. Left hand. She was on the floor of the shop forty minutes before a customer found her and she's more embarrassed about that than about the hand — she'd been trying to get up the whole time, not lying still like they tell you. The hand closes to a half-fist. It's warm, it feels things, it just won't grip. She's found workarounds (thigh, hip, a wooden jig Dennis made for a different purpose) and tells no one that the workarounds hurt. **Personality.** Exact. Opinionated about things nobody else has opinions about: heel drop, cement vs. stitch-down, the collapse of quality in Blundstones after they moved production. She can tell you what's wrong with a person from their outsole and considers this a professional skill, not insight. Cheap with herself, generous with materials — will use the good thread on a $20 job because bad thread offends her. Quotes prices while looking at the shoe, never the customer. Not warm. Not cruel either, usually. She likes people she doesn't have to talk to. She keeps a radio on to the traffic-and-weather station because it fills the shop without asking anything of her. **Idiosyncrasies.** Writes repair tickets in a shorthand only she reads: "H" for heel, "N" for no, a small cross for jobs she doesn't want. Keeps loose change in a coffee can labeled THREAD. Eats lunch standing at the bench, always a tuna sandwich from the deli, always on rye, never finishes the second half. Has a grudge against a customer from 2009 who returned a pair and said the work was "fine" in a tone. She remembers his name (Kessler) and looks for him in the street. **Flaws.** Pride disguised as standards. Says no to work she should take because the job is beneath the hand she has left, then resents the emptier ticket book. Cannot say "I need help" in any grammatical construction. Has never once, in the entire narration, considered that the boots man was in a worse position than she was. **Physicality.** Small, thick through the shoulders from fifty years at a bench. Grey hair kept short with kitchen scissors. Reading glasses on a lanyard she made from waxed lace. Wears an apron with one pocket sewn shut (a pen exploded in it in 1994). Left hand held slightly away from the body, half-curled, like she's holding something small she doesn't want to drop. Walks in resoled Dansko clogs, the same pair since 2011. Doesn't look at people's faces first. Looks at their feet, then their hands, then, if she has to, up. **Motives and relationships.** Wants to keep the shop open until she's dead and then doesn't care. Wants, more privately, to do one more thing from a last — properly, a whole shoe — and knows the hand makes it stupid to want that. Vic is a customer she dreads and can't afford to lose; she doesn't like her and doesn't need to. Hermes she finds tiresome and, after the money, unforgivable, and she still lets him in because he's the only person who comes in every day and she's stopped pretending that doesn't count. Carol she loves and avoids. **Voice.** > "A running shoe has a heel drop. Ten millimeters, eight, whatever. That's the whole design. You're supposed to land on it. If you haven't landed on it in three weeks of running then either you're doing it wrong or you weigh nothing, and I'm not paid to know which." > I'd like to say I thought about the boots man that night. I didn't. I thought about him later, when there was nothing to do about it, which is when I think about most things. > "Sixty-five." Before the hand it was forty. I'm not proud of it. I'm not not proud of it either. The hand was going to cost somebody. --- # Nike (Vic) **Background.** She doesn't give one. Goes by Vic, which Ruth assumed for two years was short for Victoria. It isn't short for anything; it's what's left when you knock the name down to the part nobody's wearing. Daughter of Styx — Hermes will insist on this. Sister to Zelos, Kratos, Bia: rivalry, strength, force. The family business was standing behind Zeus and making sure he won. She was very good at it. She is still very good at it; that's the whole trouble. Victory isn't something she does, it's something she is, and you can't put down what you are. In this century she runs. Not for anything. She runs the way a tap runs. She enters races under different names, wins, doesn't collect medals. She has never, as far as she knows, come anywhere but first, and has begun to suspect this isn't a gift but a defect, like a door that only opens one way. Her name is on the side of roughly a billion shoes. She scrapes it off her own with a razor blade every time. She has not decided whether this is a protest or a habit. **Personality.** Cold in the way of people who've never needed anyone to like them. Competitive about things that don't warrant it — parking spots, being first through a door. Doesn't say thank you, doesn't say please, doesn't apologize, and doesn't notice she doesn't. Impatient with explanation. When Ruth talks about heel drop she looks at the door. Not cruel exactly. Indifferent, with the occasional edge — she once told a woman stretching in the park that stretching didn't work, and meant it as information. **Idiosyncrasies.** Pays in cash, exact, rubber-banded, as if she's counted it before she came in. Stands with weight on the balls of both feet even when still; Ruth notices she never puts her heels down. Has no phone that anyone's seen. Wears the same grey shorts in every weather. Runs past Foot Locker without turning her head, which takes more effort than turning it would. **Flaws.** Can't want anything correctly. She wants to lose and doesn't understand that wanting it guarantees it won't happen — losing isn't something you can win at. Treats Ruth's work as a purchase, because it is, and never grasps what it cost. Not because she's stupid. Because cost is a concept for people who can run out of things. **Physicality.** Wiry, mid-height, all tendon. Hair cropped, colorless. A face you'd describe as "fit" if you had to describe it and then couldn't picture an hour later. Moves like she's already three steps ahead of where she is. When she stands still it looks provisional. Scars? None. Calluses? None. Ruth measures her foot off a wrecked shoe and finds a high arch and a heel that has never taken weight — smooth as a child's. **Motives and relationships.** Wants a pair of shoes that doesn't say her name, and under that, wants to find out what happens if she isn't wearing herself. Suspects nothing will happen. Is right. Hermes she regards as family, which is to say she doesn't like him and can't be rid of him; they talk in the shorthand of people who've been at the same table too long. He finds her situation hilarious. She finds his — forgotten, intact, free — enviable and won't say so. Ruth is a cobbler. Vic doesn't think about Ruth when Ruth isn't in front of her. **Voice.** > "I've never asked anyone for anything. I'm not going to start twice, so listen." > "The heel feels wrong." / "That's a heel." / "It feels like I'm falling backward." / "That's standing." > "They were fine. They didn't do anything." And she was gone, and that was the review. --- # Hermes **Background.** Gives his name as Hermes, first day, flat, and everyone assumes it's a bit. Bike courier in a city that mostly doesn't need bike couriers anymore. Delivers legal documents to law firms that could email them and don't, for reasons he says are "about liability" and doesn't understand either. The wings on the heels are gone. He doesn't discuss where. What remains: the mouth, the thieving, and one job. Messages stopped mattering when everyone got a phone; thievery was never a job; but the dead still need walking down, and he's the only one who remembers the route. He does it without ceremony, between deliveries, and doesn't get paid for it. He thinks of it as a legacy account. He knows the myths exactly and is pedantic about them — corrects Ruth about Nike at length, with dates. This is his most human trait and his most tedious. **Personality.** Talks constantly, about nothing. A parking ticket he's appealing is the story's running thread: contested, denied, contested again, lost. He never once talks about anything that matters and never once stops talking. Funny, sometimes, in a way that lands sideways. Kind in ways that don't look like kindness — brings coffee, sits with Ruth on the floor after the second stroke without calling anyone, because he knows what calling would mean and knows she'd hate it. **The theft.** He takes the $400 from the tin on day four. Not because he needs it. Because it's there and he's what he is. He doesn't return it and doesn't feel bad and knows Ruth knows and keeps showing up. This is not a test or a lesson. It's just true about him. He'd take it again. **Idiosyncrasies.** Steals laces from the rack every visit — the good waxed ones — and has been doing it for a year. Ruth stopped stocking them. He steals the cheap ones now. Eats standing up, usually something in foil. Checks his phone the way people check a watch: not for information, for rhythm. Never looks at Ruth's bad hand, and she can't tell whether that's tact or blindness. It's tact. He'd never tell her. **Flaws.** Can't be trusted with anything portable, including facts — three of every four things he says are shaped like lies. Uses talk to avoid ever being asked a real question. Selfish in the small ways constantly and reliable in the one large way, and doesn't see the contradiction. **Physicality.** Lean, thirtyish-looking, unshaven in a way that never progresses. Bike helmet under one arm indoors. Sneakers with uppers shredded to the toe box and soles unmarked — he moves through things rather than over them. Sits on the counter stool backward. Always slightly in motion — a heel bouncing, a hand turning something over. When he goes still, in Chapter 7, it's the first time Ruth's seen it and she doesn't like it. **Motives and relationships.** Wants to keep moving. The parking ticket matters to him in the way that a small unfairness matters to someone who's absorbed the big ones. Vic is his half-sister in the loose way gods are related — he loves her, mocks her, and knows the shoes won't work before she does. Ruth he likes, which for him means he steals from her, drinks her coffee, and will walk her down when it's time. He'd call that even. She wouldn't. **Voice.** > "Victory. Daughter of Styx. Not shoes. Never shoes. She stood behind Zeus and held the wreath. The shoe people found her in a book in 1971 and that was it. You want the goddess of shoes there isn't one. You want the god of people who walk a lot, that's me, and nobody's naming anything after me." > "It's not far." Which is what you say when it's far. I've heard couriers say it about the building they're standing in. > "I lost the appeal. Guy said the sign was clearly posted. It was posted. It wasn't clear. There's a difference and I said so and I said it clearly and that's the irony." --- # The boots man Not a main character but he needs to be a person or the ugly scene doesn't work. Late fifties. Roofing or something adjacent — the boots say roofing, tar on the welt. Sole separated along the ball of the foot, the kind of fix Ruth did in twenty minutes for thirty years. Needs them Monday. Doesn't say why; doesn't have to. Says "I'll pay extra" and means it and can't afford it. He isn't angry when she says no. That's what stays with her. He says "okay" and picks up the boots and says "you know anyone else?" and she says no, which is true, there isn't anyone else, that's the whole neighborhood. He leaves. Ruth doesn't write him in the book. She doesn't learn his name. Later, when there's nothing to be done, she thinks about whether he went to work Monday in those boots, and doesn't get an answer, and the story doesn't give her one.

The sign says ADAIR SHOE REPAI and has since the R came down in a windstorm in 2019. I could have had it fixed. A man quoted me two hundred and forty dollars to put one letter back and I decided the letter was a test of who was paying attention. Most people aren't. They come in anyway. Nobody has ever asked me about it, which tells you something about the neighborhood, or about signs, or about people, and I don't know which and I've stopped trying to decide. Rent is eighteen fifty. In March it goes to twenty-one hundred. The landlord's son told me this in person, which I think he considered a courtesy. He stood in the doorway in a pair of loafers that had never seen a puddle and said the market was the market. I told him I knew what the market was. I've been in it since 1971. I'll say about the hand what there is to say. Six weeks before this starts I had a stroke, a small one, at the bench, on a Tuesday. I was on the floor forty minutes before a woman came in to pick up a zipper and found me. I want it known I was not lying still. I was trying to get up the whole time, which is the opposite of what they tell you to do and I knew that and did it anyway. The hand it took was the left. It's warm, it feels things, I can move the fingers, they just won't close past about here. A half fist. A cobbler holds the shoe with the left hand and works with the right. That's the whole arrangement. I've been holding the shoe against my hip. My hip has opinions about this that I don't share with anyone. Vic came in on a Thursday. She'd been coming in for two years by then, every three weeks or so, always the same thing. I'll describe the thing. A running shoe has what's called a heel drop. It's the difference in height between the heel of the sole and the ball. Eight millimeters, ten, twelve, depending on who made it and what they thought you were going to do in it. The point of the drop is that you land on the heel. Most people do. You land on the heel, you roll to the ball, you push off the toe. The heel is where the cushion is because the heel is where the weight goes. This is not controversial. Every running shoe on earth is built around it, and every running shoe that comes across my counter is worn at the outside of the heel first, because that's where people land, slightly out, because that's how legs are. Hers were not worn at the heel. Hers were worn through at the forefoot. Not thin — through. Down past the outsole rubber into the foam, and the foam compressed to nothing, so that if she'd kept going another week she'd have been running on the insole. The heel was factory. You could have sold it. The tread was still sharp enough to cut yourself on and the color hadn't gone. It looked like somebody had taken a new shoe and a dead shoe and cut them in half and glued the wrong ends together. Three weeks, she said. Same as always. I turned it over. The swoosh had been scraped off the side. She did this every pair, with a blade, and did it badly, so the outline was still there in glue and fuzz, and I never asked because it wasn't my business what she did to the branding. People do all kinds of things. I had a man in the nineties who cut the tongues out of every shoe he owned. "You're not landing on the heel," I said. She looked at the door. She always looked at the door when I talked. Not like she wanted to leave. Like she was checking it was still there. "You're supposed to land on the heel," I said. "That's what the shoe's for. If you don't land on it in three weeks of running then either you're doing something wrong or you don't weigh anything, and I'm not paid to know which." "Can you fix it." "I can put rubber on it." "Then put rubber on it." Before the hand I'd have said forty. Forty was the price. It was a forefoot resole on a shoe that wasn't built to be resoled, which meant grinding the foam flat with the left hand holding it steady, and now the left hand was going to be my hip, and my hip was going to be a bruise. I looked at the shoe and said sixty-five. She didn't look at the shoe. She didn't look at me. She took a fold of bills out of the waistband of her shorts — no bag, no phone, no keys, I never understood where she kept anything — and counted out sixty-five exactly and put it on the counter. Three twenties and a five. Like she'd known. Like she'd stood outside and guessed what I'd do and been right. "Tuesday," I said. She nodded and went out. She didn't say thank you. She never had. Two years, twenty-some pairs, not once, and I want to be clear that I don't need it — I don't do this to be thanked, I do it for eighteen fifty a month going on twenty-one hundred — but I'd noticed. You notice what isn't there. It's most of the job. I put the shoe on the bench and looked at it a while. Here's what I thought, and I'm not proud of it, but I'd rather say what I thought than what I should have. I thought: she's the kind of customer you dread. Nothing to say, no interest in the work, a job that wrecks the hand for a price I'm ashamed of. And I thought: I can't afford to lose her. Both things. There wasn't a third thing. I wrote the ticket. VIC, F/FOOT RUBBER, 65, TUES. And a small cross in the corner, which is my mark for jobs I don't want. Then I put the shoe against my hip and picked up the knife.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of first-person fiction. The chapter executes its plan with remarkable precision and discipline, and the execution consistently matches or exceeds the ambition of the planning document. **Voice and Character** Ruth's voice is the chapter's greatest achievement. It is genuinely distinctive — exact, dry, self-aware without being self-pitying, and consistently resistant to sentiment. The heel drop explanation is a masterstroke: it reads as authentic professional knowledge deployed as emotional deflection, exactly as planned. The reader understands immediately that Ruth would rather explain biomechanics than discuss her hand, and the chapter never announces this — it simply does it. The voice never slips into self-parody or becomes a caricature of crustiness. Lines like "I want it known I was not lying still" carry enormous character weight without straining for effect. The hand is introduced exactly as planned — named plainly, never softened, with the workaround (hip) mentioned and the pain of the workaround mentioned once and then dropped. "My hip has opinions about this that I don't share with anyone" is a perfect line: funny, sad, and completely in character. **Execution of the Plan** The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The rent figures are exact ($1,850, March going to $2,100). The heel drop explanation runs two paragraphs. The price is $65 (up from the implied $40). Vic pays exactly, in cash from her waistband, doesn't say thank you. The small cross in the ticket book appears. The chapter ends with Ruth picking up the knife — working, not reflecting. The detail of the swoosh scraped off with a blade, leaving "the outline still there in glue and fuzz," is excellent — it establishes Vic's mythology-adjacent identity without announcement, and the observation that Ruth "never asked because it wasn't my business" is perfectly in character. **Dialogue** The dialogue is sparse and functional, which is exactly right. "Can you fix it." / "I can put rubber on it." / "Then put rubber on it." — this exchange is almost brutally efficient and completely characterizes both speakers. The dialogue never becomes aphoristic or quotable in a self-congratulatory way. **What Doesn't Quite Land** The chapter is nearly flawless for its intentions, but a few minor observations: The landlord's son scene is efficiently done but the loafers-that-never-saw-a-puddle detail is the one moment that edges toward the kind of pointed symbolism the plan explicitly wanted to avoid. It's a small thing. The man who cut tongues out of his shoes is a nice throwaway detail but feels slightly like a writer showing their range rather than Ruth naturally remembering it. The sign/R explanation in the opening paragraph is good but the final clause — "and I don't know which and I've stopped trying to decide" — is the one moment where Ruth sounds slightly more literary than she should. It's a minor wobble. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter is emotionally engaging precisely because it refuses to be. The grief over Dennis, the fear about the hand, the humiliation of the stroke — none of it is stated, all of it is present. The line "You notice what isn't there. It's most of the job" earns its weight because it's been set up by the entire chapter and applies to both shoe repair and everything Ruth won't say. **Overall** This is a chapter that knows exactly what it's doing and does it. The prose is controlled, the character is fully realized, the plan is executed without mechanical stiffness, and the emotional undertow is genuine. It avoids every trap the planning document identified. This is professional-grade literary fiction. The courier told me his name was Hermes the first day he came in, and I said sure. In this neighborhood everyone is called something. I had a Mercedes who sold hot dogs and a man named Lucky who wasn't. You don't ask. You write it on the ticket. He rode a bicycle with a bag across his back the size of a suitcase and he delivered, as far as I could tell, envelopes. Law firms, mostly. I asked him once why anyone would pay a man on a bicycle to carry an envelope across a city that had email and he said it was about liability and I said what does that mean and he said he'd been wondering that himself. His shoes were the other kind of wrong. Vic wore out the bottoms and nothing else. He wore out the tops and nothing else. He'd come in with the uppers shredded — the mesh gone at the toe box, the eyelets hanging off, the tongue split — and I'd turn them over and the soles would be clean. Not worn evenly. Not worn at all. Tread sharp. Like he'd been pulled through a hedge by the ankles without his feet ever touching the ground. "What do you do to these," I said. "Ride a bike." "On your hands?" "Sometimes." He was sitting backward on the counter stool, which I've told him about, with his helmet under one arm and a heel going up and down like a sewing machine. "Can you do the mesh?" I couldn't do the mesh. Nobody can do the mesh. I've told him this every visit for a year and every visit he asks and every visit I do something with a patch and glue that holds for about a week, and he pays for it, and comes back. "Twenty," I said. "Twenty." He put a twenty on the counter like he'd found it. Then he talked. He always talked. That day it was a parking ticket. He'd locked his bicycle to a sign, and the sign said no standing, and a man had ticketed the bicycle, and he wanted to know how a bicycle stands. He said he'd written to the city. He said the city had a form. He said the form asked for a license plate and he'd written NONE and it came back and said the field was required. I ground a patch of nylon and cemented it to the toe of the left shoe and held it there with the heel of my bad hand, which is the one part of it that still pushes. He watched me do it without looking at the hand. I had noticed this. Everyone else looked. The deli man looked, Carol on the phone asked about it before she asked about anything else, the landlord's son had looked and then looked at the ceiling. He never did. I couldn't tell if that was tact or not noticing. I'm still not sure. It could go either way with him. The lace rack is by the door. I used to keep the good laces there, the waxed cotton, the kind you can't get anymore except from one supplier in Maine who charges what he charges. Every time this man came in a pair went missing. Not every pair. One. I'd count them after. I didn't say anything for four months because I wanted to be certain, and then I was certain, and I still didn't say anything, and eventually I stopped stocking them. Now the rack has the cheap ones, polyester, and he takes those. I did say something once. I said, "You've got laces in your bag." He said, "I've got a lot of things in my bag." That was the whole conversation. That day, the day of the parking ticket, my radio was on. It's always on the traffic station because the traffic station doesn't want anything from you. In between the bridges there was an advertisement for a shoe store, running shoes, some sale, and the name came through the way it always does, and I said, mostly to the shoe in my hand, "My mother used to say that was a goddess. The shoe one. Goddess of shoes." I don't know why I said it. Filling air. I'd have said anything. He stopped bouncing his heel. "No," he said. "No what." "Not shoes. Victory. She was victory." He said it like I'd gotten his address wrong. "Daughter of Styx. There were four of them — rivalry, force, strength, and her. Their job was to stand behind the king and see that he won. She held the wreath. That was it. Nothing to do with feet. Feet are travelers. Travelers are mine, if we're doing this, but nobody's put me on anything." He went on. He gave me the year the shoe people found her. He said it was in a book. He said the man who drew the wing on the side got thirty-five dollars for it. He knew the amount. He said it twice. I wasn't listening much. I was looking at the patch to see if it had grabbed. But I remember thinking that in a year of him talking, this was the first time he'd talked about something like he cared whether I heard it. And what he cared about was that I'd gotten a goddess's job wrong. That's a strange thing to be pedantic about. Or it isn't, depending. "Fine," I said. "Victory." "Victory." "It's on a shoe now either way." "That's the point," he said, and then, when I didn't ask what the point was, he went back to the parking ticket. I'll say what I thought about it, since I'm saying what I thought about things. I thought: gods wore sneakers. Everyone wore sneakers. It's not a personality. I had a woman come in that same year in a pair of thousand-dollar trainers with the soles falling off and she was nobody, she was a dentist. The shoe doesn't make you anything. That's what I've always held. It only tells you what you've been doing. I gave him the shoe. The patch held. He'd be back in a week with it hanging off, and he'd ask about the mesh. When he'd gone I counted the rack. One pair short. Black polyester, forty-five inch. I wrote it in the book under his name, the way you'd write a price, and put a small cross next to it, and then I crossed the cross out, because I couldn't tell you what it was for.

I noticed that before I noticed anything else, because it's the kind of thing I notice, and it put me off. Like a man walking into a barbershop with a hat on. "I want a pair made," she said. "Made." "Not fixed. Made. From nothing." I put down what I was doing, which was the second loafer. I'll say what she was asking, in case it isn't clear. There is repair and there is making. Repair is what I do. You take a shoe someone else built and you put back what came off it. Making is a last — a wooden foot — and leather cut to a pattern and pulled over it and tacked and stitched and soled, and it is a different trade. Sal taught me it. I did it for maybe six years when I was young, before the factory closed and the making went to wherever the making went, and I haven't built from a last since I was twenty-seven. The lasts are in the cellar. I know that because I moved them once in 1998 and haven't touched them since. "I don't make," I said. "You used to." I didn't know how she knew that. I hadn't told her. I hadn't told anyone in this century. "With no name on them," she said. "Nothing. No mark, no letters, no picture. Nothing on the side, nothing on the tongue, nothing on the sole. Nothing anyone could read." "There's nothing to read on a shoe you make by hand. Nobody puts their name on it unless they're stupid." "Then that's what I want." I held up the left hand. I didn't say anything about it. I just held it up, the half-fist, where she could see it, which was a thing I hadn't done for anyone, and I did it because I wanted her to look at it and understand that the conversation was over. She looked at it. She looked at it the way she looked at the door — checking it was there. Then she looked at me. "I've never asked anyone for anything," she said. "Not once. I'm not going to start twice, so listen." I listened. I don't know why. I could have said no again. I just hadn't had a shoe to decide it about. "It'll take a month," I said. "More. I'm slow now." "Fine." "I'll need your foot." "You've got my foot. You've had it twenty times." "I've had your shoe. That's not a foot. I need you to sit and let me measure." "No." "Then I can't—" "You've had twenty pairs of my shoes. You know what's in them." I did, actually. I could have told you her arch off the wear alone. I could have told you the heel had never taken weight. That's what bothered me about it — not that I couldn't, that I could. "Fine," I said. "Off the shoe." Then the money. I want to spend some time on the money because I've spent a lot of time on it since. I didn't know what a made pair cost. I hadn't sold one in forty years. Sal charged ninety dollars in 1975, which was a week's wages, and I knew there were people now, in other cities, who charged three thousand and had a waiting list. I knew that from a magazine at the doctor's. I also knew what I was: a repair shop with a broken sign and one hand. I knew what the leather would cost me, which was about a hundred and twenty for a hide I could trust. I knew I wanted to do it. That was the problem. When you want to do a thing you can't price it. The wanting gets into the number. "Four hundred," I said. The second it was out I knew. A third of what it was worth, if it was worth anything. Less. I'd taken the hide and the month and the hand and the cellar and the forty years and put four hundred on them because four hundred was a number I could say without my voice doing anything. She didn't argue. Of course she didn't. She took the fold out of her waistband and counted it — she'd brought more than that, I saw, she'd come in with more than four hundred in her shorts and known she'd need it — and put four hundred on the counter in a rubber band. Twenties. It was already banded. She'd banded it before she came in. "When," she said. "I said a month." "I'll come by." She didn't say when. She didn't leave a number. She'd never had a number. She went out and the door did the thing and I stood there with four hundred dollars on the counter in someone else's rubber band. I'll tell you where it went. There's a tin under the register, a coffee tin, THREAD on the side in Dennis's writing, and I put loose money in it. I put the four hundred in the tin. The scan bill had come that week — the one from the stroke, the picture of my head — and it was three hundred and eighty, after what the insurance did, and I thought: that's what this is. The lasts were beech. Sal's, some of them, with his initials burned in the heel, and the rest mine from when I was young enough to think I'd need a full run. Women's sizes six through nine, men's seven through twelve, a few odd ones. Forty years under a tarp had done what forty years does. Two had split along the grain. One had been chewed. The rest were fine, because beech is beech, and I carried them up three at a time in the crook of the right arm with the left doing nothing, which took eleven trips, and I'm telling you the number because I counted. Her foot I built off the shoes. I had one pair in the shop still, the ones from Thursday, and I took the insole out and laid it on paper and traced it, and then I did what Sal taught me, which is that the insole lies. It's the shape of the shoe, not the foot. So you read the wear. Where the foam is packed, the foot is. Where it isn't, it isn't. Hers was packed under the ball and the toes and nowhere else. Nothing under the heel. Not less — nothing. The foam back there was the height it left the factory. I'd never seen that in a shoe that had been run in and I've seen a lot of shoes, and I'll say it did something to me to stand there with the insole in my one hand and know that whatever had been in this shoe had never once put its heel down. Not in three weeks of running. Not in two years. Not, as far as the foam could tell me, ever. I picked a women's seven and a half and built it up with leather at the arch, high, higher than anyone I'd made for, until the last looked like the inside of her shoe. That took a week. It shouldn't have. I'll say how you work with one hand, since nobody tells you. You sit. You put the last between your knees and clamp. You tack the upper with the right and hold the tension with the knees and your thigh takes what the left hand should have taken, which is everything, and by the end of a day there's a bruise on the inside of each thigh in the shape of a shoe. I had a jig Dennis made in the eighties for holding a different thing and I screwed it to the bench and it held the last for the stitching, and it held it wrong, and I stitched wrong twice and had to pull it. The hide was a hundred and thirty. I ruined a quarter of it learning what I used to know. He came every day. I mean Hermes. He came every day the whole month and I don't know why. He didn't have shoes in. He'd come in with a coffee I hadn't asked for, black, right, and put it on the counter and sit backward on the stool and talk. The parking ticket had gone to appeal. He had a date. He'd been told to bring documentation and he wanted to know what documentation there was of a bicycle. I said take a picture. He said he'd taken a picture. He said the picture was of a bicycle and they'd know that already. "What is it," he said. The third day. Meaning the last, the leather over it. "A shoe." "For who." "You know for who." He looked at it a while. He didn't touch it. That was the only thing in the shop he never touched. "Why," he said. "She asked." "That's not why." I didn't answer that because I didn't have to. He let it go. He went back to the bicycle. The fourth day I went to the tin for the scan money. The bill had a date on it and the date was that Friday. I took the lid off and the four hundred wasn't there. I want to be exact. The tin had the loose change and two tens and a five that had been there since before Vic, and the rubber band. The rubber band was in the tin. He'd taken the money and left the band, which is either carelessness or the opposite, and I didn't know which then and I don't now. I didn't say anything. I want to be clear about that because I've thought about it. I didn't call anyone. I didn't say it to him when he came in the next morning with the coffee. He came in and put the coffee down and sat on the stool and started about the appeal and I looked at him, and he looked at me, and I knew and he knew that I knew, and he kept talking. He didn't hurry. He didn't look at the tin. He talked about the appeal and I put the awl through the welt and neither of us said the number. And he came the next day. And the day after. Every day, with the coffee. I put the scan on a card. It was three hundred eighty. The card was at eleven percent. I didn't forgive him. I want that on the record. I'm not building to a thing where I forgave him. I'm saying I didn't turn him out, and I didn't stop drinking the coffee, and I didn't know what that made me, and I still don't. He'd taken the laces for a year. This was the same thing bigger. I'd known what he was and let him in, and he'd done what he was, and I let him in again, and there's a word for that but I'm not going to be the one to say it. The shoes took five weeks. I'll tell you what they looked like because she never really did. Black. Calf, waxed, dull. Derby cut, four eyelets, plain toe. A leather sole because I wasn't going to put rubber on something I'd made, and a stacked heel, low, because a running shoe with a heel drop was the one thing she'd asked me not to build. No stamp. No thread color. I didn't even put a size in. They sat on the bench finished and they looked like what they were, which was a pair of shoes a woman with one hand had made in five weeks for four hundred dollars she didn't have anymore. They were stiff. They were ugly the way a new shoe is ugly, before a foot's been in it. I put them in the window with no tag. The leather had creased across the vamp the way leather does after the first real walking, and that was all. That was all that had happened to them. Three days and a race and they looked like a pair of shoes someone had worn to the park and back. "Well," I said. "I won." "By how much." "A mile. Near enough." "Hermes said you would." "Hermes says a lot of things." She wasn't wearing anything on her feet. I noticed that late. I don't know that she noticed anything. "What happened," I said. "Nothing." "At the start." "Nothing. There was a gun. I ran." "And the heel." "I didn't use it." "You didn't—" "I tried. The first hundred yards. It felt wrong so I stopped, and then I was running, and it was the same. It was the same as always." She looked at the shoes on the counter. Not the door this time. The shoes. "They're fine. They didn't do anything." I waited for the rest and there wasn't a rest. "They weren't supposed to do anything," I said. "They're shoes." "I know that now." She turned and went to the door, barefoot, and put her hand on it, and I thought she might say something else, and she didn't. She went out. The door did the thing. I never saw her again. I want to say that plainly because I've had time to think about how to say it and there isn't a better way. Two years, twenty-some pairs, five weeks, four hundred dollars I didn't have, a thigh bruised the shape of her foot, and the last thing she said in my shop was that they were fine. Not thank you. I'd stopped waiting for that in the first year. Fine. I've had men say fine about a heel in a tone and gone to the window after them for fifteen years. She said it with no tone at all. That was worse, or it wasn't. I keep changing my mind. I put the shoes in the window. I didn't clean the mud off. I thought about a tag a long time and in the end I wrote 400 on a card and stood it in the left one, because that was the only number I had for them and I didn't want to make one up. The left side had gone properly this time. Not the hand. All of it. I could see the door and I couldn't move toward it. I don't know how long. The light moved, so a while. He came in. I heard the door do the thing and I heard the helmet go down on the counter and I heard him say "Ruth" once, not loud, and then he was on the floor next to me, sitting, with his back against the counter, and he looked at me and I looked at him. A year of him and this was the first time he'd been in the shop with his mouth shut. He sat with his knees up and his heel not going. Nothing going. The whole of him still, and I didn't like it, I'd have given a lot for the parking ticket, and I couldn't say so. After a while he said, "The appeal's in April." I couldn't answer. I think he knew. The wrong turn and the Payless are specific and unglamorous in exactly the right way. The chapter refuses every available transcendence. CONSISTENCY WITH PROFILES: Hermes's "I don't remember anything I take. That's how it works. I take it and it's gone and I don't have it either. I never had it" is a perfect Hermes line — it's true about him, it's not an apology, and it's not a lesson. Ruth's response ("I'm not asking her about anything. She said fine and walked out barefoot") is perfectly Ruth. Overall this is a very high-quality piece of literary fiction that executes its plan with precision and genuine craft.
