# Day 9 The TV was on when I got up and it was on when I went to bed and I don't think Dad turned it off in between. Namibia first. A beach outside Walvis Bay, sardines, a line of them along the sand exactly like Cormorant, the same overlapping ripple, the same gulls, except the gulls were different gulls and the people had different shovels. Then Chile. Then a stretch of Hokkaido where they'd brought in earth-movers and the man on the TV said *unprecedented* in Japanese and then the translator said it. There were structures off every one of those coasts. Namibia had two. Chile had five, in a line. There was a graphic with a globe and red dots on it, and all the dots were in water, and the man with the graphic said that like it meant something and didn't say what. Then the UN. Then a general with a lot of ribbons who wouldn't say the word *weapon* and wouldn't say the word *not*. Then a man in Florida standing in surf up to his knees firing a rifle at a thing eleven kilometres out, and the reporter treating it as a human-interest story. "See," Dad said, from the chair. "See. That's American." "He's shooting at it, Dad." "I'm just saying." His cousin Wade in Halifax texted at noon: *navy going to fire on one tomorrow, heard from a guy at Shearwater, don't tell anyone.* Dad told everyone. He read it out loud at the Irving to three people and the girl behind the counter, and by two o'clock it was around the whole cove that the navy was going to fire on one tomorrow, and by four Wade had texted again saying *maybe not tomorrow* and Dad didn't read that one out. The smell was total by then. I've tried to describe it to people who weren't here and I can't. It's not a fish smell. Fish is a clean smell, a cold one. This was under everything — in the car, in the closets, in the bread. The town had stopped noticing it and started noticing when it changed. Behind the ballfield, past the sign Gerry sponsors, they'd brought in two bulldozers from Bridgewater and dug a pit the size of a hockey rink and were pushing herring into it with the blades, and the sound of that, the wet give of it, is the other thing I can't describe. The gulls were dying too. Not many yet. But you'd see one on a roof, sitting wrong, and the next morning it'd be in the gutter. The federal team arrived at the fire hall at eleven in a white truck and a van and a refrigerated trailer, and the woman running it came to the station at one and knocked, which nobody does. "Priya Raman," she said. "DFO. You're Dr. Dorey." "Nell." "Okay." She was tall, close-cropped, in field pants that had been wet more than once, with reading glasses pushed up into her hair that she'd clearly forgotten were there. She looked at the whiteboard — THINGS I DON'T KNOW, fourteen items now — for a second longer than she needed to and didn't comment. "We're collecting from every die-off site on the shore," she said. "I'd like your samples. Everything from day five on, chain of custody, we'll take it to St. Andrews." "Sure," I said. I gave her the herring and the mackerel from the beach — the whole bodies, the ones I'd already been through, gutted and useless. I kept the heads. I didn't tell her I'd kept the heads. I had eleven of them in the walk-in in a crisper drawer and I don't fully know why I held them back except that she'd knocked, and she was polite, and she had a refrigerated trailer, and I had a crisper drawer. She looked at the bags. "These have been on ice? Not fixed?" "Ice." "Since the fifth." "Yes." "I hear you. But — okay. So the soft tissue's four days autolysed. The livers will be gone. That's not going to give anyone a finding, Nell, that's just decomposition." I should have fixed them. I knew that when I didn't do it. I had formalin. I had gutted sixteen fish under a bad lamp and looked at their livers and written *liver* and moved on, and I hadn't fixed a single one because I'd been tired and because it was, I'd thought, one night, and I'd do it properly in the morning. "I had a hundred and eighty fish and one pair of hands," I said, which was true and not the point. "Sure," she said. She hadn't learned yet what mine meant. "What are you seeing?" "Nothing. Gills clean. Guts full. No lesions." "Same as everywhere." She wrote something on the back of her hand. "Okay. Thank you. I'll be at the hall." I watched her carry my useless fish to her truck and I was angry at her, and I knew it was the wrong direction, and it didn't help. Dad came home at six from driving to Yarmouth. He'd been gone since seven. Gerry had asked him the night before — "young fella, I need a driver" — and Dad had said yes the way he says yes to Gerry, which is before the sentence is finished. He came in smelling of diesel instead of fish, which was a change, and sat down heavily in the chair, groaning, like it was a joke. "Good run?" "Fine." "What was it." "Herring. Mackerel. Some haddock." "From where." He turned the TV up. I knew. I'd known when Gerry asked him. Gerry had a walk-in full of stock frozen the week before the structures came, and he had a loan against the plant, and thirty-one people, and a town where nobody was going to buy a fish off a beach. And there were restaurants in Yarmouth, and past Yarmouth, Boston, where the fish came in boxes with a date on them and nobody asked which date. I could have said something. I said, "You want supper?" He said, "I could eat." At the station, the pollock was hanging in its tank, alive, indifferent, and it hadn't eaten in four days because I only had flake. It would need pellets. The nearest pellets were in Bridgewater, an hour each way, and I sat in the car in the dark outside the plant and thought about whether one fish was worth two hours, and then I drove.

# Day 14 I did twenty-two heads before I thought to open an ear. I want to be honest about that number because it's embarrassing and because it's the truth of how the work actually goes. You don't have an insight. You have a crisper drawer and a bad lamp and a Wednesday, and you do the thing you know how to do, and you do it again, and somewhere around the twentieth time you notice you've been doing the wrong thing. The heads were from the fifth, on ice, then in the walk-in at two degrees, and Priya was right that the soft tissue was going. But heads keep better than bodies — bone, cartilage, the stuff in the skull is protected — and I'd told myself that was why I kept them. I set up at nine with the scalpel, the fine forceps, the dissecting scope Sadie had cracked the stage on in April, and a squeeze bottle of formalin for what I wanted to hold onto, which by then I'd learned to want. Herring head, three-year fish. Skin off the operculum. Lift the gill arches: pink, clean, I'd seen it sixteen times. Open the buccal cavity: fine. Cut down through the cranium along the midline, which on a herring is like cutting a walnut shell with a butter knife, and lift out the brain, which is the size of a lentil and looked like a brain. Nothing. Formalin. Next. By head eight my hand was cramping. The lamp is on a gooseneck and the gooseneck doesn't hold, so every ten minutes I was pushing it back up and it was coming down again like something tired. The plant smelled of formalin over the smell of everything else, which was almost a relief, the way a burn is a relief from an itch. Head twelve I did a mackerel, for variety. Same. Around fifteen I stopped and ate cheese and crackers standing at the window and looked at the three of them out past the shelf and said, out loud, "What did you do," and then felt like an idiot and went back. Head twenty-two, I don't know why. I'd taken the brain out and was sitting there with the empty cranium under the scope, and behind where the brain had been, on either side, there are two small chambers — the inner ear, the labyrinth — and in a healthy fish they hold the otoliths, which are three little stones of calcium carbonate that I had spent six years of my life sectioning and reading like tree rings. I know otoliths. I've handled thousands. You lift them out with fine forceps and they're smooth and white and heavy for their size, and they *click*, a tiny click, when you set them in a dish. I went in with the forceps and came out with grit. I sat back. I looked at the grit in the forceps, and I looked at the head, and I went in again, on the other side, and it was the same. Not one broken stone. Powder. Fragments. Like someone had taken a hammer to a shell. I did head twenty-three in about four minutes. Same. Twenty-four, mackerel: same, and the mackerel's sagittae are bigger and I could see the fracture lines under the scope, radial, from the centre out. I went to the walk-in and got a whole herring I'd been saving, one of the last, and opened it not for the guts this time but for the swim bladder, which sits above them like a long silver balloon, and which in every fish I'd done I'd noted as *intact* and moved past. It was intact. It was also, when I held it to the lamp, full of blood. Haemorrhaged from the inside, the whole lining, so that it looked less like a bladder than a bruise. Then the lateral line. It runs down each flank, a canal under the skin with pores, and it's how a fish hears water — pressure, movement, the shape of the thing coming. I cut along it and lifted the skin and the canal was torn. Not cut. Torn, along its length, the way a seam goes when you pull the fabric too hard. I said, "Lateral line," out loud, in an empty fish plant, to nobody, and then I heard myself and felt stupid, and then I sat down on the floor. Not poison. Not heat. Nothing in the gills. Nothing in the guts. Every organ that hears — every structure built to take pressure from water and turn it into information — burst. From the inside. From something in the water so loud that the ears of animals designed to listen to it had come apart. They'd died of hearing something. I sat on the floor for a while and then I got up and wrote it on the whiteboard under THINGS I DON'T KNOW and then crossed it out and wrote it again on the other side. Except. The livers. I had a note from day five that said *liver* and nothing else, and I'd let Priya tell me it was autolysis, and it might have been. But I'd had one fresh liver out that morning and it was pale — not the dark red-brown of a herring liver but a putty colour, and it had come apart on the forceps like wet bread. Pressure doesn't do that. Sound doesn't do that. I sat with it for twenty minutes and I could not make it fit, and in the end I wrote *livers — friable, pale — ???* under the crossed-out line and left it there, where it still is. Then I got the hydrophone. It's from 2006. It works about a third of the time. I ran it out the window on its cable into the cove off the wharf and sat with the meter and my headphones and got what I'd got on day one, which was nothing. Not quiet — nothing. No shrimp. No wave noise against the pilings. A flat line, for four minutes. Then a single pulse, so low I felt it in my chest before I heard it, and the meter went to the top of its range and stayed there for two seconds and came down. I didn't call Dad. I called the fire hall. Priya picked up. I told her. There was a pause. "We got that Tuesday," she said. "Off the shelf. Same signature. I was told not to release it." "You —" "I'm telling you now. Which is also not releasing it. So." I hung up on her. I'd like to say it was about the pulse. It was about *Tuesday*. At the tank, the pollock had turned in the water, nose to the window, and was holding there, facing out, and I told myself fish don't do that, and I turned the light off.

The line "You don't have an insight. You have a crisper drawer and a bad lamp and a Wednesday" is genuinely excellent: specific, funny, true, and entirely in character. The procedural detail is handled with real skill. The descriptions of otolith extraction, the lateral line anatomy, the swim bladder hemorrhage — these are accurate enough to feel authoritative without becoming a textbook. The moment of discovery is earned: "I went in with the forceps and came out with grit." That sentence lands because of everything that preceded it. The escalation from grit to fractured sagittae to hemorrhaged swim bladder to torn lateral line canal is well-paced and builds genuine dread. The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The plan specified: twenty-two heads before opening an ear, the otolith discovery, the swim bladder hemorrhage, the lateral line, the "lateral line" spoken aloud moment, the liver anomaly that doesn't fit, the hydrophone pulse, and the call to Priya. All of these are present and executed with care. The plan's note that "the livers are wrong too — pale, friable — and that doesn't fit pressure, and she can't make it fit, and she writes it down and moves on" is honored precisely, and this unresolved detail is one of the chapter's strongest elements — it resists the tidy revelation. The metaphors are restrained and consistently land. "Like cutting a walnut shell with a butter knife" is apt. "The lamp is on a gooseneck and the gooseneck doesn't hold, so every ten minutes I was pushing it back up and it was coming down again like something tired" — the personification of the lamp as tired is subtle and effective, not overwrought. "Like a long silver balloon" for the swim bladder is precise. "The way a seam goes when you pull the fabric too hard" for the torn lateral line canal is exactly right. None of these feel forced. The emotional beats are well-calibrated. Nell sitting on the floor after the discovery is earned. The whiteboard moment — writing it under THINGS I DON'T KNOW, crossing it out, writing it on the other side — is a perfect character detail that was established in the profile and pays off here. The ending with the pollock facing the window is quietly ominous without being overwrought, and Nell's self-correction ("I told myself fish don't do that") is characteristic of her voice. The dialogue is minimal but excellent. Priya's two lines are perfectly in character: "We got that Tuesday. Off the shelf. Same signature. I was told not to release it." And then: "I'm telling you now. Which is also not releasing it. So." This is exactly the Priya from the character profile — following rules she thinks are stupid while acknowledging the absurdity. Nell's response — hanging up, and the admission that it was about "Tuesday" not the pulse — is a small, sharp character moment. The chapter's one potential weakness is that it is almost entirely interior and procedural, with very little external action. But this is by design, and the plan explicitly called for it. The question is whether the chapter earns its length, and I think it does — the procedural accumulation creates genuine tension, and the discoveries feel like real discoveries rather than planted revelations. The ending with the pollock is the only moment that edges toward the slightly too-neat — the fish facing the window as Nell turns off the light has a symbolic weight that the rest of the chapter deliberately avoids. But it's restrained enough not to tip into sentimentality. Overall, this is a chapter that demonstrates genuine craft: a distinctive voice, accurate scientific detail used for emotional effect, consistent characterization, and a structure that earns its length. It avoids the pitfalls the plan warned against — no aphorism, no wonder-as-ear-bleed, no symmetry payoffs. The unresolved liver mystery is a particularly strong choice. "The left one's leaning," to the girl behind the counter, while she waited for her coffee, and the girl said, "Is it," and I was behind her with a bag of pellets from Bridgewater and I went out to the pumps and looked. It was. Barely. You had to line it up against something — I used the flagpole on the fire hall — but the left one, the smallest, which had stood dead plumb for nineteen days, was off. Two degrees, maybe. Less. The way a fence post goes after one winter. Nobody at the fire hall would say anything. Priya wasn't there; one of her people, a young man with a clipboard, said the assets were "under continuous observation" and that any change would be "communicated through appropriate channels," and I said, "It's leaning," and he said, "I hear you," and I realized where he'd got that. The Wentzells were packing a trailer when I got home. Tanya had it backed up to the door and Kayden was carrying out a TV and Dex was sitting on the step with a plastic bin of Lego in his lap, not moving. I said hello. Tanya said they were going to her sister's in Truro for a bit. Kayden said nothing and didn't look at me. By evening the TV was back in the house and the trailer was still there, hitched, and it stayed hitched, loaded and unloaded, for the next seven days, like a question nobody wanted to answer out loud. Dad said at supper that he was going out to them things in the morning. There was a Coast Guard notice — a two-kilometre exclusion zone around each one, posted at the wharf, on the radio, everywhere. He knew about it. He said so. He said the Coast Guard could come and stop him if they wanted and he'd like to see them try with one helicopter, and he said it with his mouth full, and I knew from the set of him that this wasn't a thing he'd decided that day. "I'll come," I said. "You don't have to." "I know I don't." I went because I was afraid he'd go alone. I want to be clear that I wasn't curious. I'd been curious on day one. By day twenty I was tired and I had a whiteboard full of things I didn't know and I did not want to be any closer to the source of them. But he can't swim and won't wear a jacket and *Merle* is thirty years old, and there was nobody else. We left at six in a flat calm. No helicopter. The sounder was still "broke" — the column empty from the wharf to the shelf, not one mark — and he'd stopped mentioning it. We ran for forty minutes without talking, past where the Coast Guard notice said we couldn't be, and the thing got bigger the way a mountain does, which is to say it didn't seem to, and then it did all at once, and then it was the only thing there was. He cut the engine at maybe fifty metres. It was July. It was eighteen degrees on the water when we left. Our breath showed. I watched Dad exhale and saw it, white, going away from him toward the thing, and I looked at my own hands and they were red with cold. There was frost — actual frost — on the rail on the side facing it. The surface wasn't slate up close. It wasn't any colour I could hold onto. It was the colour of the inside of your eyes when you press them shut. No seam, no join, no texture I could find with my eyes at fifty metres, and it went up and I didn't look up because looking up made the boat feel small in a way I couldn't afford. The water at the base was the worst part. It was thick. Not weed — bodies. Herring, mackerel, things I'd never seen alive, a seal, a lot of gulls, packed to the hull of the thing like a raft, and none of it was moving. Not rocking. Not drifting. The swell we'd come in on stopped somewhere behind us, and the water around the base was as still as the water in my tank, and it was full of dead things, and it did not smell, and that was the part I couldn't make sense of. Everything else on the shore had stunk for two weeks. This didn't. Dad drifted us in. "Dad." "I just want to see." He got the gaff off the rack. He leaned out over the rail, over the raft of dead things, and he reached, and I said his name again, and he put the hook of the gaff against the side of it and pulled. Nothing. No sound. Not the sound of metal on — whatever it was. Not the sound of the gaff itself, which I'd heard rap on the gunwale a thousand times. He hit it again, harder, and it made no sound, and he stood there with the gaff against it and said, "See," like he'd proved something, and I have still not worked out what. We came home. He started the engine, and the engine sounded like an engine, and by the time we were a kilometre out our breath was invisible again and my hands were pink. We argued the whole way in about Gerry's truck. I don't know who started it. I said something about Yarmouth and he said Gerry was paying Tanya Wentzell out of that and I said that wasn't the point and he said what was the point then, Nellie, and I couldn't say it, I couldn't say *you know what's in the truck*, because he did know, and saying it wouldn't have made him not know, it would only have made me the one who'd said it. So we argued about the route instead. Whether he should take the 103 or the shore road. For forty minutes. That night the tank heater failed. I don't know why. It was a cheap one and the plant's wiring is old and it was twenty-one days into the end of the world. In the morning the pollock was on its side on the gravel and the water was fourteen degrees. I lifted it out and looked at it for a while and then I put it in a bag and put it in the walk-in with the heads, because I didn't know what else to do with it, and it's still there.

# Day 24–25 Brayden Hiltz bet him twenty dollars, and Kayden Wentzell went off the government wharf at four in the afternoon in his hoodie with his phone in a Ziploc bag. I wasn't there. I got it from Dot, and then from Brayden's video, which was on everyone's phone by five. You can see him on the edge, skinny, talking fast — "no, literally, I'm going, I'm going, film it" — and then he's in, and the water closes over him without a splash, the way it had been doing for three weeks, like it was thick. Then nothing for eleven seconds. Brayden counts them out loud. Then Kayden comes up. He comes up screaming. Not hurt-screaming. Not the sound a kid makes when the water's cold. He comes up with his mouth already open and the sound already going, and he gets to the ladder and he's saying it before he's out, "It talked, it talked, it — no, listen, it *talked*," and Brayden is laughing and then stops laughing, and the video ends because Tanya Wentzell has arrived from across the road and slapped her son across the face hard enough that the phone hears it. I watched it four times. He came to the station at seven. I don't know if his mother knew. He stood in the door in a dry hoodie with his hair still wet and his hands going in the pockets, and he said, "Doctor Dorey," with the smirk, and then the smirk didn't hold. "It wasn't a sound," he said. "It was in my teeth. It was — okay, you know when there's a truck going by and you feel it in the window? Like that but it had — it had *shape*. It stopped and started. It was like it was waiting for me to say something." "Kayden." "I'm not lying." "I didn't say you were." "You're thinking it." I was. I want to be honest. He lies about everything small — where he was, whose drone that was, whether he's eaten — and he sounds exactly the same when he's lying as when he isn't, so I'd stopped being able to hear the difference. I said I'd think about it. He said, "Right," and left, and I didn't think about anything else for the next fourteen hours. Priya's divers went down at nine, off the same wharf, with a boat and a line and a real hydrophone. Two of them. They were under fifty-one seconds. The first one came up and got his mask off and sat on the swim step with his head between his knees and said *pressure*, and the second one said *nausea*, and then they both said nothing, and Priya stood on the wharf writing on her hand and didn't look at me. I didn't sleep. Dad's old drysuit was in the shed under the lobster traps. He'd bought it in 1998 to work on *Merle*'s hull and worn it twice. It was made for a man with a chest like a barrel and it fit me the way a tent fits a pole. I got into it at five in the morning in the dark with the station light on and a roll of duct tape for the wrists, and I want to say I did this because I'm a scientist and there was a phenomenon. I did it because a sixteen-year-old had gone in with a Ziploc bag and I hadn't. The water off the station wharf was full of bodies. I'd known that. I'd looked at it for three weeks. Going into it is different. They were at the surface and under the surface, drifting, soft, and I went down the ladder into them and they moved aside the way clothes move in a washer, and something brushed my faceplate, and I made myself not look at what. Two metres down I heard it. Kayden was right that it wasn't a sound. My tinnitus — I've had it for years, from a dive in Passamaquoddy — is a sound. This wasn't. It was the pulse from the hydrophone but from the inside, in the bone behind my ears, in my jaw, in the fillings, and it wasn't one pulse. It was one and then a gap and then a different one, lower, and then a gap, and the gaps were the thing. The gaps were exact. They were the length of a breath. They were the length of a *reply*. Every time one stopped I felt the space where I was supposed to put something, and I didn't have anything, and it started again. I'd like to describe it as awe. It was closer to being in a room with someone standing too near you in the dark. I think I was down forty seconds. I don't know. At some point my body decided it wasn't doing this anymore and started kicking without me, and the suit was full of air in the wrong places and I couldn't get my head up, and the bodies were everywhere, and I breathed water. I remember thinking, very clearly, *Dad can't swim*, and then hands. Not his. One of Priya's — the one who'd said *nausea* — had come down the wharf at dawn to check the line and seen a drysuit that fit nobody go off the ladder, and he went in after me in his shorts. He got me to the ladder and Priya got me up it and I lay on the planks and threw up seawater and something came out of my right ear that wasn't seawater. It was blood. I'll say this once because I know how it sounds and I don't want it to sound like that. My eardrum burst. It's an injury. It happens to divers. It hurt, it bled, Priya packed it, it took three weeks to heal and I still can't hear a phone ring on that side. It was not a sign. It was not the price. It was a woman in a suit that didn't fit going down too fast into water she shouldn't have been in, and I want that on the record because everything else about that morning I can't put on any record at all. Kayden was on the wharf. I don't know how long he'd been there. He was standing back by the shed with his hood up and his hands in his pockets and he waited until Priya had finished with my ear and then he came over and looked down at me. "Told you," he said. "Yeah," I said. He nodded, once, and went home across the road, and the trailer was still hitched in the driveway, and it was six-fifteen in the morning, and it was talking.

# Day 27 By the twenty-seventh it had words, and Priya put them through a speaker in the fire hall so the whole town could hear. She didn't want to. She said so, flatly, to me and to nobody else, standing in the hall doorway with her travel mug: "This is going to go badly and I've been told to do it anyway, so." Then she went in and set it up. A hydrophone off the government wharf on two hundred metres of cable, a laptop, a PA borrowed from the Legion. Fifty or sixty people on folding chairs. Gerry in the front row with his jacket on. Dad beside him. Me at the back with my ear packed and the whole right side of my head sounding like a shell. It started with the pulse. People shifted. Then the pulse thinned, and rose, and became a voice. I'd like to say it sounded like nothing on earth. It sounded like the marine VHF. Exactly. The cadence of it — the flat, clipped, over-and-out rhythm every fisherman on the shore has heard every day of his life — and under that, threaded through it, something else. A sing-song. Rising at the ends. A tune I half knew and couldn't place until Dot Hiltz's sister said, out loud, "That's *Theodore*," and it was. *Theodore Tugboat*. The kids' show. Somebody's boat had had a radio picking up a Halifax station for ten years and the thing in the water had learned English from Channel 16 and a cartoon about a harbour. "*Harrow Cove, Harrow Cove,*" it said, in the VHF voice, and half the room flinched, because that's how you call a boat. "*Are you the wet.*" Nobody moved. "*Are you the wet. Are you the wet. The loud is quiet now. Good. The loud is quiet, good, good.*" I understood it before anyone. The loud. The things that made noise in the water. The things with ears and swim bladders and lateral lines that rang like bells when it spoke. The loud was the fish. The loud was quiet now, and that was *good*. It said it the way the tugboat said things. Kindly. Pleased. Gerry laughed first. It came out of him like something he'd been holding — one bark, and then he couldn't stop, and he put his hand over his face and his shoulders went, and he said, "The *wet*. Christ almighty. The *wet*," and then the room went. Not everyone. Dot didn't. Tanya Wentzell didn't, sitting with Dex asleep on her. But enough. Dad laughed. I heard him. The big laugh, the one from the wharf. Brayden Hiltz filmed it. I've thought about that laughing more than about anything else this month. It wasn't cruel. I don't think it was even really funny. It was fifty people who had shovelled a town's worth of dead animals into a pit and lost a plant and a season and a way of living, hearing the thing that did it ask, in a cartoon voice, whether they were the ocean. If it was funny it wasn't what it was. So it had to be funny. "*Are you the wet,*" it said again, into the laughing, patient. Priya took me down to the wharf after. She had a second rig — a speaker, waterproofed, on a line — and she said if I wanted to answer it, this was how, and she said it without looking at me, and I understood it was the closest she'd come to an apology for Tuesday. I got down on my knees on the planks with the microphone and I talked into the water. I said we were not the wet. I said the loud were not the wet either. I said the loud were fish, and I said the word *fish* slowly, and then I said it again, and I tried to explain what a fish was to something that had lived in oceans and had never once noticed one, and I heard myself — *small, with scales, they swim* — and I sounded like Sadie describing the job to her boyfriend. It answered. Not to that. "*Harrow Cove. The cold part. Are you the cold part.*" "I don't know what that means." "*The cold part is small. The cold part is quiet. Good. Are you the wet.*" "No. I'm — there are people. On the land. The land is separate from the water. We —" "*The loud is quiet now. Good.*" Round and round. It wasn't ignoring me. That's what took me a while to understand, kneeling there with my knees going numb. It wasn't refusing to answer. It was answering. It was answering the questions it had, in the order it had them, and mine didn't land anywhere it had a place for. I was saying *fish* into a thing that had a category for water and a category for noise and was trying, patiently, to work out which one I was. I waited for it to say it was sorry. I want to be honest about that. I knelt there for forty minutes with my ear packed and I waited for the word, because that's what I'd have said, and that's what a story would have it say, and every gap it left I thought *here*, *now*, and it said *good*. It wasn't going to. It didn't have the thing that says sorry. It had never done anything wrong, in whatever sense it had of wrong. It had come to say hello to an ocean and the ocean had been full of small loud things and now it wasn't, and that was better, and it was pleased. My wanting it to be sorry was the childish part. I knew that, kneeling there. It didn't help. Dad came down when I'd stopped. He stood over me and listened for a bit to the speaker still going — *are you the wet, Harrow Cove, are you the wet* — and he said, "Sounds like my old Icom. The one before this one. Sounds exactly like it. I'm just saying." He was right. It did. In the morning the Wentzells' trailer was gone from across the road. So was Tanya's car. Dex's bin of Lego was gone from the step. Kayden wasn't. He was sitting on the step where the bin had been, in his hoodie, with his phone in his hand, not on, and when I came out to the car he didn't look up, and I didn't go over, and I've been asking myself since what kind of person doesn't go over.

# Day 30 A month. Priya had it on a schedule by then — a dive at eight, off the government wharf, twenty minutes, two divers, hydrophone and speaker down on the line. Ottawa wanted daily. I was on the schedule because I'd been down and come back and because, Priya said, it seemed to aim at me, and I said I didn't want to, and she said she knew, and she said she'd go with me, and I resented that and was grateful for it and didn't say either. She was a better diver than I'll ever be. I watched her check my suit — a proper one now, hers, borrowed, that fit — and check her own without looking at it, and she put her hand flat on the wharf plank before we went in and said, "I'm scared of it. So you know." "Okay," I said, and it was the first time I'd said it her way. The bodies had thinned. Not gone. Something was taking them now — something was eating again, out there, or the current had come back, or both — and the water going down was water and not a washer full of clothes. I went down the ladder with my ear still packed and taped and Priya beside me, and at two metres I felt it in my jaw. It knew we were there. I can't defend that sentence. It turned. Whatever it was doing in the water — the pulse, the shape, the VHF sing-song coming up the line to the surface where the laptop was taking it down — it turned toward the two of us the way you feel someone in a dark room turn toward a sound you made. "*Harrow Cove. The cold part.*" Priya's hand on my arm. She heard it too, then. I'd wondered. "*The loud is quiet. Good. The wet is quiet. Good.*" A gap. The gap the length of a breath. "*Say it again. Bigger.*" It hadn't asked that before. "*Say it again bigger. Yes. Harrow Cove. Say it again bigger. Yes.*" I understood it the way I'd understood *the loud* in the fire hall — before I could have explained it, and with the same drop in my stomach. It had said hello. The hello had gone through a whole ocean and burst the ears of everything that could hear it, and the ocean hadn't answered, because the ocean was water and water doesn't. So: louder. Say it again, bigger, and this time the wet would hear. I had no way to say no. That's the truth of it. I had a microphone on a line and a vocabulary made of Channel 16 and *Theodore Tugboat*, and it did not have *no*. It had *good* and *quiet* and *yes*. I had no right to say it for anyone — for the shore, for Chile and Namibia and Hokkaido and the red dots on the globe — and there was nobody down there but a half-deaf fish scientist who'd been wrong about her own data and a federal employee who'd sat on a pulse for six days. I said it anyway. I said, "No," into the water, and I said, "Quiet," because that was a word it had, and I said, "Quiet is good, don't say it bigger, quiet," and I heard how I sounded and I kept going. The gap. "*Good,*" it said. Pleased. Kind. The way it said everything. "*Quiet. Good. Harrow Cove. Good.*" I don't know what that meant. I don't know if it heard me or if it heard the wet finally answer or if *good* is just the sound it makes. Priya squeezed my arm once and pointed up and we went. Dad wasn't on the wharf. I'd known he wouldn't be. Gerry had a run to Yarmouth and Dad had said yes before the sentence finished, and he'd left at six with the reefer full of whatever's left in a walk-in twenty-nine days after the last fresh fish came in, and I'd stood in the kitchen and said, "Drive safe," and he'd said, "I'm just saying," to nothing, out of habit, and gone. I got out of the suit on the wharf and Priya took the hydrophone to the hall to send the file to people who'd tell her not to release it, and I stood there wet in the July sun and looked at the three of them past the shelf. The left one was still leaning. Two degrees. The same two degrees. Nothing else had changed and nothing else was going to and I understood, standing there, that I would be looking at them for the rest of my life and that was just the view now. Kayden was on the Wentzells' step. Same hoodie. A duffel bag beside him this time, packed, the zip open. Not vibrating. That was the thing. His leg wasn't going. His thumbs weren't going. He was sitting on the concrete step of an empty house with his hands in his lap like someone waiting for a bus that doesn't come through here, and he'd been there, I think, since I'd seen him from the car three mornings ago, in the way that mattered. I went over. "Truro?" I said. "She called. She's coming back for me Sunday." He said it like he'd been saying it all week. He sounded exactly the same as when he lies and exactly the same as when he doesn't. "You want a ride somewhere?" "Where." "I don't know. Somewhere." He got in. I drove. I took the shore road, not the 103, and I don't know why that mattered and it did. We went past the ballfield where the pit was covered now and Gerry's sign was still up, and past the plant with the doors chained, and past Cormorant, where the beach was sand again and the gulls had come back, a few of them, and were standing on it not eating anything. He said, "So what'd it say." I kept driving. "Down there. Today. What'd it actually say." I thought about *say it again bigger*. I thought about *good*. I thought about a sixteen-year-old on a step with a duffel bag whose mother was coming Sunday. "It said it was sorry," I said. He looked at me for a while. Then he looked out the window at the three of them, standing where they'd stood, and I couldn't tell if he believed me, and I've been asking myself since whether that was a kindness or just the easiest thing I had.

The chapter opens with a clean, declarative sentence — "A month." — that earns its brevity. The prose throughout maintains the voice established in the character profiles: Nell is sharp, self-aware, defensive, and honest about facts while dishonest about herself. The line "I resented that and was grateful for it and didn't say either" is exactly right for her character, and it's shown through action and admission rather than explained. The dive sequence is the chapter's centerpiece, and it handles the alien communication with admirable restraint. The voice's grammar — "Say it again. Bigger." — is genuinely unsettling because it's so plausible: something that learned English from marine VHF and a children's show would sound exactly like this. The interpretation Nell offers ("It had said hello. The hello had gone through a whole ocean and burst the ears of everything that could hear it") is earned by the preceding chapters' groundwork and doesn't feel like a cheat. Crucially, the chapter doesn't resolve whether Nell's "no" worked — "I don't know what that meant" — which is the correct choice. The Priya moment — "I'm scared of it. So you know." / "Okay," I said, and it was the first time I'd said it her way." — is a small, perfect beat. It does character work, relationship work, and tonal work simultaneously without announcing itself. The Ambrose absence is handled well. He's not there because he's driving Gerry's truck, and Nell says "Drive safe" and he says "I'm just saying" to nothing — this is exactly the kind of specific, slightly absurd detail that makes the story feel lived-in rather than constructed. The Kayden scene is where the chapter stakes its claim. "He was sitting on the concrete step of an empty house with his hands in his lap like someone waiting for a bus that doesn't come through here" — this is the chapter's best sentence, and it earns its slight poeticism because it's grounded in the physical and the specific. The observation that he's not vibrating, that his leg isn't going, is the right way to show that something has broken in him. The lie at the end — "It said it was sorry" — is the chapter's moral center, and the plan called for it explicitly. The execution is clean: Nell thinks through what she knows ("say it again bigger," "good"), thinks about the boy on the step, and chooses the lie. The final sentence — "I've been asking myself since whether that was a kindness or just the easiest thing I had" — is Nell being honest about her dishonesty, which is her defining characteristic. It doesn't resolve into wisdom or condemnation. It just sits there. The shore road detail ("I took the shore road, not the 103, and I don't know why that mattered and it did") is a small risk that pays off — it's the kind of thing people actually do and actually feel, and it resists explanation. Weaknesses: The paragraph about having "no right to say it for anyone — for the shore, for Chile and Namibia and Hokkaido and the red dots on the globe" edges toward the expository. It's the chapter's most tell-heavy moment, where Nell explains the stakes rather than letting them be felt. The "half-deaf fish scientist who'd been wrong about her own data" is also slightly on-the-nose self-description, though it's in character for Nell to think this way. The structures being described as "the left one was still leaning. Two degrees. The same two degrees." is good — the repetition of the plan's detail lands. The dialogue is sparse and functional throughout. "Where." / "I don't know. Somewhere." is exactly right — it doesn't over-explain the gesture of the ride. Kayden's "She called. She's coming back for me Sunday" sounds exactly like someone who's been rehearsing a lie until it sounds like truth. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the dive happens, the "say it again bigger" question is asked, Nell says no in inadequate language, the voice says "good" ambiguously, Ambrose is absent, Kayden is on the step with the duffel bag, the lie is told. The plan's note that "she doesn't know if he believes her" is preserved in the final line. The prose avoids the pitfalls the plan warned against: no standing in water listening, no symmetry payoff, no apology-aliens (the "good" is kind but not apologetic), no ear-bleed-as-wonder. The ending is genuinely uncomfortable rather than elegiac. This is a chapter that trusts its reader, trusts its character, and doesn't flinch from its own implications. It's not perfect — the expository paragraph about Chile and Namibia is the weakest moment — but it's very good. # Brainstorming **The prompt's core hook:** Three blood-drop emojis, no words, just after midnight. The ambiguity is the whole engine. Who sends this? Why? The comedy and darkness both live in the gap between what the recipient *assumes* and what it *actually* means. **Possible meanings of 🩸🩸🩸 (cast wide):** - A period emergency — a friend needs tampons at midnight. The most mundane, most British, most YA-real reading. - A blood pact / oath among friends that's finally being called in. - Literal blood — someone's hurt, someone's done something. - A code from a group chat: "code red," previously agreed, now forgotten by everyone except the sender. - A vampire-obsessed younger sibling or mate doing a bit. - A wrong number that the recipient decides to respond to anyway. - A blood donation reminder gone rogue (the NHS Give Blood app sends emojis now?). - A boyfriend/girlfriend who "bled" for someone — metaphorical, melodramatic. - Nosebleed. Just a nosebleed. Sent by someone who wants attention. - A dare: three drops of blood = the three of us, one of us has to do the thing tonight. **Protagonist options:** 1. **Priya**, 16, insomniac, chronically overthinking, lives in a Midlands town where nothing happens. Gets the text from Mo, her best mate since Year 7, who is *not* a texter. Panics. 2. **Fin**, 17, in his last summer before Sixth Form results, working at a big Tesco. Gets the text from his ex, Saskia, who he blocked and then unblocked in a moment of weakness. Deeply unreliable narrator about his own feelings. 3. **Dee (Deirdre, never say it)**, 15, youngest of four in a chaotic Glaswegian-Irish family in Coventry. Gets it from her older brother's group chat by mistake — she's been added to "THE PACT" by accident. 4. **Rosh**, 16, hospital-adjacent — mum's a nurse, so blood is boring to her — gets the text from a boy she's been talking to for three weeks and has never met in person. The emojis are meant to be hearts. He's picked the wrong red thing. Or has he? 5. **Twins**, one narrating — the text comes from the other twin, who is *supposed* to be asleep in the next room. **Tone landmarks (darkly comic British YA):** Think *The End of the F\*\*\*ing World*, *Derry Girls*, Holly Bourne's edge, Patrice Lawrence's grit, *Sex Education* dialogue rhythms. Dry, mordant, self-aware first-person narration. Real stakes underneath the jokes. Adults who are useless or absent in specific, believable ways. Setting details that are aggressively unglamorous: Greggs, a retail park, a bus that doesn't come, the smell of a leisure centre. **Plot skeleton A — "The Pact":** Four friends made a blood pact at 13 (pricked fingers with a compass, very unhygienic, one of them fainted). The pact: if any of them sends 🩸🩸🩸, the others drop everything and come, no questions. Three years later, they've drifted. Then at midnight, the text. The narrator has to (a) work out who sent it (it came from a group chat where two people have new numbers), (b) get out of the house, (c) find the others, (d) discover what's actually happened. Reveal: the sender's situation is both smaller and larger than expected — e.g., she's about to be moved by her dad to another city and wanted one last night; or she's done something she can't undo (shaved her head? set fire to something? confessed to a teacher?); or she's actually in danger and the comedy curdles. **Plot skeleton B — "Wrong Number":** The text is a wrong number. Narrator, insomniac and bored, replies "wrong number but are you ok?" A conversation unfolds over one night with a stranger who might be in trouble or might be winding them up. Structure: eight chapters = eight hours to dawn. Twist: the stranger is closer than they think (someone from school, a neighbour, the narrator's own estranged sibling). Risk: too much texting, not enough action. **Plot skeleton C — "Nosebleed / Period / Anticlimax":** The whole story is the narrator's escalating catastrophising over what turns out to be a request for tampons. Comic, but 8000 words of anticlimax is a hard sell — unless the tampon run becomes the adventure (breaking into a Boots? bribing a night-shift worker? a neighbour with a scary dog?) and along the way the *real* story is what the friends say to each other. **Plot skeleton D — "The Thing We Did":** The 🩸🩸🩸 is a threat. Three friends did something last summer — an accident, a prank that went wrong, a cover-up. Someone else knows. The emojis arrive on the anniversary. Darker, thrillery. Comedy comes from the friends' utter incompetence at being blackmailed. **Plot skeleton E — Hybrid:** Blood pact framing (A) with a mundane-then-not-mundane reveal. The sender, Jess, is on the roof of the disused leisure centre. She sent the text because she wanted them there. It looks like a suicide thing; it's actually that she's been told she has a chronic illness (something with blood — anaemia, leukaemia scare, a clotting disorder) and didn't know how to say it, so she said it in the only language they had. Comedy: they arrive with wildly wrong ideas (one brings a shovel, one brings a first aid kit, one brings a Bible he's never opened). Darkness: real fear. Ending: dawn, the four of them, nobody knowing what to say, someone makes a terrible joke, it lands. **Character ensemble sketch (for A or E):** - **Narrator: Tash**, 16, sardonic, secretly the softest of them, has been avoiding the group because she's got a new "cooler" friend circle and feels guilty about it. - **Jess**, the sender. Loud, chaotic, the one who instigated the pact. Hasn't been in school much lately (everyone assumed she was skiving). - **Kwame**, the anxious one, now doing a very serious Duke of Edinburgh and has a *plan* for everything except this. - **Bex/Rebecca**, who's changed her name to Rebecca and gone posh since her mum remarried, and is mortified to be climbing out a window at 12:40am. **Comic set-pieces to potentially use:** - Sneaking out past a parent asleep in front of *Homes Under the Hammer* repeats. - The only transport is a stolen (borrowed) mobility scooter / a Lime bike with 4% battery / a dad's Skoda that nobody can drive. - A fox. There's always a fox. - Misreading the emoji as an invitation to something else entirely. - A very earnest conversation held while hiding from a PCSO. - Group chat archaeology: scrolling up to find the original pact terms, written in 2019 in text speak. - An adult (night-shift petrol station worker) who becomes an unlikely oracle. **Structural options for 8 chapters:** - **Real-time countdown:** 12:04am → 6:30am, each chapter a segment of the night. - **Alternating past/present:** Odd chapters tonight, even chapters flashback to the pact and the drift. Risk: slows momentum. - **Rotating POV** across the four friends. Risk: hard to build voice in 1000 words each. - **Single POV, linear, with embedded texts/screenshots** as texture. **Title ideas:** *Three Drops*, *Pact*, *No Questions*, *Code Red (Not That Kind)*, *Blood, Just After Midnight*. **Endings:** - Bittersweet dawn: the truth is out, nothing is solved, but they're back. - Comic sting: after everything, someone realises the text was sent by Jess's little brother playing with her phone. (Undercuts the emotion — probably not.) - Ambiguous: Jess is fine tonight. Tonight is all they've got. The last line is another text, months later: 🩸🩸🩸 — and Tash is already putting her shoes on. # Reflection The wrong-number idea (B) is charming but risks being eight chapters of screen-reading; the intimacy is real but the *Britishness* and the *comedy* would have to come almost entirely through voice, with no physical set-pieces. It's a good short-short but a weak 8000-worder. The blackmail thriller (D) has propulsion but leans away from YA's emotional register into genre; "darkly comic" could tip into just "dark," and I'd worry the comedy feels bolted on rather than arising from character. The pure anticlimax (C) is the funniest single idea and the most honest about what a midnight 🩸🩸🩸 usually means, but 8000 words of build-up to tampons needs a second, hidden story underneath it or it deflates. Actually — there's something in *using* the tampon reading as the first wrong guess in a longer chain of wrong guesses. That preserves the joke without hanging the whole story on it. The blood pact (A/E hybrid) does the most work. It gives the emojis a *meaning the characters agreed on*, so the text isn't ambiguous to them — it's a summons — which converts ambiguity into urgency and gets people out of the house fast (crucial for pacing). It creates a built-in ensemble with built-in history and built-in drift, so every reunion beat is doing double duty. It's very YA: the sacredness of a stupid thing you did at 13. And the childish literalness of "blood" as the code gives the reveal — that the actual problem is *literally* about blood — a satisfying click without being a twist that cheapens what came before. The illness reveal is the risk. It could be maudlin. It works only if Jess is not a saint — if she's a bit of a nightmare for summoning them like this, and they're allowed to be annoyed at her while also being terrified. The comedy shouldn't stop at the reveal; it should get *sharper*, because that's how these kids actually cope. The alternative reveal (she's being moved away) is lower-stakes and gentler; the "she did something she can't undo" reveal is funnier but flimsier. Illness earns the darkness in "darkly comic" if handled with a light, unsentimental hand, and it justifies why she couldn't just *say it in words*. Single POV is the right call for voice and word budget. Tash-as-narrator works because her guilt about drifting gives her a private arc that runs alongside the group's public one — she's the one who nearly didn't come. Linear, real-time structure with the pact backstory delivered in fragments (a scrolled-up group chat, a memory triggered by a place) rather than a full flashback chapter keeps momentum. Pacing across eight ~1000-word chapters roughly wants: (1) text + panic + who-sent-this + getting out; (2) collecting the first friend, comic transport; (3) collecting the second, friction, the drift made explicit; (4) the search — wrong location, wrong theory (the tampon guess, the boyfriend guess); (5) finding Jess, misreading the scene, peak dread; (6) the reveal, the shift in register; (7) the long night talk, jokes as armour, Tash's confession; (8) dawn, cold, unresolved but rejoined, the last-line echo. The midpoint (end of 4 into 5) needs the hardest tonal turn; chapters 6–7 need to resist the urge to explain feelings and let the dialogue carry it. The set-pieces that earn their place are the ones that also reveal character: Kwame's over-prepared rucksack says he's been waiting to be needed; Rebecca climbing out a sash window in a silk pyjama set says she hasn't changed as much as she pretends. The fox and the petrol-station oracle are texture — keep one, not both. Adults should be present only as obstacles or as one brief unexpected kindness. The ambiguous-loop ending (another 🩸🩸🩸 months later, shoes already going on) is the strongest closer: it reframes the emojis from omen to promise, and it lets the story end on motion rather than resolution, which suits both the genre and the age group.

Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Plot:** The blood pact story. Four friends — Tash (narrator), Jess, Kwame, Rebecca-formerly-Bex — made a pact at 13: send 🩸🩸🩸 and the others come, no questions. Three years on, drifted. The text arrives at 12:04am from Jess. Tash nearly doesn't go. She goes. The night is a search that gets the theory wrong repeatedly (tampons, a boy, a stunt, self-harm) before finding Jess on the roof of the derelict leisure centre, where the truth is that Jess has been told she has a blood cancer scare — tests pending, results Monday — and the pact was the only language she had for asking them to be there. Nothing is fixed. They get through to dawn. Months later: another text, and Tash's shoes are already going on. **Voice:** First person, present tense, Tash. Dry, quick, self-lacerating, fond underneath. Short paragraphs. Jokes that arrive a beat after the fear. She notices brands, smells, the specific squalor of a Midlands town at 1am. She lies to the reader about her own motives and gets caught out by other characters. **Tone:** Darkly comic first, moving. The comedy never stops after the reveal — it changes function, from deflection to care. No adult explains anything. No epiphany speeches; feeling is carried by what people do with their hands and what they choose to joke about. The word "cancer" gets said exactly once, by Jess, badly. **Style choices:** Embedded texts sparingly — the original 2019 pact message scrolled up in Chapter 1 is the key artefact. Real-time structure, one night, chapter headings as timestamps. Setting: fictional town of Kettlewood, retail park, canal, the closed Kettlewood Leisure Centre. One fox. One petrol-station night worker as the single adult with a line that matters. **Aim for:** Momentum from the first page; each friend collected reveals who they've become; Tash's private guilt (the new friend group, the ignored messages) surfacing sideways rather than declared; a reveal that lands as a *click* not a twist; an ending on motion. **Avoid:** Maudlin illness beats, saintly Jess, a chapter of flashback, an adult saving anyone, the "it was the little brother" undercut, resolving the medical question either way. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — 00:04.** Tash, awake, scrolling, the text from Jess in the dead group chat "BLOOD SISTERS (+kwame)". Immediate dread, then bargaining: it's a joke, it's a mis-send, it's 2019. She scrolls up to the original pact message (misspelt, all caps, "NO QUESTIONS NO EXCUSES NO PARENTS"). Confesses to the reader she's left Jess on read four times since Easter because Holly and the Sixth Form lot don't rate her. Kwame replies "On my way" instantly. Rebecca replies "Is this real". Tash puts her shoes on while telling herself she isn't going. Sneaks past Mum asleep under a *Homes Under the Hammer* repeat. **Chapter 2 — 00:31.** Kwame's house. He's at the gate in a full DofE rucksack — head torch, foil blanket, a trowel, Kendal Mint Cake. Comic inventory; also the sting that he's clearly been waiting years to be summoned. Transport problem: no buses, Tash's bike has one pedal. They "borrow" his nan's mobility scooter, tandem, 8mph. Kwame's theories, all catastrophic. Tash's, deliberately mundane: "It's tampons, Kwame." The fox watches them pass. **Chapter 3 — 00:58.** Rebecca's new house on the posh estate. She descends from a sash window in silk pyjamas and a school blazer, furious, hissing about her stepdad's Ring doorbell. Friction: Rebecca on Tash's new friends ("Holly Marsh thinks Jess is 'a lot'. You *agreed*"). The drift made explicit in a three-way argument on a mobility scooter. Where is Jess? Not answering. Rebecca knows Jess has been off school "weeks, actually" — Tash didn't know. First real crack. **Chapter 4 — 01:40.** Wrong locations. Jess's house: dark, her mum's car gone. The canal bridge where they used to sit: empty, a Greggs bag. Theories escalate — a boy, a stunt for TikTok, worse, unspoken. The 24hr Esso. Scooter battery dying. The night worker, Marek, sells them Lucozade and, unasked, says the kid in the Adidas jacket went past an hour ago "towards the old pool, with a bottle." He says: "Go and get her, then." Tash realises where. The chapter ends running. **Chapter 5 — 02:15.** Kettlewood Leisure Centre, closed since 2020, fence, the way in they always knew. Kwame's head torch on the drained pool: empty, echoing, smelling of chlorine ghosts. Voice from above. Jess on the flat roof, legs over the edge, bottle of Echo Falls. Peak dread — every wrong theory converges. Comedy sours: Kwame reaching for the foil blanket, Rebecca whispering to call someone, Tash saying "Don't" to everyone including herself. They climb up. Jess: "You took your time." **Chapter 6 — 02:40.** The roof. Jess is annoyed they've made it "a thing." Won't say it. Makes them guess; the guesses are all wrong and she mocks each. Then, flat: bruises she didn't get, nosebleeds, bloods at the GP, a referral, a consultant who used the word "haematology" and then a worse one. Results Monday. Mum's at A&E doing a shift, doesn't know Jess is out. Jess: "I sent it because it was funny. Blood. Get it." Nobody laughs. Then Kwame does, horribly, and it breaks the seal. Tash notices she's holding Jess's wrist and can't remember taking it. **Chapter 7 — 04:10.** The long stretch till light. They don't talk about Monday. They talk about everything else: the pact origin (Rebecca fainting, the compass, the tetanus panic), who Kwame fancies, Rebecca admitting the silk pyjamas are her mum's. Jokes get crueller and kinder. Jess corners Tash: "You left me on read." Tash's non-apology, then real one, badly done, in the dark. Jess: "I know Holly Marsh is fit, Tash, I'm not blind." Kendal Mint Cake passed round like communion. Rebecca's stepdad's Ring app pings — she's been rumbled. She turns her phone off. **Chapter 8 — 05:52.** Dawn over the retail park, grey then pink, deeply unbeautiful and they say so. Cold, hungover on nothing, four people under one foil blanket. Jess says she'll tell her mum today, maybe. They climb down. The mobility scooter is dead; they push it. At the Esso, Marek looks at them and pushes four sausage rolls across the counter and doesn't charge. Walk home. Nothing resolved. Cut to: October, 23:58, Tash in bed. The group chat lights up. 🩸🩸🩸. She's already got one shoe on before she reads who sent it.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human might approach this piece A human writer given "The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸" would probably not start with a beat sheet. They'd start with a memory: a specific friend who sent weird texts, a specific derelict building they broke into at fifteen, a specific night bus that never came. The piece would be built outward from two or three details they *know* are true — the sound a chain-link fence makes when you climb it, the taste of Echo Falls warm — and the plot would be found while writing, not before. A human would also probably not know what the emojis meant when they started. They'd let the ambiguity sit on the page longer than is comfortable, possibly all the way to the end. They might write a version where Jess never explains herself. They might write a version where it *was* tampons and the story is about how four people can be terrified for two hours and then have to pretend they weren't. A human writing darkly comic British YA would be drawing on having *been* that age in that place — which means the jokes would be the jokes actual sixteen-year-olds make (crueller, dumber, more repetitive, in-jokes the reader isn't let in on), and the boring parts would be boring in specific ways. They'd remember that most of a night out consists of standing about. They'd remember that friends at sixteen are frequently horrible to each other with no redemptive arc attached. Crucially: a human would be willing to let the piece be *smaller* than its premise. Eight thousand words is a lot of room to fill with meaningful incident; a human might fill some of it with nothing, on purpose, because nights like this are mostly nothing. # Telltale LLM approaches, and why they'd hurt this piece **Structural symmetry.** LLMs love the shape of things: setup–complication–reveal–resolution, one friend per chapter, the midpoint turn landing exactly at the midpoint. Real stories lurch. For this piece, over-symmetry makes the night feel authored rather than lived; the reader can feel the outline under the prose. **Every detail load-bearing.** In LLM prose, if a fox appears, it's *the* fox; if someone eats mint cake it's communion. Nothing is just there. Humans include details that mean nothing — the wrong bus number, a bin that's been knocked over — and the meaninglessness is what makes the world feel real. Darkly comic writing especially depends on the accidental and the irrelevant. **Emotional literacy.** LLM characters know what they feel and can articulate it in clean, quotable lines. Sixteen-year-olds mostly can't. They say the wrong thing, or nothing, or something aggressive that means "I love you." A Tash who "confesses" and a Jess who accepts is therapy, not fiction. **Wrapping with a bow.** The impulse to close every loop: the guilt gets apologised for, the adult is kind, the sausage rolls are free, the coda reframes the emoji as a promise. Each individually is fine; together they add up to a story that reassures. The prompt's genre is *darkly* comic. Reassurance is the enemy. **Performative restraint.** "The word cancer gets said exactly once, badly." This is restraint as a rule, announced. Real restraint is invisible; a writer either handles it lightly or doesn't. Rules like this tend to produce a self-conscious beat where the reader can feel the writer *not saying the word*. **Brand-listing as texture.** Greggs, Lucozade, Adidas, Esso, Tesco, Echo Falls, *Homes Under the Hammer* — this is Britishness as a shopping list. Humans use one or two of these because they're true, not six because they signal place. Also: *Homes Under the Hammer* isn't on at midnight. It's Channel 5 documentaries about lorries, or QVC, or the shopping channel with the rings. Wrong-but-plausible details are how you can tell. **The resonant final image.** "One shoe on before she reads who sent it." LLMs are drawn to the sting, the button, the line you can quote in a review. Human endings are often flatter, stranger, or stop a beat too early. **Tonal announcement without tonal risk.** Calling something darkly comic and then being careful not to actually be dark — no real cruelty, no real transgression, everyone fundamentally decent. The genre needs a moment where the reader thinks "that's too far" and the story doesn't apologise. **Sentence-level habits.** Triads. Fragments for emphasis. The wry one-line paragraph after a long one. "Somewhere, a fox." Similes stacked three deep. Present tense as a default for immediacy. These aren't wrong individually but as a default register they produce prose that sounds like every other dry-first-person-YA voice generated in the last few years. # Deep dive: where the intention and plan fall into these traps **The plan is a beat sheet.** Chapters 2 and 3 are "collect friend, reveal trait via costume/props." Chapter 4 is "wrong locations, oracle, run." Chapter 6 is "the reveal." Chapter 7 is "the talk." Chapter 8 is "dawn, coda." It's a screenplay structure, and screenplays are the most LLM-friendly form because they're already outline-shaped. It will read as competent and slightly airless. **The ensemble is a sitcom.** Anxious one, posh one, chaotic one, sardonic narrator. Each has a *costume* (rucksack, silk pyjamas, Adidas jacket) and a *bit*. The plan even says "each friend collected reveals who they've become," which is a line from a writing guide. Real friend groups have two people who don't really like each other and never have, and someone whose personality is mostly that they're there. **Marek is a magical helper.** The night-shift worker who has noticed the girl, knows where she went, delivers the gruff imperative ("Go and get her, then"), and later gives free food. He's a device wearing a hi-vis. He also displaces the kids' agency — they don't work out where Jess is, an adult tells them. And the free sausage rolls at the end are pure bow. **The mobility scooter is a sketch.** Tandem, 8mph, battery dies at the convenient moment, pushed home at dawn. It's funny in a plan. In prose it's a lot of words spent on a vehicle gag when the actual comedy of being sixteen at 1am is that you *walk*, for ages, and it's cold, and someone needs a wee. **Kwame's rucksack is an inventory joke.** Head torch, foil blanket, trowel, mint cake. This is the "comic list" beat and it's the single most recognisable LLM humour move. The mint cake then returns as "communion" — which is the second most recognisable move: the prop that comes back Meaning Something. **Rebecca's costume comedy.** Silk pyjamas plus school blazer is a visual gag that tells you the writer is thinking in pictures rather than in what a sixteen-year-old would actually grab. The "she's her mum's pyjamas" reveal is a small bow tied on a small joke. **Tash's arc is a moral loop.** She drifted, she feels guilty, she's called out, she apologises badly, she's implicitly forgiven ("I know Holly Marsh is fit, Tash, I'm not blind"). That last line is a *very* LLM line — the wounded party deflecting with generosity and wit. It absolves Tash. Real Jess might not. **The roof image is stock.** Legs over the edge, bottle in hand, "You took your time." It's every teen-drama rooftop. The misread-as-suicide beat, converging with "every wrong theory," is efficient but predictable, and the plan flags it as "peak dread" as if dread were a dial. **The reveal is too clean.** Bruises, nosebleeds, bloods, referral, haematology, results Monday. A neat clinical staircase, and "Monday" gives the story a tidy horizon it then decorously refuses to resolve. Real medical uncertainty is messier: a phone call that said "probably nothing but," a repeat test with no date, a mum who's downplaying it, a Google spiral. Also — nurse mum on an A&E shift while daughter panics about blood is an irony the plan is a bit pleased with. **"Jokes as armour."** The intention names this. Naming it means the writing will perform it. Every post-reveal joke will feel like it's been told to Do The Armour Thing. **The wrist.** "Tash notices she's holding Jess's wrist and can't remember taking it." Body-acts-before-mind is a stock emotional beat. Real teenagers on a cold roof are more likely to not touch, or to shove, or to put a hood up. **The dawn.** "Deeply unbeautiful and they say so." Undercutting the sunrise is now as clichéd as the sunrise. The plan is aware of the cliché and swaps in the meta-cliché. **The coda.** October, 23:58, 🩸🩸🩸, shoe on. This is a bow that thinks it's an open ending. It resolves the story's thesis (the emoji is now a promise) and rewards Tash's arc (she's a good friend now). It's the line an editor would love and a reader would forget. **Voice default.** "Dry, quick, self-lacerating, fond underneath. Short paragraphs." This describes *Fleabag*, *Derry Girls*, Holly Bourne, and roughly every AI-generated YA voice. It's not wrong for the piece; it's just that with no further specificity it'll land as pastiche. **Timestamp headings.** Device-y. Fine, but it's the kind of frame that makes the story feel like a product ("real-time thriller!") rather than a memory. # Brainstorm: making it more human **Break the collection structure.** - Rebecca doesn't come. She replies "Is this real," then nothing, then at 3am a single "sorry x". Three on the roof, not four. The absence is the drift, and it never gets addressed. - Or Rebecca comes but leaves at 2am because her stepdad's found out, and the story doesn't judge her for it. - Or Kwame is already there when Tash arrives — he lives closest, he didn't wait — so Tash's whole "I nearly didn't come" is undercut by the fact that nobody noticed she was late. **Kill or degrade the oracle.** - Marek is rude, or asleep, or a kid Tash's age doing a shift he shouldn't be, and he doesn't know anything. - They find Jess because Kwame checks Snap Maps, which is what actually happens, and there's a beat where they realise they could have done this at 12:05 and skipped two hours of driving round — and that the pact's "no questions" clause is why nobody did. That's a joke with teeth. - Or Jess's location has been *on* the whole time and Tash had muted her. **Replace the scooter with walking.** Or with something scarier and truer: one of them has a provisional licence and takes a parent's car, no supervising adult, and there's a stretch where it's genuinely dangerous and nobody's laughing. Darkly comic includes *actually dark*. **Make the props stupid, not useful.** Kwame's rucksack has his retainer, a half-eaten Boost, his brother's vape he's confiscated, and a copy of *Of Mice and Men* with his GCSE annotations. Nothing in it helps. The foil blanket, if it exists, is used wrong. **Let the wrong theories be uglier.** Not just "a boy, TikTok, worse." Tash thinks: attention. She thinks it and it's cruel and she's a bit right — Jess *does* want attention, because she's terrified, and wanting attention when you're terrified is fine. The story shouldn't punish Tash for thinking it or exonerate Jess for wanting it. **Move Jess off the roof edge.** She's lying on her back in the deep end of the drained pool, staring up, and they don't see her until they're standing over her. Or she's on the roof but in the middle, eating Wotsits, not remotely near the drop, and the dread was entirely theirs. The story about the friends' projection becomes clearer. **Muddy the medical.** "Probably nothing but they want to do it again." No Monday. A leaflet with a purple logo she's folded into a tiny square. Her mum's been "weird about it," which might mean it's bad or might mean her mum is bad at things. The friends' relief that it's "probably nothing" lands wrong — Jess sees it as them being glad they can go home — and there's a genuine flash of hatred. **Let Jess be a nightmare.** She summoned three people at midnight and won't say why for forty minutes and mocks every guess and is, for a stretch, actively horrible to Tash: "You only came because Kwame did." No wit, no generosity. Tash has nothing to say back. That silence stays unfilled. **Don't absolve Tash.** Cut "I know Holly Marsh is fit." Jess never says it's fine because it isn't. Tash apologises and Jess says "yeah" and that's the whole exchange. Months later they're friends again anyway because that's how it works, and the story doesn't explain how. **Let a joke die.** Kwame does a bit and nobody laughs and he does it again, worse. That's what happens. **Include the nothing.** Twenty minutes at a bus stop that says the next bus is in 320 minutes. Someone needs a wee behind Currys. A conversation about whether a specific teacher is divorced, in full, that goes nowhere and is the most alive scene in the piece. Phone at 6%, then 4%, then Tash puts it face-down so she can't see. **Two of them don't get on.** Kwame and Rebecca have unrelated beef from a party in Year 10 and it keeps surfacing sideways all night and is never resolved. It's got nothing to do with Jess. **Let an adult intrude wrongly.** Jess's mum rings at 3am. Jess answers on speaker by accident. Lies fluently while three people listen. Mum says "love you" and Jess says "yeah" and hangs up and nobody knows where to look. **Real register.** Midlands 2020s teenage speech, used accurately and sparingly. Swearing that's actually how they swear. Slang that'll date the piece — good, that's what human writing does. **Vary the prose rhythm.** One chapter that's nearly all dialogue, no narration. One long paragraph where Tash rambles for 400 words about something irrelevant because she's scared. Drop the one-line-zinger paragraphs as a default. Try past tense and see if it stops sounding like a monologue. **Real late-night TV.** Mum asleep in front of *Traffic Cops* or a *Come Dine With Me* marathon or the ring channel. **Alternative endings.** - End on the walk home, mid-sentence, before they split up. - End with Tash getting back into bed and her mum, awake, saying nothing about it, ever. - The coda exists but the text that arrives in October is not 🩸🩸🩸 — it's Jess sending a bad meme, unprompted, and Tash sends one back. That's the reconnection. No emoji reprise. - Or the coda is 🩸🩸🩸 and Tash looks at it and the story ends before she moves. - Or the last line is a fact: the leisure centre got demolished in the spring. Nothing about the friends. **Cut what the intention names.** "Jokes as armour," "pact as language," "omen to promise." If the plan can articulate the theme this cleanly, the writing will over-deliver it. Let the reader have that. **Ditch the timestamps.** Or use them wrong — one chapter's heading is just "later" because Tash's phone's died and she doesn't know.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt.
