# Four Carla brought a cake. She always does. It was in a tin on the passenger seat and she handed it to me before she'd said hello, the way you'd hand someone a baby so you could get your coat off. "Pão de ló," she said. "Mum's. Don't let it sit." Then she went past me into the hall and I heard Ines say "Carla," and I heard Carla say "Nêna," and there was the sound of the hug — Carla's hugs have a sound, one pat, hard, between the shoulders — and I stood in the porch with the tin and the cold coming in behind me and I thought: she'll see. Carla sees everything. She'll see in about four minutes. — She didn't. Or she saw something else. We had lunch, then a walk that Carla decided on and led, then wine at four because Carla said it was dark enough. Ines was easy the whole time. Laughed at Carla's stories, asked after Tomás at university, remembered the name of the woman at the council Carla can't stand. Didn't interrupt once. Didn't say *um*. Sat with her hands on her knees while Carla talked, and listened, and I watched Carla watch her, and I waited. In the kitchen, while Ines was upstairs, Carla dried a glass she'd already dried and said, "She looks well." "Yeah." "No, Daniel. She looks *well*. Better than — I don't know. Years." She put the glass down. "And you look like something the cat brought in and left." "I haven't been sleeping." "Why not." I'd rehearsed this. In the car, in the cellar in Corby, in the front room at five in the morning. I had a version that was calm and specific. And what came out was that she stands at the foot of the bed, and she doesn't blink, and her feet are cold, and I heard it as I said it, heard it land in Carla's kitchen-tidy silence like a man describing a dream at a bus stop. "Right," Carla said. Which is what she says. "I know how it —" "Right. So she's calmer. She's sleeping. She's playing the piano again. And you're the one who looks like death. Remind me who I should be worried about." She said it gently, which was worse. Then she said, "Did you ever talk to anyone? After. They said you should." "About what." She looked at me for a second too long, the way she does, and then Ines came down and asked who wanted more wine. — The roast was at seven. Ines made it. She'd never made a roast in her life that didn't involve at least one thing on fire and a joke about it, and this was fine, it was all fine, the potatoes were right, and Carla said so and Ines said "thank you" without doing anything to it. Carla was telling the dog story. There's a dog story in every family and this is theirs: the summer their dad left the side gate open and the dog got out and was gone two days and turned up in the church car park, sitting outside the door like it had come for mass. Carla tells it with the priest's voice. I've heard it maybe nine times. "And Dad's standing there in his slippers —" "With the lead," Ines said. "He'd brought the lead." "He'd brought the lead, in case, and Father Ryan says —" "Poor Rex," Ines said. Smiling. Into her wine. Carla stopped. It was a small stop. A quarter of a second. Her mouth stayed open for the next bit and the next bit didn't come, and I watched her face do a thing I'd never seen it do, which was go completely still, the way a face goes when the body has understood something before the head has. Then Carla said, "Bica," in an ordinary voice. "It was Bica." "Bica," Ines said. "God. Yes." She laughed. "Rex is the one in the photo." "Rex died before you were born." "I know. I don't know why I said that." Easy. Unbothered. She reached for the gravy. Carla looked at her for one more second and then at me, and I was already looking at her, and something went between us across the table that neither of us had a word for and wasn't going to find one. Then I heard myself say, "Anyone want more potatoes," and Carla said "Yes," and passed her plate, and told the rest of the story, and did the priest's voice, and it was fine. — She left Sunday morning. She was meant to stay till Monday. "Work thing," she said, in the hall, with her bag already on her shoulder. "Simon's dropped a grievance on my desk and I've got to — you know." Ines said of course. Ines hugged her, and Carla did the one pat, and then Carla turned to me. She held on. Longer than she does. Longer than the pat. Her arms round me and her face against my shoulder and I could feel her breathing, and she didn't say anything, and I didn't, and I understood — or I'll say I understood; I don't know what she'd say — that she'd seen it and she wasn't going to say so, and that this was as far as she could go, and that she was sorry. Then she let go and said "Right" and went out to the car, and drove off too fast, the way she does. — That night Ines didn't get up. I lay awake for it, for a while. I did the breathing. I listened for the mattress. Around one I stopped being able to and I went under, all the way, for the first time in — I'd have to count — and I dreamed I was standing at the foot of a bed. That's all. Just standing, in a low light, looking down at something I couldn't make out. It didn't feel like anything. When I woke the light was full and I was alone and the sheet beside me was warm, warm the way a chair is when someone's just got up, and I put my hand on it flat, and then I heard her downstairs, and I heard the kettle, and I heard Carla's cake tin being opened, and I lay there with my hand on the warm place and thought about how long a mattress holds heat, which I don't know, which isn't a thing I know. Monday there was a text. *Call me if you need to. C.* I read it in the car outside a house in Kettering. Then I put the phone face-down on the passenger seat and went in and did the survey.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of fiction writing. Let me work through it carefully. The chapter opens with a beautifully observed detail — Carla handing over the cake tin "the way you'd hand someone a baby so you could get your coat off" — which is the kind of simile that earns its place because it's precise, character-revealing (Carla's practicality, her way of managing situations), and slightly funny without straining for effect. It lands. The structure of the chapter is elegant: the arrival, the failed attempt to communicate with Carla in the kitchen, the roast, the dog-name moment, the departure, the night, the aftermath. Each section does work. Nothing is decorative. The kitchen scene where Daniel tries to tell Carla what he's seen is one of the chapter's finest moments. "I heard it as I said it, heard it land in Carla's kitchen-tidy silence like a man describing a dream at a bus stop" — this is exactly right. The simile works because it captures the social humiliation of the supernatural, the way horror becomes absurdity when spoken aloud in daylight. Carla's response — "Right. So she's calmer. She's sleeping. She's playing the piano again. And you're the one who looks like death" — is pitch-perfect dialogue. It's what a sensible person would say. It's also devastating because it's not wrong. The dog-name moment is handled with surgical restraint. "A quarter of a second. Her mouth stayed open for the next bit and the next bit didn't come" — the prose slows to register the exact duration of the wrongness. Carla's face going "completely still, the way a face goes when the body has understood something before the head has" is a genuinely good observation about how shock works. Then the recovery: Ines's "Easy. Unbothered. She reached for the gravy." The gravy is perfect. The mundane object doing the work of horror. The exchange across the table — "something went between us across the table that neither of us had a word for and wasn't going to find one" — and then Daniel immediately saying "Anyone want more potatoes" is one of the best moments in the chapter. It's the cowardice of ordinary life, the way people retreat into the social rather than face the unspeakable. It's also consistent with Daniel's character: he sees, he stores, he doesn't act. Carla's departure and the long hug is handled well. The prose here is careful not to over-explain: "I understood — or I'll say I understood; I don't know what she'd say" is a nice epistemic hedge that keeps Daniel's unreliability in view. The dream — standing at the foot of a bed, looking at something he can't make out — is quietly devastating. The story doesn't announce it. It just sits there. The ending with the warm sheet is excellent. Daniel's hand on the warm place, then his mind going to the technical question of how long a mattress holds heat — "which I don't know, which isn't a thing I know" — is exactly right for his character. He retreats into the measurable when the unmeasurable is too close. The repetition of "which I don't know" has the quality of someone trying to stop themselves from thinking something. The text from Carla and Daniel's non-response — reading it in the car, putting the phone face-down, going in to do the survey — closes the chapter on exactly the right note of ordinary avoidance. Weaknesses: There are almost none of significance. The section breaks (em-dashes) are used well to control pacing. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: Carla's arrival, the kitchen conversation, the roast, the dog-name error, Carla's early departure, the hug, Daniel sleeping, the dream, the warm sheet, the text. Every element from the plan is present and executed. The dialogue is consistently strong — Carla's voice in particular is exactly as described in the character profile. Ines's "Easy. Unbothered" moments are chilling precisely because they're not performed as chilling. One very minor note: "like something the cat brought in and left" is a slightly familiar phrase, though it's appropriate to Carla's voice and the slight staleness is arguably intentional. This is a negligible concern. The chapter is faithful to the writing prompt, the plan, and the character profiles. It achieves the stated aims: claustrophobia, a Daniel who is not simply good (his retreat into "anyone want more potatoes" is a small moral failure), the horror tangled with ordinary life. The wrongness is tasteful in the best sense — it's not tasteful-as-euphemism but tasteful-as-precise. # Five I did a thing on the Wednesday that I'm not proud of, and I'm putting it down because leaving it out would be a kind of lie, and I've decided I'm not doing that here. She was at the sink. I was at the table with the paper I don't read. She was talking — she talks more now, in the evenings, in these long even runs with no *ums* in them — about the woman two doors down whose fence I'd looked at once, and how the woman had stopped her in the street to ask after her, and how kind people were, and she said, "It was like that after the Hendersons' party, do you remember, on the tenth, everyone rang for a week —" "Twelfth," I said. She stopped. Hands in the water. "The Hendersons'. It was the twelfth. You said the tenth." I knew what I was doing. I'll say that. The Hendersons' is the party where she said the thing about me, to the table, laughing — *Daniel doesn't like people, he likes watching them* — and I laughed, and we drove home, and neither of us has said a word about it since, and I've never forgotten the date because I looked at it on the calendar afterwards, alone, as if the date could tell me something. She'd know it. Of all the dates in eleven years, she would know that one, because she'd lain awake on it too. I know she did. I heard her. So I said *twelfth* and I watched her face for the gap. I've done this to people before. Not often. At work, at dinners. You wait for someone to finish and then you put the small true thing down in front of them and you watch what happens to their face, the flicker, the recalculation, and it's not that I enjoy it. It's that it's mine. It's the one thing in a room I can be sure of. Her face did nothing. Not nothing the way a person's does when they're covering. Nothing the way a wall does. She looked at me, pleasant, and said, "Was it? The twelfth. God, my memory," and went back to the plates, and I sat there with the paper and I didn't know what I'd been hoping for. That she'd flinch. That she'd say *you know why I remember that one*. That she'd say *what are you doing*. I sat there for a while and then I said I'd take the recycling out, and I stood by the bins in the dark for longer than the bins needed. — That night I didn't do the breathing. I didn't pretend. I lay on my back with my eyes open and waited for it, and I thought about how many nights I'd spent on my back in this room listening for one thing or another, before and after, and how a marriage is mostly that, if you're honest, lying next to someone and listening. She got up a little after two. I heard the mattress this time because I was listening for it and not for my own breath. I heard her feet on the boards and I heard nothing else, no shifting, and then she was where she stands, and the light was behind her, and I let it go on for what I'd guess was a minute. Then I sat up and put the lamp on. I don't know what I thought would happen. That she'd startle. That she'd blink and put her hand up and say *what* in the voice you use when you've been caught at something. Instead the lamp came on and she was standing there in the yellow light, hands down, hair loose, T-shirt, bare legs, bare feet on the boards, and she looked at me exactly as she'd been looking at me in the dark. The light didn't change anything. That was the worst part of it, if I'm choosing. I'd thought the light would. "What are you doing," I said. "Looking at you." She said it the way you'd say *making tea*. Not a confession, not a challenge. An answer to a question. I sat there. The lamp hummed, it does, it's cheap. I could hear the boiler ticking down in the kitchen and a car on the main road and my own heart, which I don't usually hear. "Why." She didn't answer that. She went on looking, and the look was — I've tried to get this right and I can't, quite — it was interested. Not hungry. Not cold. Interested, the way you'd look at something you were learning, a face, a piece of music, the movement of a wall under load. "Ines," I said. "What do you want." And her face changed. It wasn't much. Her head came forward a degree, the way mine does when I'm listening, and something happened round her eyes that I can only call attention. Like I'd said a word she'd heard before and nearly knew. Like someone at the edge of a language, at the stage where you catch the shape of a sentence and none of the meaning, and you lean in, and you wait for the rest of it to make sense. She waited. I didn't say anything else. I didn't have anything else. And then it went. Whatever it was went out of her face like a cloud off a window, and she was Ines, or she was the thing that does Ines, and she smiled, tired, fond, a wife at two in the morning, and said, "You should sleep, Dan. You look terrible." She got back into bed. She turned on her side, away. Her feet found my leg. Cold. I left the lamp on. I sat with my back against the headboard and my knees up and I watched the shape of her under the duvet till the window went grey, and she didn't move, not once, and I didn't either. — It was the next day, the Thursday, that I noticed the shadows. I'd come home at three. I don't remember why. I'd finished a job and not gone on to the next one and driven back and let myself in and she was out, she'd left a note, *shop, back soon*, in handwriting that was hers, and I'd gone to the back window to see if Mo was on the wall. He was. Then the boy started. Four o'clock. *Thock. Thock.* The panel jumping a bit each time where the post's gone soft. And then I looked down at the lawn and the shadow of the fence was across it, all the way across, nearly to the step, and it had been nowhere near when I'd come to the window, and I stood there and worked out from the angle how long that was, and it was a long time, and I didn't remember any of it. Not one thought. I'd been standing at the glass with my hands at my sides looking out at a cat on a wall for the better part of an hour, and I hadn't noticed, and I hadn't shifted, and I couldn't have told you what I'd been looking at, only that I'd been looking.

# Six Friday I got the boards up. I'd been meaning to since September. I took the Friday off — rang in, said a personal day, which I've never said in nineteen years, and Marion on the desk said "Right you are" like it was nothing. Then I went up to the landing with the crowbar and the torch and the meter and I did the job I'd have done in someone else's house, and I did it well, and I'm going to put it down because it's the one thing from this week I'm sure of. The stain on the bathroom ceiling is fourteen inches at its widest, brown going to yellow at the edge, darker on the left. Darker on the left means the water's coming from the right. Above the bathroom on the right is the airing cupboard and above the airing cupboard is the loft hatch and the pipe run to the tank goes along the joist there, a twenty-two-mil copper rising main with a compression fitting where it meets the elbow. I've known this since September. I didn't need the boards up to know it. I got the boards up anyway. Three of them, tongue and groove, original, nails not screws, and the second one split along the grain when I levered it, and I looked at the split and thought it was a clean split, a good one, the wood had wanted to go that way. Under the boards the joist was wet along eight inches. Not soaked. Dark. When I put the meter to it the needle went to the top of the yellow and sat there. The compression nut on the elbow had a bead of water on its underside, one bead, and I watched it and it didn't fall, and after a while another one formed beside it and they joined and the joined one fell, and I counted, and the next one took a hundred and ten seconds to fall. So that's the rate. That's the whole leak. One drop every hundred and ten seconds since September, and a stain fourteen inches wide. I could have tightened it. I had the spanner. I sat on the landing with the spanner in my hand and the torch across my knees and I didn't, and I don't know why, except that it seemed important to know what it was first, all of it, before I changed anything. — I've had three nights now. I want to say that plainly. I lay down Wednesday and Thursday and I didn't sleep on either and Friday I didn't lie down. It doesn't feel like anything. That's what nobody tells you. I'd thought it would be like the films, shaking, seeing things, but it's not. Everything's very clear. Everything's a bit far off and very clear, the way a room looks through the wrong end of binoculars, and I can see the grain in the split board and the bead on the nut and I can count things, I can count very well, and I don't feel anything about any of it. The feeling is what goes. Not the seeing. Ted was on the wall when I went down for water. He looked at me through the glass. I looked back. Ginger, hunched. I said his name and he didn't move and I thought, he never did come when you called, and I went back up. — She found me on the landing. Around four. The boy had started. I heard her on the stairs and I knew from the stairs it was her, the real one — I don't know how I knew. The weight. She stops on the fourth step. She's always stopped on the fourth step because it creaks and she's spent eleven years thinking that if she pauses it won't, and it always does. It did. She stood at the top and looked at the boards up and the torch and me sitting there and she said, "Dan," in a voice with a wobble in the middle of it, and I knew. She went into the bathroom and sat on the edge of the bath, under the stain, with her hands between her knees. I followed her in and stood against the sink. "I keep waking up standing," she said. I didn't say anything. "In the bedroom. I'm — I go to sleep and then I'm standing and I don't know how I got there, I don't know how long, and I'm looking at you, and I don't know why I'm looking at you." She was looking at the floor. She was doing the thing she does with the kids, saying it to the tiles. "It's every night. Isn't it. You know it is. You've been —" She stopped. "You've been pretending." "Yes." "How long." "A few weeks." She nodded like that was a number she'd expected. Then she said, "I'm frightened," and it came out plain, no joke on it, and I've been married to her eleven years and I've never heard her say a thing like that without a joke on it, not once, and I went and sat next to her on the edge of the bath and put my arm round her and she leaned in. She was exactly her body. That's what I kept thinking. The shoulders, the weight of her head on me, the way she fits. I've held her a thousand times and it was that. Warm through the T-shirt. Her hand came up and held my wrist the way she does. And I believed her. I want that down. I believed every word and I sat there believing it, and it didn't change anything I'd decided, and I knew that too, and I held her tighter because of it. She said, "I'm sorry," into my shoulder. I said, "It's all right." Which it isn't. — The toast burned. Later, in the kitchen, when she'd gone up and I was making her something because that's a thing you do. I stood and watched it go from brown to black under the grill and I didn't move to stop it, I watched it, and I could smell it and see the smoke start off the edge and I knew what she'd have said. *The toast is expressing itself.* Every time. Eleven years. I opened my mouth to say it, to the empty kitchen, to see if it was still a thing that could be said, and it wasn't. My mouth was open and nothing came. I put the black toast in the bin and did two more slices and took them up. She was asleep. Properly, on her side, mouth a bit open, eyes shut all the way. I checked. I stood at the foot of the bed with the plate and I checked, and then I saw where I was standing and I went and sat in the chair by the window instead. The boiler came on at half five. I heard the pipes go. I counted the clicks as it fired — it's five, it's always five — and I got to five and then I went on, six, seven, past where the clicks stopped, counting the quiet where they'd been.

# Eight I could breathe. I know how that sounds. But since August there's been something low in my chest, a weight, like the last cup of the reservoir never came up, and I've breathed round it for three months the way you learn to walk on a bad knee. And I woke and it was gone. Just gone. I lay in the dark and breathed all the way down, right to the bottom, like an idiot, like someone showing off in a lesson, and I nearly laughed. That's how it was. I nearly laughed, and only then did I look up. Daniel was standing at the foot of the bed. The hall light was on behind him the way it always is, because I don't like feeling for the wall, and it made him a shape and a bit of hair and two points. Grey T-shirt. Bare legs. Hands down. And I thought: oh, love. Because he's been so worried. I know he has. I've watched him not sleep — I've watched him from wherever I've been, which I can't tell you about, it's like trying to describe the taste of the inside of your own mouth — and I've watched him get thinner and greyer and more precise, the way he does, the way he goes when he's frightened, counting things. He's been counting things for a month. And now here he was, up in the night, checking on me. Standing there like a dad at a cot. I nearly said his name. I got as far as the D in my mouth. — The thing about eight-year-olds is they'll tell you exactly what's wrong if you don't look at them while they do it. So I look at the music. I say "bar twelve again," and they say their mum's got a new boyfriend and he's got a dog and they hate the dog, and I say "bar twelve," and we go from there. I've never known how to do that with Daniel. He's always looking. There's nowhere to put your eyes. I've been thinking about his hands on my chest. On the bank. I don't remember it; I've been told. Carla told me, in the hospital, in the voice she uses for facts. Six minutes. His hands on my sternum and his mouth on mine and him counting, of course counting, and a woman with a dog calling the ambulance. I've tried to feel it, like you'd try to feel a bruise you can't see. I can't. It's just a thing I know about my own body that somebody else told me. And I've thought about what he was looking at before he looked up. He's never said. I've never asked. That's us. That's eleven years. — His feet were bare on the boards. That's not a thing you notice about a person, it's a thing you know, like which stair. Daniel's feet are always cold. He shifts. He stands at the counter shifting from one to the other like a boy waiting outside a head's office, and in bed he pulls them up, and in the night if he gets up for anything he's back in thirty seconds with his knees to his chest and his feet on my calves going *God*. Always. It's the most Daniel thing about him. I've told the kids about it, I've said, my husband has feet like a fish, and they've laughed. He wasn't shifting. He was standing on the bare boards in November in the middle of the night with his feet together and he wasn't shifting and the two points where the light was weren't going in and out, and I lay there and knew it. I did. I'm not going to pretend I didn't. Something in me went very still and clear and knew it the way you know a chord's wrong before you can say which note. And I thought: don't. Not tonight. I'm so tired. I've been gone since August and I've just come back and I can breathe and he's *here*, he's standing right there, and whatever else is true he's still the shape of him in the door with the light behind. I'll look properly in the morning. I'll look in daylight, when things look like themselves. I closed my eyes. I'm going to be honest about why, because I've had a night to think and there isn't a version where I come out well. I closed them because I was tired. I closed them because I love him. I closed them because I didn't want to know. And I lay there and tried to find where one of those stopped and the next one started and I couldn't, they were all the same thing, one thing, and I don't have a name for it and I don't think there is one. After a while the mattress took him. His side. He turned away. His feet didn't come. I lay with my eyes shut till the birds. — He was down before me. I heard the kettle. The kitchen was grey, the boy already at the fence — early, for him, it wasn't nine — *thock*, *thock*, the panel jumping where the post's gone. Daniel was at the counter with two mugs. He'd put mine on my side. He had the sugar out. He doesn't take sugar. Nineteen years in the same firm and he's never once taken it; he reads the ingredients on things. He had a teaspoon in the bag and he put one in his and stirred it, round and round, looking at nothing, and then he looked up and smiled at me. Tired. Fond. A husband in a kitchen. I didn't say anything. I got the oatcakes down. Three packets, one behind the other, the way he'd stacked them. I opened the front one and put four out on the counter with the butter, standing, the way I do, and I ate one, and it was fine, and the crumbs went everywhere. The wall outside was empty. I noticed that and then I didn't think about it. He said, "You slept." "I did," I said. "You?" "Like the dead," he said, and drank his coffee, and I said, "Good," and passed him the plate.

[Analysis] This is an exceptional piece of writing that executes its plan with remarkable precision and restraint. Let me work through the key elements. **Voice and Character** The Ines voice is everything the plan promised: warmer, more digressive, funnier, and crucially different from Daniel's clipped precision. The digression about eight-year-olds and the "bar twelve" technique is perfectly placed — it reveals her pedagogy, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of her own failure with Daniel in one compact passage. The detail about telling her students "my husband has feet like a fish" is exactly right: it's the kind of thing a person says to children, intimate and slightly embarrassing, and it makes her real in a way Daniel's chapters couldn't. The voice is consistent throughout and never slips into Daniel's register. **The Horror** The horror here is handled with extraordinary discipline. The chapter never names what's happening. Ines's recognition — "I knew it the way you know a chord's wrong before you can say which note" — is the right metaphor for her: musical, precise, and immediately suppressed. The decision to close her eyes is rendered with genuine moral honesty: "I closed them because I was tired. I closed them because I love him. I closed them because I didn't want to know. And I lay there and tried to find where one of those stopped and the next one started and I couldn't." This is the thematic heart of the story made flesh, and it earns its weight. The plan specified that the chapter should be "honest that these are the same thing" — love, exhaustion, and not wanting to know — and the prose delivers this without editorializing. **The Wrongnesses** The plan's wrongnesses are deployed with care. His feet not shifting is the key tell, and it's set up beautifully with the "fish feet" detail earlier in the same chapter. The sugar in the coffee is the final wrongness — quiet, domestic, devastating. "He doesn't take sugar. Nineteen years in the same firm and he's never once taken it; he reads the ingredients on things." This is Daniel-as-was, and the sugar is the marker of what he's become. The empty wall (the cat gone) is noted and then deliberately not thought about, which is exactly right. **The Ending** "Like the dead," he said, and drank his coffee, and I said, "Good," and passed him the plate. This is a near-perfect ending. It's ordinary, it's devastating, it's funny in the darkest possible way, and it doesn't announce itself. The plan called for "something ordinary she says to him across the kitchen, and his answer" — and "like the dead" as his answer is better than anything the plan could have specified. It's the kind of line that rewards rereading. **Weaknesses** The section break structure (the em-dashes) is slightly mechanical — three sections of roughly equal weight. The middle section (the digression about Carla's telling her about the CPR) is the weakest: it's necessary information but it sits slightly more expository than the rest. "That's us. That's eleven years" is the one moment where the prose tells rather than shows, and it's a small but real lapse. The metaphor "like the last cup of the reservoir never came up" is slightly strained — "cup" is an odd unit for reservoir water — though "breathed round it the way you learn to walk on a bad knee" is excellent. **Plan Adherence** The chapter follows its plan with impressive fidelity. The reservoir weight lifting, the hall light, Daniel standing still, the feet not shifting, the almost-said name, the eyes closed for all three reasons, the sugar, the oatcakes, the empty wall, the boy starting early, the last line being ordinary dialogue — all present and executed. The plan's instruction to avoid "the pronoun-swap ending as final line" is honored; the ending is dialogue, not revelation. **Overall** This is writing of genuine quality. The restraint is real restraint, not performed restraint. The horror is earned. The ending is devastating without being theatrical. The voice is distinct and consistent. The small failures (one expository sentence, one slightly strained metaphor) are minor against the achievement of the whole. [Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of horror fiction that operates almost entirely through restraint, accumulation, and the precise observation of domestic detail. The story takes the possession horror premise and executes it with genuine literary sophistication, refusing the genre's usual shortcuts in favor of something far more unsettling. The narrative voice is the story's greatest achievement. Daniel's voice as a surveyor—someone professionally trained to read evidence, measure decay, and quantify damage—is not merely a character detail but the story's structural spine. His habit of counting, measuring, and cataloguing ("one drop every hundred and ten seconds since September, and a stain fourteen inches wide") creates a man whose coping mechanism is precision, and the horror emerges precisely when precision fails him. The compression fitting, the stain, the boards he keeps meaning to get up—these are not decorative details but load-bearing elements of character and theme. The story's central conceit—that the possession works through sleep, through the unconscious surrender of the self—is handled with remarkable intelligence. The final chapter's reversal, where we see events from Ines's perspective and discover that Daniel has been standing at the foot of the bed, is genuinely earned. The story has been building toward this symmetry from the first chapter, and the final line ("Like the dead") lands with the weight of everything that preceded it. The Carla chapter is particularly strong. The dog's name—Bica versus Rex—is a masterclass in how to deploy a horror beat without telegraphing it. Carla's face going "completely still, the way a face goes when the body has understood something before the head has" is exactly right. Her early departure, the long hug, the text—these are all perfectly calibrated. The oatcakes are a brilliant recurring motif. Three packets stacking up, the detail of how Ines used to eat them (standing, crumbs everywhere, butter off the knife), and then in the final chapter Ines eating them exactly that way again—this is the story's emotional resolution, and it's devastating precisely because it's ambiguous. Is this Ines returned, or the thing that has learned Ines so thoroughly it can perform her perfectly? The chapter eight perspective shift is a bold structural choice that pays off. Ines's voice is distinct from Daniel's—warmer, more associative, less precise—and her deliberate choice to close her eyes rather than confront what she sees is the story's most psychologically complex moment. "I closed them because I was tired. I closed them because I love him. I closed them because I didn't want to know." This is genuinely nuanced writing about how love and denial are sometimes indistinguishable. The dialogue is sparse but effective. "You should sleep, Dan. You look terrible" is chilling precisely because it's so ordinary. The Hendersons' party gambit—Daniel testing her with a date he knows she'd remember—is a beautifully observed moment of marital cruelty dressed as investigation. Some minor criticisms: The cat (Mo/Ted—the name changes, which may be intentional given the story's themes of identity but reads as a possible error) is used effectively but the symbolism is perhaps slightly too on-the-nose. The story occasionally risks over-explaining its own emotional logic ("I've always thought a thing was one or the other. It isn't"), though these moments are rare and the observation is usually earned. The pacing in chapters 5 and 6 slows slightly as Daniel's sleeplessness accumulates, though this mirrors his psychological state effectively. The ending is genuinely masterful. "Like the dead" as the final line, spoken by Daniel, with Ines saying "Good"—the story refuses to resolve whether this is horror or reunion, whether Daniel is lost or found, whether Ines is back or something else is wearing her. The warm mattress, the sugar in the coffee, the empty wall—these details accumulate into an ending that is both emotionally satisfying and deeply unsettling. The metaphors consistently land. The reservoir, the stain, the compression fitting, the split board—these are not decorative but functional, each one doing double duty as character revelation and thematic statement.
