Model Output:
# Brainstorming **The prompt line.** "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" is a classic noir description of a femme fatale, gender-flipped. It's retrospective — someone is describing a man they've already lost or already been ruined by. The line implies a narrator who knew better and went anyway. That gives us the emotional engine: desire that knows it's a mistake. **Who says the line?** Options: - A first-person narrator looking back after the fact (classic noir voice-over structure — *Double Indemnity*, *Sunset Boulevard*). We know it ends badly; the question is how. - A third-person close narrator, present tense, so the "bad ideas" are still unfolding. - The line could be the *last* line rather than the first — we spend eight chapters learning why he earns that epitaph. **Setting possibilities.** - Contemporary city, rain-slick, post-industrial — a mid-sized rust belt city rather than LA/NYC to avoid cliché. Pittsburgh, Cleveland, Baltimore. Bridges, rivers, shuttered steel. - A coastal town off-season — motels, a boardwalk shuttered for winter, casinos two towns over. - Desert border town — heat noir instead of rain noir. - Near-future with a slight technological chill (surveillance, gig economy) — neo-noir often uses this. - 1990s — pre-smartphone, pagers, payphones, the last era when "disappearing" was plausible. Also coincides with a specific era of queer precarity (post-AIDS-crisis, pre-marriage-equality) that could deepen stakes without becoming an "issue" story. **Narrator candidates.** 1. **A repo man / skip tracer** — finds people for a living, gets hired to find *him*, and finds him too well. 2. **A night-shift ER nurse** — patches up a man with a knife wound who won't give his name. Medical noir; the nurse sees bodies all night, this one's different. 3. **A bartender at a dying gay bar** — the bar is about to be sold; the man walks in with a scheme to save it (or to use it). 4. **A parole officer** — the man is his client. Power imbalance, professional ruin, the obvious "bad idea." 5. **An insurance adjuster** — very *Double Indemnity*. Boring, careful man meets chaos. 6. **A locksmith** — literally opens doors he shouldn't. Nice metaphor; a man who breaks into things falling for a man who breaks things. 7. **A pawnshop owner** — the man comes to hock something that isn't his. 8. **A translator / court interpreter** — hears everything, says nothing. **The "him."** - A small-time grifter with one big con left. - A man on the run from a brother/partner/husband he stole from. - A former cop, now disgraced. - A getaway driver, aging out. - A musician who owes money to the wrong people. - Someone who is *not* what he seems — the twist being he's the one who's been cased, not the caser. **Plot shapes.** - **Heist gone wrong.** He pulls the narrator into a job — robbing a specific person (an ex, a boss, a landlord). It works, then doesn't. - **Body in the trunk.** Something already happened before chapter one; the narrator helps clean up. - **Insurance/inheritance scheme.** He wants the narrator to help him claim something — a dead man's identity, a dead husband's estate. Queer angle: an unrecognized partner locked out of an inheritance, so he needs someone to *impersonate* a family member or to forge. - **Missing person.** He hires the narrator to find someone; the someone is himself, or is dead by his hand. - **Blackmail.** He's blackmailing someone closeted and powerful; the narrator gets caught in the middle. - **Reverse noir.** The narrator is the dangerous one; "he" is the one who gets ruined; the narrator doesn't realize he's the femme fatale until too late. **The queerness — how central?** Options range from incidental (the romance is simply between two men) to structural (the plot mechanics depend on legal/social invisibility of queer relationships). The structural version has more noir bite: noir is about people the system doesn't protect making their own justice. A queer couple who *can't* go to the police, *can't* inherit, *can't* be each other's next of kin — that's noir-native. **Tone.** - Hardboiled, clipped, Chandler-esque metaphors. Risk: pastiche. - Lush, melancholy, more Patricia Highsmith / *Carol* / Denis Johnson — interiority over quips. - Dry, funny, self-aware — the narrator knows he's in a noir and hates it. - Dreamy, fragmented — Wong Kar-wai / *Happy Together* neon melancholy. **Ending possibilities.** - He dies; narrator survives, wrecked (classic). - Narrator dies; he narrates from beyond (*Sunset Boulevard* trick). - He betrays narrator; narrator lets him, knowingly. - Narrator betrays him — turns him in, or takes the money. - They both get away — but the last chapter makes clear it won't last; the getaway is itself the bad idea. - Ambiguous: he vanishes, narrator waits, cigarette burning down. - Quiet inversion: after all the crime, the actual "bad idea" was the domesticity — he asks the narrator to stay, and that's the thing that gets someone killed. **Structural ideas for 8 chapters.** - Chapters alternate: odd chapters present-day (aftermath, narrator being questioned or waiting), even chapters the past (how it happened). Converge in 7–8. - Straight chronological with the retrospective voice — cleaner for 8000 words. - Each chapter titled by a cigarette count or a time of night. - Each chapter anchored to a location: the bar, the motel, the car, the river, the house, the hospital, the bus station, the bar again. **Images/motifs.** - Cigarettes obviously — the narrator doesn't smoke and starts; or quit and restarts; the final image is him lighting one alone. - Rain vs. heat. - Bridges (crossing, jumping, tolls). - Keys and locks. - Mirrors/reflections in wet streets. - A specific object that changes hands: a lighter, a watch, a ring that isn't legally a wedding ring. - Hands — the narrator notices his hands before his face. **Specific concept sketches:** *A. The Locksmith.* Late 90s, Pittsburgh. Narrator Danny, 40, runs a locksmith shop inherited from his father, closeted-ish, careful. A man named Cal comes in wanting a safe opened. The safe belonged to Cal's dead partner Marcus; Marcus's family has seized the house and everything in it because Cal has no legal standing. Cal wants to break in and take what's his. Danny knows it's theft under the law. He goes anyway. Inside the safe is something neither expected (money that isn't Marcus's; evidence Marcus was involved with people who want it back). The family, the creditors, and the two of them collide. *B. The Nurse.* Night-shift nurse Ray stitches up a man who pays cash and gives a fake name. The man comes back. Ray starts covering for him — falsifying charts. Man is a courier for something. Ray's professional ruin is the "bad idea." Ends with Ray treating him one last time and not being able to save him, or choosing not to call it in. *C. The Skip Tracer.* Narrator finds people who skipped bail. Hired to find a man; finds him in a week; doesn't turn him in. Starts feeding the bondsman false leads. The man is running from a violent ex-partner who is also the person who posted bail (control via money). The narrator has to decide whether to hand him back. *D. The Reverse.* Narrator is the smoke-and-bad-ideas one, narrating about a quiet man he ruined. Line is spoken about the quiet man ironically at the end — "he was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, by the time I was done with him." # Reflection The prompt line is doing a lot of work — it's a voice line as much as a description. Whoever narrates has to be someone capable of that sentence: wry, a little bitter, retrospective, in love. That immediately favors first-person past tense with a knowing voice. The line also implies that the narrator is *not* smoke and bad ideas himself — he's the steady one, the one with a shop or a job or a routine, which is what makes the contrast legible. That rules out the Reverse concept (D) as the main approach, though the irony is tempting; it undercuts the prompt rather than fulfilling it, and at 8000 words there isn't room to earn a double inversion. On tone: pure hardboiled pastiche is the biggest risk. Eight chapters of Chandler metaphors will exhaust a reader and read as costume. The Highsmith/Denis Johnson register — melancholy, precise, occasional dry humor, real interiority — will hold up better and suits romance, which needs the reader to feel the pull rather than admire the prose. The noir should live in the *situation* (people outside the law's protection, moral compromise, fatalism) and the *imagery* (night, weather, rooms), not in wisecracks. On setting: 1990s rust belt is strong. It solves the practical problems (no phones, disappearing is plausible, cash economy) and gives the queer element structural teeth without lecturing — in 1996 a surviving partner genuinely had no claim, couldn't be next of kin, could be evicted by the family. That's a noir-grade injustice that doesn't require a villain to be cartoonish; the family can be ordinary and grieving and still be the antagonists. It also makes "can't go to the police" a real constraint rather than a contrivance. Pittsburgh specifically gives bridges, rivers, hills, steam, a city that feels like it's already been left. Concept A (the Locksmith) feels like the strongest spine. The profession is thematically loaded without being cute — a man who opens things for a living, who has kept himself locked — and it gives a concrete, small-scale crime that two people can actually commit in one night. The inheritance-theft premise is *sympathetic* crime, which is important: the romance needs the reader to root for the bad idea. The safe as a MacGuffin gives a clean midpoint reveal that escalates stakes (what's in it isn't what Cal said, or Cal lied about why he wants it). And the twist space is rich: Cal might have been half-honest — he did love Marcus, and Marcus did owe money to people, and the safe was always about the money as much as the memory. That's the noir turn: the bad idea is partly a con, and the narrator has to decide if it matters. Concept B (the Nurse) is good but the "patching up a stranger" beat is well-worn and the escalation is less concrete. Concept C (the Skip Tracer) has a nice built-in tension but the found-him-in-a-week structure front-loads the plot; the middle would sag. Pacing over eight chapters at ~1000 words each: that's tight. Each chapter needs one scene, one location, one turn. Roughly — meeting; the ask and the refusal; the yes; the job; what's inside; the fallout closing in; the choice; the aftermath and the line. The alternating-timeline structure is appealing but at this length it would fracture momentum; better to run chronological with a brief frame in chapter one (the narrator already knows how it ends) and a return to that frame in chapter eight. The retrospective voice does the double-timeline work for free. The ending should not be the getaway. Noir romance earns its ache by denying the reader the thing they want while making the wanting worth it. But killing him outright is the expected move. More interesting: he leaves with the money and the narrator lets him — even helps — knowing he's been used and choosing to believe it was also real. The narrator keeps the shop, keeps one thing of Cal's, starts smoking. The last line can be a variant of the prompt, but the story should arguably *open* on it so the reader carries the fatalism through, and close on something quieter — the lit cigarette, the narrator becoming, a little, the thing he loved. Things to guard against: making the family villains rather than obstacles; over-explaining the legal situation (one exchange should do it); letting Cal be only charming — he needs a scene where he's petty, tired, or afraid so the love is for a person and not a silhouette. And the sex/intimacy should be present but oblique — noir is about what's withheld, and the romance should be felt in hands, keys, the way he lights a cigarette off the narrator's stove.

Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention I'm writing a first-person, past-tense noir romance in the retrospective voice — the narrator already knows how it ends, and the reader will too from the first line. That fatalism is the engine; the pleasure is in watching him walk into it anyway. The prompt line opens the story. The last line will be quieter and will not repeat it. **Plot.** Pittsburgh, October–November 1996. Tom Rusnak, 41, runs the locksmith shop his father left him on the South Side. Cal Mercer walks in wanting a safe opened. The safe is in a house that belonged to Marcus Hale, Cal's partner of nine years, dead six weeks; Marcus's sister has taken possession because Cal has no legal standing to anything. Cal says the safe holds letters, photographs, a ring. It does. It also holds $38,000 that Marcus owed to a man named Doyle, and Cal knew. The crime is sympathetic; the lie inside it is the noir. The ending is not the getaway and not the death: Cal leaves with the money, Tom lets him and helps him, and stays. Tom keeps one thing. Tom starts smoking again. **Voice.** Highsmith and Denis Johnson over Chandler. Precise, melancholy, occasionally dry. Metaphors earned and sparing — no more than one or two hardboiled flourishes per chapter, and they should come from Tom's actual world (locks, brass, tumblers, his father's hands). Tom is a careful man; his sentences should be careful too, with the occasional break where feeling gets through. Dialogue clipped, people not saying the thing. **Queerness.** Structural, not thematic. The 1996 legal reality — a surviving partner who can't inherit, can't be next of kin, can be locked out of his own house — is what makes the crime necessary and what makes the police unavailable. One exchange establishes it; nobody lectures. The bar exists, the codes exist, the caution exists; they're furniture, not subject. **What I'm aiming for.** Cal must be a person, not a silhouette: a scene where he's petty, a scene where he's frightened, a scene where he's tired. Marcus's sister Linda must be grieving and ordinary, an obstacle rather than a villain. The intimacy should be felt through hands, objects, and proximity, with the sex itself oblique. Each chapter is one location, one scene, one turn. The safe-opening should be genuinely procedural — the one place Tom is fully competent and fully alive. **What I'm avoiding.** Pastiche wisecracks. Rain in every chapter (it should rain twice, meaningfully). Explaining the law. A cartoon loan shark — Doyle's threat arrives through a subordinate and a gesture, never a speech. A twist that makes Cal a pure con man; the letters have to be real and Tom has to know they're real. A last line that recycles the prompt. **Motifs.** Cigarettes (Tom quit eight years ago; Cal lights his off Tom's gas stove; the final image). Keys and the shop's dead display safe. Marcus's overcoat. Hands. Bridges crossed at night. The residence hotel Cal lives in, with the broken neon. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Rusnak & Son.** Opens on the line. Tom's shop near closing, a Tuesday in October, first rain. Establish Tom: the father's shop, the father's habits, the ledger, the eight years without a cigarette, the apartment upstairs, the careful life. Cal comes in with a key that fits nothing and asks about safes — Moslers specifically, older residential ones. Won't say where the safe is. Tom knows what that means and says no. Cal buys a padlock he doesn't need, leaves a book of matches from Lucky's on the counter. Tom keeps them. Ends with Tom upstairs, not smoking, turning the matchbook over. **Chapter 2 — Lucky's.** Friday. Tom goes to the bar he goes to twice a month and sits where he always sits. Cal is there, or arrives, and it isn't a coincidence. He tells the story straight: Marcus, the restaurant on Murray Avenue, the aneurysm, the funeral where Cal sat in the last pew, the day Linda changed the locks on the house in Squirrel Hill while he was at work. One exchange covers what Cal is legally: nothing. The safe holds letters, photos, Marcus's ring. Tom says no again, more slowly. Drives Cal to his residence hotel on the North Side, broken neon. Cal's hand on the dash. Tom drives home over the bridge and does not go in. **Chapter 3 — Beechwood Boulevard.** Tom cases the house alone, telling himself he's just driving. Watches Linda and her husband carrying black trash bags to the curb — Marcus's clothes. Waits until they go in, takes an overcoat from a bag. Brings it to Cal's room. Cal's reaction is not gratitude: he's angry, petty, snaps at Tom for pitying him, then puts the coat on and can't speak. Tom says yes. Later, at Tom's stove, Cal lights a cigarette off the burner and Tom watches his hands. First kiss, brief. Tom's first turn from careful. **Chapter 4 — The Mosler.** The job, one long night. Rear door, a Schlage Tom's father could have done blindfolded. The safe in Marcus's study: a 1950s Mosler, three-wheel. Tom's competence and calm — the one chapter where he is entirely himself. Cal holding the flashlight, not speaking. The door opens on letters, photographs, a ring in a box — and eleven banded stacks of cash. Tom looks at Cal's face and Cal isn't surprised. Headlights on the street. They take everything and go. Tom's van, lettered with his own name, on a street where vans get remembered. **Chapter 5 — Upstairs.** Tom's apartment, 2 a.m. The confrontation, low-voiced. Cal admits it: Marcus borrowed from Doyle to keep the restaurant open, died owing, Doyle sent a man to the funeral. Cal knew the money was in the safe; he didn't lie about the letters. He's frightened in a way he wasn't before, and tired, and it's the most honest he's been. Tom reads one letter and it's real. He hides the money in the dead display safe downstairs — the one his father used for show. They sleep together; the prose stays on the window, the streetlight, Cal's back. Tom doesn't sleep after. **Chapter 6 — Visitors.** Three days. A detective named Kowalczyk comes to the shop about a break-in in Squirrel Hill — professional entry, a van seen. Tom is calm because he has been calm his whole life. Then a man in a good coat comes in asking after Cal by name, buys nothing, sets a book of Lucky's matches on the counter and lights one and lets it burn to his fingers before he leaves. Linda calls the shop about rekeying — she doesn't know who Tom is; her voice is only tired. Cal doesn't come that night, or the next. Tom sits with the display safe and understands he's been used and that it was also real, and that these aren't opposites. **Chapter 7 — Eleventh Street.** Cal at the shop door at 3 a.m., a cut over his eye. Doyle's man found the hotel. He needs the money and the 5:40 Greyhound to anywhere south. He asks Tom to come — and means it, which is the worst part. Tom knows he'd be smoke inside a month. He opens the safe, gives Cal the money and Marcus's coat, keeps the ring without asking. Drives him across the river to the station. In the car Cal lights his last cigarette and hands it to Tom, and Tom takes it. The bus. Cal does not look back, and Tom watches long enough to be sure. **Chapter 8 — Rekey.** Three weeks on. Kowalczyk stops coming. Doyle's man comes once more; Tom says he doesn't know where Cal is, and it's true, and the man can tell. Linda comes in to have her locks rekeyed and says something small and human about her brother. Tom does the job for cost. He finds the letters Cal left in the coat pocket — not taken, left — and doesn't read them again. The shop at closing, first snow. Tom opens the drawer, finds the matchbook, buys a pack across the street. Lights one at the counter where Cal stood. Ends on the shop, the smoke, the sign with his father's name, Tom staying.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This A human writer given "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" would probably not start with a plan. They'd start with a person — someone they knew or half-knew, a man at a bar in 1994 who said one thing they've never forgotten. The story would grow crooked around that memory. It would have a scene that doesn't strictly need to be there but is the reason the writer wanted to write it. It would have a detail so specific it couldn't be invented (the brand of the space heater, the way the bar's bathroom door didn't latch). And it would have at least one place where the writer clearly didn't know what to do and just wrote through it, leaving a seam. Human writers of this kind of story — Highsmith, Denis Johnson, Garth Greenwell, Jean Genet in a different register — also tend to be *less fair* than a planner. They have a favorite character and it shows. They let scenes run long past their "function." They include the boring day. They contradict their own theme. Their narrators lie a little, or misremember, or notice the wrong thing in the middle of the important moment. And crucially: they don't know, while writing chapter three, exactly what chapter eight is going to do with the ring. A human would also be more comfortable with the story being *about something else* than it appears. The prompt says noir romance; a human might discover halfway through that it's actually about the father, or about the city dying, or about how Tom has never once in his life said what he wanted out loud, and let the noir plot become the excuse rather than the point. # Telltale LLM Approaches — Generally **Symmetry and closure.** LLMs love bookends, callbacks, motifs that pay off exactly once in the final chapter. Every object introduced gets used. Every thread gets tied. Real stories leave things on the table. **Thematic underlining.** The prose tells you what it's about. A character will think a sentence that is the theme. A final image will be explicable in one clause. Humans trust the reader more and trust themselves less. **Even distribution.** Each chapter gets one scene, one turn, one location, roughly equal weight. Real stories are lumpy — a 400-word chapter, a 2000-word one, a scene that's mostly one person not talking. **Safe emotional register.** The melancholy is tasteful. The anger is justified. Nobody is ugly for longer than a beat before being redeemed by context. Sex is "oblique" in a way that's really just absent. Cruelty is gestured at, not committed. **Competence porn and tidy procedure.** The character who's good at a thing is *shown being good at it* in a controlled set-piece. Nothing goes wrong that the plot didn't need to go wrong. **Impressive sentences at the expense of momentum.** Metaphor density. The "one perfect line" per paragraph habit. Adjective-noun-adjective-noun rhythm. Sentences that end on the strong word every time so the prose sounds like it's landing punches. **Characters who are legible.** Everyone's motive is nameable. The femme fatale lied *about this specific thing* for *this specific reason*, disclosed in a confession scene. **Period detail as checklist.** 1996: payphone, Greyhound, no cell phones — all deployed as plot lubricant rather than lived texture. **The wise, wounded narrator.** Sad but never pathetic. Used but never humiliated. Complicit but never actually contemptible. He gets the last word and it's a good one. **Dialogue that is "clipped, people not saying the thing."** This is itself a cliché now. Real evasive dialogue is *weirder* — people say too much about the wrong thing, repeat themselves, make jokes that don't land. # Deep Dive: Where the Plan Falls Into These **The structure is too clean.** Eight chapters, eight locations, eight turns, each about 1000 words. The plan even names the shape: meeting / ask / yes / job / reveal / pressure / choice / aftermath. That's a screenwriting beat sheet. The reader will feel the machinery. Chapter 6 in particular — three visitors in sequence (cop, thug, sister), each doing one thing — is a checklist scene. **Every object pays off.** Matchbook in Ch1 → Ch6 (thug's matchbook) → Ch8 (buys cigarettes). Overcoat Ch3 → Ch7 (given back) → Ch8 (letters in pocket). Display safe Ch5 → Ch7 → Ch8. Ring Ch2 → Ch4 → Ch7. Stove-lit cigarette Ch3 → last cigarette handed over Ch7 → lights one Ch8. This is *tidy*, and tidy is the enemy here. Noir is about loose ends. Grief is loose ends. Somebody should keep something that never comes up again. Something should be lost stupidly. **The "Cal must be a person" note is a checklist too.** "A scene where he's petty, a scene where he's frightened, a scene where he's tired" — assigning one flaw per chapter is exactly how an LLM manufactures roundness. A human Cal is petty *while* frightened, funny *while* lying, and does something in chapter two that only makes sense in retrospect and maybe never fully. **The reveal is over-motivated.** Ch5: Cal confesses everything — Doyle, the restaurant, the funeral, "he didn't lie about the letters." That's a deposition. It explains the mystery so the reader can file it. More human: Tom never gets the full story. Cal tells two versions on two nights and they don't match. Tom picks one to believe and knows he's picking. **Tom is too dignified.** He's the careful one, the steady one, wry and observant. He gets used and responds with rueful acceptance. He never begs. He never does anything humiliating. He never gets it *wrong* — never reads a situation badly, never says something stupid to Cal that he can't take back, never is boring or needy or jealous of a dead man. The plan says "Tom keeps the ring without asking" as if that's a quiet noble act. It could instead be a small theft, a grubby thing he's ashamed of. **The father is decorative.** "Rusnak & Son," the father's hands, the father's habits — but the father never *does* anything to the story. In a human draft he'd either become the secret subject or be cut. What did the father know? Did Tom bring anyone upstairs while the old man was alive? Is the shop a life or a sentence? **The queerness is "structural not thematic" — which risks being neither.** The plan is careful (LLM-careful) not to lecture. Fine. But the danger is that it becomes tasteful furniture: one exchange about legal standing, then it recedes. In 1996 Pittsburgh this would have been *in the body* — who Tom looks at in the shop, what he does when Kowalczyk uses the word "roommate," whether Tom has ever been in a hospital room when he wasn't allowed to be. It should be uncomfortable somewhere, not just sad. **Linda is being handled with tongs.** "Grieving and ordinary, obstacle not villain" — and then she gets one humanizing line in Ch8 and Tom does the job at cost. That's the plan performing fairness. A human writer might let Linda be genuinely unpleasant *and* right. Or let Tom hate her unjustly. Or give her the best line in the story and no redemption. **Doyle's man with the burning match** is a nice image and a very LLM one — the menacing gesture in lieu of menace. Real intimidation is duller and more frightening: he asks about Tom's mother. He comes back and buys a padlock. He knows the name of the bar. **Sex is "oblique — window, streetlight, Cal's back."** This is the safe choice dressed as an aesthetic one. Greenwell and Johnson would not look away. The story is *about* desire that knows better; if the desire is offstage, the knowing-better has no weight. It doesn't need to be explicit but it needs to be *present*, awkward, specific — a bad moment, a good one, something Tom hadn't known he wanted. **The ending is the "quiet noble sacrifice" ending.** Tom lets him go, keeps the shop, lights a cigarette, "Tom staying." It's the safe version of unsafe. It resolves the romance into wisdom. Noir doesn't do wisdom. The reader should leave slightly unsure whether Tom did the right thing, or whether Tom even *chose* — maybe Cal just left and Tom's narration is dressing it as a choice. **The retrospective voice is doing a lot of hedging.** "Tom already knows how it ends" lets the prose be wise about everything. It also drains suspense. A human would let the narrator's knowledge be *partial* — he knows how it ended for him, not for Cal. He doesn't know if Cal's alive. **The prose intentions are a taste checklist.** "Highsmith over Chandler," "one or two flourishes per chapter," "metaphors from his world." This produces controlled, well-mannered prose. It won't produce the sentence that makes a reader stop. Permission needed to be occasionally over the top, occasionally flat, occasionally wrong. # Brainstorming: Making It More Human **Break the symmetry.** - Let one chapter be very short — Ch6 as four paragraphs, or the bus station as 300 words. - Let one chapter be two scenes badly joined, or a scene that's just Tom doing inventory while thinking. - Drop one motif entirely. The matchbook could just never come up again. The ring could be given to Cal and never mentioned. - Put the line "cigarette smoke and bad ideas" *not* first — maybe in Ch3, said to Cal's face as a joke, and Cal doesn't laugh. **Let Tom be worse.** - He lies to Cal about something small in Ch2 and never corrects it. - He's jealous of Marcus and reads the letters *because* of that, not out of tenderness. - He says something cruel about the dead man during the confrontation. - He calls the hotel after Cal's gone, twice, hangs up. - He considers turning Cal in — not for justice, out of spite — and only doesn't because he's a coward. - He keeps the ring and it's not romantic; it's the only thing in the story he takes for himself and he can't explain it. **Let Cal be less explicable.** - Two versions of the Doyle story. Or no confession — Tom pieces it together and might be wrong. - Cal has a habit that's unattractive and un-noir (bad teeth, talks about his mother, watches game shows in the hotel). - Cal is funny. Actually funny, not wry. The plan has no jokes. - Cal asks Tom to come with him and Tom can't tell if it's real — and neither can the reader, and the story doesn't settle it. - Cal does something kind that serves no plot purpose. **Let the crime go wrong in a small, dumb way.** - Tom cuts his hand on the Mosler and bleeds on Marcus's desk. - They leave the padlock from Ch1 on the kitchen table. - Linda's dog. There's always a dog. - Tom, mid-job, notices a photograph and stops working for two minutes and Cal has to say his name. **Make the queerness live in the body and the room.** - Kowalczyk says "roommate" and Tom watches himself agree. - Tom went to a hospital once for someone and was not let in. He never says who. - The bar has a specific rule about the back door. - The father knew. Or the father found something and they never spoke of it and the shop is the silence. **Complicate Linda.** - She's not grieving in a way Tom finds acceptable — she's angry at Marcus, and she's *right* about some of it. - She says something homophobic that's also true about Cal. - Tom overcharges her. **Make the menace mundane.** - Doyle's man is polite and mentions Tom's father by name. - He comes to Lucky's and sits down. - Nothing happens to Tom. That's worse. **Let the sex be in the story.** - One paragraph that is direct. Not a window. - It's awkward once. Tom hasn't in years. - Afterward Cal smokes and talks about Marcus and Tom lies there and it's the loneliest he's been. **Unsettle the ending.** - Tom doesn't know if Cal made the bus. Never finds out. - Or: a postcard, no return address, something banal on it. Tom reads it too many times. - Or: Tom smokes but the story doesn't make it mean anything. He just does now. - Or: the last line is about the father, or the lock, or the weather — not about Cal at all. - Or: Tom admits, in the last paragraph, that he might be lying about one of these things. **Roughen the voice.** - Allow Tom a run-on when he's upset. Allow a paragraph that's just facts. - Allow him to say "I don't know why I did that" and mean it. - Let one metaphor be bad and let it stay. - Let him notice the wrong thing during the kiss. **Cut what the plan is proud of.** - The burning match. The "stays" ending image. The "Tom becoming the thing he loved" — that's a thesis, not a feeling. If the story works, the reader gets there without being told.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention The story stays what it was: Tom Rusnak, locksmith, South Side of Pittsburgh, fall 1996. Cal Mercer walks in wanting a safe opened. Marcus is dead six weeks, Linda has the house, the safe holds letters and it holds money and Cal knew. Cal leaves with the money. Tom stays. That spine is sound and it serves the prompt — a steady man narrating the mistake he chose. What changes is everything around it. **The line.** It opens the story, but it isn't wisdom. It's the sentence Tom has been saying to himself for months, and the story is him testing whether it's true. He'll say a version of it to Cal's face in Chapter 3 as a joke, and Cal won't laugh, and Tom will know he's got something wrong. The story never confirms which one of them the line is really about. **Voice.** First person, past tense, retrospective but *partial*: Tom knows how it ended for him. He does not know if Cal is alive. He admits, more than once, that he doesn't understand why he did a thing. The prose is plain and precise most of the time — a careful man's sentences — but it's allowed to run on when he's shaken, allowed to be flat for a paragraph of facts, allowed one metaphor per chapter that's a little too much and stays. No wisecracks. Real jokes, though: Cal is actually funny, and Tom is funnier than he thinks. **Tom is worse than the plan had him.** He lies to Cal about a small thing in Chapter 2 and never corrects it. He's jealous of a dead man. He reads the letters out of that jealousy, not tenderness. He says one genuinely cruel thing about Marcus and can't take it back. He steals the ring — steals it, from Cal — and doesn't have a reason. He calls the hotel after Cal is gone and hangs up. He's dignified in public and not in private. **Cal is less explicable.** There is no confession scene. He tells the Doyle story twice, on two nights, and the versions don't match; Tom picks one and knows he's picking. Cal watches game shows with the sound off. He talks about his mother in Ohio. He does one kind thing that serves no plot purpose. When he asks Tom to come, neither Tom nor the reader gets to know if he meant it. **The queerness lives in the body.** Kowalczyk says "roommate" and Tom watches himself agree. Tom was once not let into a hospital room and never says whose. His father knew, or found something, and the shop is the silence they kept about it. Lucky's has a back door and a reason for it. None of this is explained; it's the weather Tom lives in. **Linda is not handled with tongs.** She's angry at her brother and she is partly right. She says something about Cal that's ugly and also true. Tom overcharges her in Chapter 8 and the story doesn't scold him. **Menace is mundane.** Doyle's man is polite, buys a padlock, and knows Tom's father's name. Nothing happens to Tom. That's the threat. **The crime goes wrong stupidly.** Tom stops working mid-job because of a photograph. He cuts his hand on the Mosler. They leave something behind. **The sex is in the story.** One direct paragraph in Chapter 5. It's awkward — Tom hasn't in years. Afterward Cal smokes and talks about Marcus and it's the loneliest Tom has been. **Structure is lumpy on purpose.** Chapters don't all get one clean turn. Chapter 6 is short and mostly Tom doing inventory. Chapter 7 is two scenes badly joined. The matchbook from Chapter 1 never comes up again. The ring is stolen in 7 and mentioned once more, flatly, in 8, and not explained. **The ending is not noble.** Tom lets Cal go, or Cal just goes and Tom's narration dresses it as a choice — the story leaves that open. Tom smokes now. The prose doesn't tell you what that means. The last line isn't about Cal. **Avoid:** callbacks that click shut, the theme stated as a thought, the burning match, "Tom staying" as image, "becoming the thing he loved," rain more than twice, any sentence that explains 1996. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Tuesday.** Opens on the line, then undercuts it: Tom saying he's been saying that to himself and isn't sure it's fair. Shop near closing, first cold rain. Tom's life in facts: the ledger in his father's hand, the apartment upstairs, the display safe with nothing in it, eight years off cigarettes and still counting. Cal comes in wet with a key that fits nothing and asks about Moslers, residential, fifties. Won't say where. Tom says no and means it. Cal is funny about being told no — a real joke, and Tom laughs and hates that he did. Cal buys a padlock he doesn't need and asks, on the way out, if Tom's father is the Rusnak on the sign or if he is. Tom says his father. That's the first lie; his father's been dead four years. Cal leaves a matchbook. Tom throws it out. Upstairs, doesn't smoke. **Chapter 2 — Lucky's.** Friday. Tom goes to the bar he goes to twice a month, sits where he sits, notes the back door and who uses it. Cal's there. Not a coincidence, and Cal doesn't pretend it is. He tells it: Marcus, the restaurant on Murray, nine years, the aneurysm on a Tuesday, the funeral where Cal sat at the back and Linda's husband nodded at him like a caterer. The locks changed while he was at work. One exchange establishes what Cal is legally, and Tom knows the answer before Cal says it — Tom has stood outside a door like that. He doesn't say whose. Cal says letters, photographs, a ring. Tom says no, slower. Cal mentions his mother in Ohio, unprompted, and it's the least noir thing anyone says all night. Tom drives him to the residence hotel on the North Side with the neon that says HOT L. Cal's hand on the dash the whole way. Tom drives home across the bridge and sits in the van with the engine off for a while and doesn't know why. **Chapter 3 — Beechwood.** Tom drives past the house on his own, tells himself it's a route. Linda and her husband putting black bags at the curb. He waits till they're in and takes a coat from a bag — a man's overcoat, good wool, cigarettes in the pocket. Brings it to Cal's room. The TV is on with the sound off, a game show. Cal isn't grateful. He's petty and mean about it, says Tom doesn't get to bring him his dead boyfriend's clothes like a dog with a bird, and Tom says something back that's worse — about what Marcus must have thought, leaving nothing to him. Silence. Cal puts the coat on anyway and can't talk. Tom says yes. Later at Tom's stove, Cal lights a cigarette off the burner and Tom says the line — smoke and bad ideas — as a joke. Cal doesn't laugh. He says, "Which one of us." First kiss, and Tom notices the wrong thing during it: the coat still smells like the other man. **Chapter 4 — The Mosler.** The job. Rear Schlage his father could have done drunk. Study, and the safe, and for two pages Tom is completely himself — the wheel pack, the contact points, the way his father taught him to listen with his fingertips. Then a photograph on the desk: Marcus and Cal at somebody's lake, young, and Tom stops. Just stops. Cal has to say his name twice. Tom slips on the last wheel and opens his knuckle on the dial and bleeds on the blotter and they don't clean it. The door opens: letters, photos, the ring in a box, and eleven banded stacks. Tom looks at Cal and Cal isn't surprised and Cal doesn't pretend to be. Headlights. They take it all. On the porch Tom realizes the padlock from Chapter 1 is on the kitchen table where Cal set it down, and they leave it. The van with his name on it, on that street. **Chapter 5 — Upstairs.** Two a.m. Not a confrontation — Tom is too tired and too scared to shout. Cal tells the Doyle story: Marcus borrowed to keep the restaurant open, died owing, a man at the funeral. Tom asks why he didn't say, and Cal says he did, he said letters, and there were letters. Tom hides the money in the display safe downstairs, the one that's never held anything. Then the sex, one paragraph, direct: Tom's hands not sure where they go anymore, Cal patient about it and then not, and something Tom didn't know he wanted and can't name after. Afterward Cal smokes at the window and talks about Marcus — how he cooked, a thing he used to say — and Tom lies there and it's the loneliest he's been in a room with another person. He reads one letter while Cal sleeps. It's real. He reads it because he's jealous, and he knows that. **Chapter 6 — Inventory.** Short. Three days. Tom does the fall inventory because it's what he does. Kowalczyk comes about a break-in in Squirrel Hill — a van, clean entry — and says "your roommate" about Cal, having asked around, and Tom hears himself say yes, roommate, and the word sits in the shop after the cop leaves. A man in a good coat buys a padlock, pays exact, and says his father knew Walt Rusnak, sorry to hear. That's all. Cal tells the Doyle story again that night on the phone and one detail is different — the amount, or who was at the funeral — and Tom notices and picks the first version and knows he's choosing. Cal doesn't come the next night. Tom does the blinds. He is not a wise man; he's a man counting deadbolts. **Chapter 7 — Eleventh Street.** Two scenes, badly joined. First: Cal at the door at three, cut over his eye, coat on. Doyle's man was at the hotel. He needs the money and the 5:40 south. He asks Tom to come. Tom will never know if he meant it. Tom asks him something stupid — did you ever, with Marcus, this — and Cal says that's not a question you ask a person, and Tom knows. He opens the display safe. While Cal's in the bathroom Tom takes the ring out of the box and puts it in his own pocket, and doesn't know why, and says nothing. Second scene: the car, the bridge, the station. Cal hands him a lit cigarette without asking and Tom takes it after eight years and it tastes like nothing. Cal gets on. Doesn't look back, or does once and Tom's not sure. The bus goes. Tom sits in the lot until it's light. **Chapter 8 — Rekey.** Three weeks. Kowalczyk stopped. The man in the good coat came once more, asked, and Tom said he didn't know, and it was true, and the man could tell, and left. Linda comes in for a rekey on Beechwood, doesn't know Tom from anyone. She says her brother was always careless with money and with people and she's not sorry the boyfriend's gone, and part of it's ugly and part of it's right, and Tom charges her forty over. The letters were in the coat Cal took — gone. The ring is in the drawer with the ledger. He doesn't take it out. He called the hotel twice the first week and hung up. First snow at closing. Tom smokes at the counter now, most nights; he doesn't make it stand for anything and neither does the story. He locks up. Last line is about the shop, or the cold, or his father's hand in the ledger — not about Cal.

# Tom Rusnak **Background.** Born 1955, South Side, the row house on Sarah Street where the shop still is. Walter Rusnak — Walt — opened Rusnak Lock & Key in 1958 after coming back from Korea and deciding he'd had enough of the mill. Tom's mother, Helen, did the books until she died in 1979; the ledger is still in her hand for the first twenty years and in Walt's for the next thirteen and in Tom's since 1992. Tom was going to leave. He had a year at Pitt, 1973–74, and a boy there named David who is the reason he came home — not because it ended badly but because it didn't end, and he couldn't stand what it was turning him into in front of his father. He told Walt the money had run out. Walt said fine and handed him a Schlage cutaway and that was the whole conversation. He has never told anyone about the hospital in 1988. A man he'd been seeing for eleven months — not David, someone from Lucky's named Ray, a bus mechanic — went into Mercy with pneumonia that wasn't pneumonia, and the sister at the desk asked Tom what he was to the patient and Tom said "a friend" and she said family only. He stood in the hall for four hours and went home. Ray died in February. Tom quit smoking the week after, and he's never made the connection out loud, and he counts the years anyway. **Personality.** Careful is the word he'd use. Cowardly is the word he uses at three in the morning. He's good with his hands and bad with his face; he has a way of going still when something lands, which people read as calm and which is actually a kind of hiding. He notices everything about a lock and nothing about what he's feeling until later, sometimes years later, and then he'll be doing something ordinary — sorting key blanks — and it'll arrive whole. He's funnier than he knows. He says dry things under his breath to customers and doesn't hear them as jokes. He's a small liar — not about anything that matters, about things that don't, which is worse: he'll say his father's alive, or that he's been to Cleveland, and then be stuck with it. He does this to keep a door closed and then can't find the key. **Idiosyncrasies.** Still sets two places at the counter upstairs sometimes without thinking. Listens to Pirates games on the radio in the shop even in the off-season — there's nothing on, he just leaves it tuned. Won't use the display safe for anything; it was Walt's and it's for show. Keeps eight years of not smoking on a page in the back of the ledger, a tick mark for every month, and has never told anyone what the marks are. Says "yeah, no" and "I'll tell you what" and then doesn't tell you what. Eats standing up. **Flaws.** Jealous in a way that surprises him — of the dead, of anyone who got to be someone's without hiding it. Passive to the point of letting things happen so he can say he didn't choose them. Petty when hurt; will say the one thing that cuts and then go quiet like he didn't. Takes things — small things, a coat from a trash bag, a ring — and can't explain it, and doesn't try. **Physicality.** Six feet but stands like five-eleven. Big hands, scarred at the knuckles, always clean under the nails because he scrubs them with a brush his father used. Going grey at forty-one in a way that looks like he did it on purpose. Reading glasses he takes off whenever someone comes in. Wears his father's canvas work coat because it fits. Moves slowly and precisely; doesn't gesture; when he does touch someone, it looks like a decision. **Motives and relationships.** He wants — he'd never say this — to be let into a room. He tells himself he wants the shop to keep going and not to be noticed. Lucky's twice a month is the whole of his social life; he knows the bartender, Denise, well enough that she pours without asking and not well enough that she knows his last name. He owes nothing to anyone and is starting to understand that as a failure. **Voice.** > "I told him no. I want that down somewhere. I told him no twice, in two different rooms, and I meant it the first time." > "My father could feel a wheel drop through a pair of work gloves. I've never known if that was true or just a thing he said to make me practice. I practiced." > "Roommate. That was the word he used, and I heard myself say yeah, roommate, like I was correcting his spelling. It sat in the shop after he left. I did the blinds around it." # Cal Mercer **Background.** Calvin Mercer, 36, born in Zanesville, Ohio, the second of three boys. Father sold farm equipment; mother, Dot, still lives in the house and still sends birthday cards to the restaurant address because he never told her it closed. Left Ohio at nineteen for Columbus and then for wherever; tended bar in four cities, waited tables in six, got a real estate license in Baltimore and let it lapse. Came to Pittsburgh in 1987 because a man he was seeing was moving there; the man left within a year, and Cal stayed, because by then he'd met Marcus Hale. Marcus was ten years older and owned Hale's, a forty-seat place on Murray Avenue that did a chicken paprikash people drove in from Monroeville for. Cal started as a waiter and ended as something the restaurant didn't have a title for — front of house, bookkeeper, the one who knew which suppliers you could stall. Nine years. They lived in Marcus's house on Beechwood, the one Marcus's parents left him, and Cal's name was on nothing, and it hadn't mattered because who thinks about that. The restaurant was dying for two years before Marcus was. Cal knew about Doyle. He didn't know how much until after. **Personality.** Charming the way some people are tall — it's just a fact about him, and he uses it because it's there. He can make anyone laugh and knows exactly when he's doing it, and there's a flatness behind his eyes while it's working that Tom sees on the second night. Underneath is a man who's tired in a way that isn't about sleep. He's been the pleasant one in other people's lives for a long time and has started to suspect he doesn't have another setting. He lies by omission, fluently, and thinks of it as kindness — not making people carry what they don't need. He is genuinely grieving and genuinely calculating and does not experience these as contradictory. He can be mean when cornered, cruel in a quick precise way, and he hates himself for it in the specific manner of someone who does it anyway. **Idiosyncrasies.** Watches game shows with the sound off — *Jeopardy*, *Wheel* — because Marcus used to yell answers at the TV and the silence is easier than the wrong voice. Smokes Merits, which he knows are a joke of a cigarette; Marcus smoked Camels and Cal switched when they got together so he'd stop stealing them. Reads the obituaries first. Calls his mother every Sunday from a payphone and tells her the restaurant's fine. Straightens things on other people's counters. Says "sweetheart" to people he's about to disappoint. Terrible at directions; has lived in Pittsburgh nine years and still gets lost in Oakland. **Flaws.** Uses people softly and calls it survival. Can't ask for anything directly — the whole story is him asking Tom for something sideways. Vain about his charm in a way that's already curdling. Makes the same mistake with the same kind of man every time: the careful one, the one who'll hold still. **Physicality.** Five-nine, narrow, the kind of thin that used to be attractive and is starting to look like something else. Dark hair going in a way he covers with product. A good face going a little soft under the jaw. Beautiful hands — Tom notices them first — long fingers, a burn scar on the left thumb from a sauté pan. Moves like a waiter still: fast, economical, never in anyone's way. Stands too close to people he wants something from and knows he does it. **Motives and relationships.** He wants the letters. He also wants the money. He wants not to be the man who sat in the last pew. Somewhere under that he wants to go home to Ohio and can't, and doesn't know that's what south means. Linda he doesn't hate; he understands her, which is worse. Doyle he's more frightened of than he'll let Tom see until Chapter 7. Tom — he likes Tom. He'd have liked Tom in another life. He's not sure this is the other life or the same one again. **Voice.** > "Sweetheart, I've been told no by better locksmiths than you. Okay, that's not true. You're the only locksmith I've ever been told no by. But I've been told no." > "There were letters. I said letters. You want to check the transcript, there were letters." > "Which one of us." # Marcus Hale (deceased) **Background.** 1950–1996. Only son of a Squirrel Hill pharmacist; grew up in the Beechwood house and never really left it. Cooked because his mother did and he was better at it. Opened Hale's in 1981 with his parents' money and ran it for fifteen years at a margin that only worked while the neighborhood was what it had been. Loud, generous, terrible with money, good at making forty people feel like the room was full. Never came out to his sister in words; brought Cal to every Thanksgiving and let the silence do it. **In the story.** He's a photograph on a desk, a coat, a ring, a stack of letters Tom reads for the wrong reason, and a debt. He's the man Tom is jealous of and the man Tom says a cruel thing about, and the story never lets Tom find out if the cruel thing was true. The letters — written to Cal over nine years, birthdays and anniversaries and one from a hospital bed after a scare in '91 — are warm and a little vain and completely sincere. Marcus called Cal "Kid" in writing and never in person. **Physicality (from photos, from Cal).** Big, bearded, a laugh you could hear from the kitchen. Wore the overcoat every winter for twenty years. **Voice (from a letter).** > "Kid — I don't write these because I can't say it. I write them because you keep them, and I like knowing there's a box somewhere with the whole argument in it. Happy nine. Don't let Sal talk you into the veal. —M." # Linda Hale Brodsky **Background.** 49, Marcus's older sister. Married to Gary Brodsky, an actuary; two kids in college. Lives in Mt. Lebanon and has spent the last fifteen years being the responsible one while her brother ran a restaurant into the ground on their parents' money. She was the one who sat with their mother at the end. She was the one who paid for the funeral. She has been angry at Marcus for a decade and had just about made peace with it when he died and left her a house full of another man's things and a stack of unpaid invoices. **Personality.** Efficient, tired, not unkind by her own account. She isn't a bigot in the way she'd define one; she'd say she didn't care what Marcus did. She did care that he never *said*, that she had to find out from a neighbor in 1988, that at every Thanksgiving there was a stranger at the table she was supposed to pretend wasn't strange. She sees Cal as one more thing Marcus was careless with, and she's not entirely wrong. **Idiosyncrasies.** Labels things. Had the trash bags at the curb sorted — GOODWILL, TRASH — in marker. Calls Cal "the boyfriend" and never his name. Drinks Tab. **Physicality.** Marcus's face on a smaller, tighter frame. Good coat, sensible shoes, hair done every two weeks. Stands with her arms crossed like she's waiting for a contractor to finish. **Voice.** > "He was careless. With money, with people, with himself. I loved him and he was careless, and I'm the one who gets to be the bitch about it. I've made my peace." > "I'm not sorry the boyfriend's gone. I'm sorry that's what I am now. Change the deadbolts too." # Detective Ed Kowalczyk **Background.** 44, Zone 4, burglary. Grew up in Greenfield, three blocks from where the break-in was. Twenty years in. Decent at his job in the way of a man who's stopped expecting it to matter. Knows the South Side; his uncle bought locks from Walt Rusnak. **Personality.** Not stupid, not cruel. Uses "roommate" because it's the word that lets everyone keep their face, and he knows exactly what he's doing when he uses it. He'd probably let this one go anyway — a dead man's boyfriend taking his own letters back isn't a case he wants to make — but he'd like Tom to know he *could*. **Physicality.** Heavy, mustache, raincoat that's seen better decades. Sits without being asked. **Voice.** > "Van like yours. Not saying yours. Saying like yours. Lot of vans." # The Man in the Good Coat **Background.** Never named. Works for Doyle, who is never seen. Fifties, Irish, dresses like an insurance man. Has been doing this a long time and has learned that the quiet version works better and costs less. He is not going to hurt Tom. He wants Tom to spend three weeks understanding that. **Idiosyncrasies.** Pays exact change. Says "sorry to hear" about everything. Knows everyone's father. **Voice.** > "Walt Rusnak. My dad bought a safe off him in '71, still has it. Sorry to hear. You'd be the son." # Walt Rusnak (deceased) He's a hand in a ledger and a scrub brush and a canvas coat. He's the reason Tom came home and the reason Tom never left again. He found something once — a letter, a photograph, the story doesn't specify — in 1980, and put it back where it was, and never said a word, and the shop has been that silence for sixteen years. Tom knows he knew. Tom has never decided if that was mercy or its opposite. > "You can feel it drop. Don't look at the dial. The dial's for the customer."

# Chapter 1 — Tuesday He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas. I've been saying that to myself for going on four months now, and I've started to wonder whether it's true or just something that sounds like it should be. It has the shape of a thing you'd say. My father had a lot of those. You can feel it drop, he'd say, about a wheel in a safe, and I practiced for years before I understood he might have made it up to keep me at the bench. It was a Tuesday in October. I know because Tuesday is when I do the ledger, and the ledger was open on the counter when he came in, and I remember putting my hand flat on the page like he might read it upside down from the door. The ledger is in three hands. My mother's for the first twenty years, small and slanted, every entry ending in a period like she was closing a door on it. My father's for the next thirteen, blocky, pressing hard enough that you can read the numbers from the back of the page. Mine since 1992. I don't know what mine looks like. You don't, about your own. The shop is Rusnak Lock & Key, Sarah Street, South Side. It has been there since 1958. There is a display safe in the front window that my father bought at an auction in Homestead and never put anything in, because it was for show, and I have kept it that way because it was his. There is an apartment upstairs where I live. There is a radio on the shelf behind the counter that stays on the Pirates station in October even though the Pirates are done, and on that Tuesday it was somebody talking about the Steelers' secondary and the first cold rain of the year was going sideways against the front glass. I had quit smoking eight years and seven months before that. I keep a count. There's a page in the back of the ledger with a tick mark for every month, and I've never told anybody what the marks are, and if I'm honest nobody's asked. He came in wet. Not umbrella-wet, walked-from-somewhere wet, his hair pushed back off his face with one hand in a way that was going to look careless and didn't. He was thin. He had on a leather jacket that wasn't warm enough, and under it a white shirt gone see-through at the shoulders, and he stood in the door and let the rain come in behind him for a second longer than a person needs to, looking at the shop like he was deciding whether to buy it. I took my glasses off. I do that. I don't know why. "You're open," he said. "Till six." He came to the counter and put a key down on it. Brass, old, a bit-and-barrel key like nothing's been made in fifty years, the kind you'd find in a drawer and not know what it went to. I looked at it because that's what I do when someone puts a key on my counter. "That doesn't go to anything," I said. "No," he said. "I know. I just like carrying it." He smiled. It was a good smile and he knew it and I knew he knew it, and it worked anyway, which is the thing about a smile like that. "I wanted to ask you about safes." "Buying or opening?" "Opening." "What kind." "Mosler. Older. Fifties, I think. The kind you'd have in a house." "Residential." "Sure. Residential." I looked at him. He had beautiful hands. I want to be clear about the order I noticed things in, because I've gone over it. Hands, then the wet shoulders, then the face, then the smile, and by the smile it was already too late but I didn't know that. On his left thumb there was a burn scar, shiny, the kind you get off a pan. "Where is it," I said. "Where's what." "The safe." He picked the key back up. Turned it over. "Does it matter?" It matters. It's the only thing that matters. A man who owns a safe and can't open it gives you an address. A man who won't give you the address is asking you to do something else. My father had a way of saying no that didn't involve the word — he'd just start putting things away — and I found myself closing the ledger. "I can't help you," I said. "You haven't heard what it is yet." "I don't need to." "It's a Mosler." "I heard." "Three-wheel, I think. I don't actually know what that means. I looked it up at the library and now I say it." I didn't say anything. He looked at me for a while and the rain hit the glass and the radio man said something about Rod Woodson's knee. "Okay," he said. "So that's a no." "That's a no." "Sweetheart, I have been told no by better locksmiths than you." He stopped. "That's not true. You're the only locksmith I've ever been told no by. I don't have a basis for comparison." I laughed. It came out of me before I had anything to say about it, one short sound, and I heard it in the shop and hated it, and he heard it too, and he had the decency not to smile again right away. "Well," he said. He looked around like he needed a reason to have come in. "I should buy something." "You don't have to buy something." "I feel like I should." He pointed at the wall rack. "What's that." "That's a padlock." "I'll take that." He paid cash for a Master No. 3 that he had no use for, and I put it in a paper bag because that's what you do, and he took the bag and stood there. "The sign," he said. "Rusnak and Son. Are you the son or the Rusnak?" "Son," I said. "My father's the Rusnak." My father had been dead four years that August. I don't know why I said it. I've thought about it more than I've thought about most things I've done, and I don't have an answer better than that it was a door, and I wanted it shut, and that was the closest one. He nodded like it was a normal thing to hear. He went out into the rain. He left a book of matches on the counter — Lucky's, the red ones — and I looked at it for a while and then I put it in the trash under the register. I went upstairs at six. I set one plate. I sat with the radio off and the window open a crack for the sound of the rain, and I did not smoke, and I want that down somewhere too.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of literary fiction that demonstrates rare control over voice, pacing, and the architecture of restraint. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Voice and Character** Tom Rusnak's voice is established with remarkable precision from the opening paragraph. The self-interrogation of the opening line — "I've been saying that to myself for going on four months now, and I've started to wonder whether it's true or just something that sounds like it should be" — immediately signals a narrator who is both retrospective and genuinely uncertain, which is exactly what the plan called for. The voice is plain and precise, with the occasional sentence that runs a little long when emotion is present. The observation about the ledger being in three hands is quietly devastating and earns its place. The detail work is exceptional: the tick marks in the ledger that nobody's asked about, the radio tuned to the Pirates station in October when the Pirates are done, the glasses he takes off when someone comes in and doesn't know why. These are not decorative details — they build a man who is defined by private rituals and small concealments. **Cal's Introduction** Cal arrives exactly as planned: charming, slightly too comfortable with being told no, funny in a way that catches Tom off guard. The "Sweetheart, I have been told no by better locksmiths than you" line lands perfectly, and the self-correction that follows is genuinely funny without being a wisecrack. The padlock purchase is exactly right — a man manufacturing a reason to stay. The matchbook left behind and immediately thrown away is a clean, unforced detail. **The Lie** The lie about Tom's father is handled with real skill. "My father's the Rusnak" is delivered flatly, and then the narration simply states the fact: "My father had been dead four years that August." No editorializing, no explanation. The subsequent reflection — "I don't know why I said it. I've thought about it more than I've thought about most things I've done" — is honest without being overwrought. This is exactly the kind of small, inexplicable lie the plan called for. **Potential Weaknesses** The observation about Cal's hands — "I want to be clear about the order I noticed things in, because I've gone over it. Hands, then the wet shoulders, then the face, then the smile" — is a strong moment, but it's also the most self-consciously literary beat in the chapter. It works, but it's the one place where the narrator seems to be performing his own interiority rather than simply inhabiting it. This is a minor criticism. The ending — "I did not smoke, and I want that down somewhere too" — is a callback to the earlier "I told him no. I want that down somewhere" construction from the character profile, and it works as a closing note, though it's slightly too neat in its symmetry. The chapter plan called for Tom to go upstairs and not smoke, and this delivers that, but the "I want that down somewhere" framing, used twice in close proximity, risks becoming a tic. **Dialogue** The dialogue is excellent throughout. It's economical, character-specific, and does real work. Cal's voice is distinct from Tom's narration without being cartoonish. The exchange about the Mosler — "Three-wheel, I think. I don't actually know what that means. I looked it up at the library and now I say it" — is perfect: it's funny, it reveals character, and it establishes Cal as someone who does his homework while maintaining plausible deniability. **Adherence to Plan** The chapter follows the plan closely and faithfully. The matchbook is left and thrown away (as planned, never to return). The lie about the father is told. Cal buys the padlock he doesn't need. The rain is present but not overdone. The "Rusnak and Son" question is handled exactly as planned. The chapter ends with Tom upstairs, not smoking, having set one plate — a detail not in the plan but entirely consistent with the character profile's note about setting two places without thinking. **Queerness** The queerness is present in the body and the weather, as intended. Tom's careful notation of the order in which he noticed Cal — hands first — does real work without announcing itself. The single plate at the end is quietly eloquent. **Overall Assessment** This is a chapter that knows exactly what it's doing and does it without waste. The prose is controlled, the voice is distinctive, the character work is precise, and the tonal register — melancholy, dry, occasionally funny — is maintained throughout. It's not a flashy chapter, but it's not trying to be. It's doing the harder thing: establishing a world and a narrator that the reader will trust for seven more chapters. # Chapter 2 — Lucky's I go to Lucky's the first and third Friday. I don't know when that started. It's on Carson under a dentist's office, down a half flight of stairs, and there's a front door on Carson and a back door on the alley, and the back door is the one most people use, and I have never once asked anybody why. You know why. It's a thing you know without being told, like which stair creaks. Denise pours me a Rolling Rock when I come in and doesn't say anything. She's poured for me for nine years and I don't think she knows my last name. I sit at the end of the bar by the wall where you can see both doors, which is not a thing I decided to do so much as a thing I've always done, and I nurse the one beer, and around ten I have a second, and around eleven I go home. He was already there. He was at a table, not the bar, with his back to the wall and a glass of something brown, and he saw me come in and lifted the glass an inch and didn't smile. That's what I noticed. Tuesday he'd smiled at everything. Friday he lifted his glass an inch and waited to see what I'd do. I want to say I thought about it. I sat down at the bar. Denise poured. I drank about a third of the beer looking at the mirror behind the bottles, where I could see him not looking at me, and then I picked up the bottle and went over, because if I'd stayed at the bar I'd have had to keep doing that all night. "This isn't a coincidence," I said. "No." "You asked around." "I asked Denise what you drank. She said the green bottle and to leave you alone." He moved his jacket off the other chair. "I'm not very good at leaving people alone. It's been mentioned." I sat. He told it straight. I'll give him that, and I've gone back over it enough times to know what I'm giving. He told it like a man who'd told it before to himself in a room with the sound off. Marcus Hale. The restaurant on Murray Avenue, Hale's, forty seats, a chicken paprikash that people drove in from Monroeville for. I knew the place. I'd never been. Nine years — he said the number and then said it again, like it was a thing he had to check was still true. The house on Beechwood Boulevard that had been Marcus's parents'. "Okay," I said. "I'll do it." He nodded at the wall. --- I don't know how we got to my kitchen. He came, is all. It was near midnight. He straightened up and let the smoke out at the ceiling and looked at me. I said it as a joke. I want that understood. I said, "You're all cigarette smoke and bad ideas," in the voice you use for a joke, and I was smiling when I said it. He didn't smile. # Chapter 4 — The Mosler The back door was a Schlage. I'd known it would be. Squirrel Hill in 1996 is Schlage or Kwikset and the Brodskys weren't Kwikset people, and I stood on the back porch under a light that wasn't on and put the pick in and thought about my father saying he could do a Schlage drunk. He said it once, at Thanksgiving, to a cousin. I don't think he was ever drunk in his life. It took me eleven seconds. I know because I counted, because counting is a thing you do with your mouth so your hands can work. He stood behind me with the flashlight off. He'd wanted to bring it on. I'd said no, and he'd said okay, and that was the last thing either of us said for a while. The kitchen was clean. Not lived-in clean — cleared. There were squares on the wall where things had been and the counters had nothing on them but a bowl of keys and my padlock, still in its paper bag, which he'd carried in for some reason I didn't ask about and set down on the table like he was home. The stove was a six-burner Garland. I looked at it longer than I should have. The study was at the front of the house, off the hall. He knew the way in the dark and I followed him and there was a moment on the stairs where his hand found the rail and stayed on it, just stayed, and I waited. Then he went up. The Mosler was in a closet behind a rack of coats, and the coats were gone, so it just sat there. Green. About the size of a small refrigerator. Nineteen fifty-something, three-wheel, the dial worn to brass at nine and three where somebody's fingers had gone for forty years. I got down on the floor in front of it and put the flashlight in his hand and said, "On the dial. Don't move it," and he didn't move it. I want to tell you about the next part, because it's the only part of any of this where I knew what I was doing. You set the wheels. You go all the way around three times to pick them up, and then you go slow. There's a place on a dial where the nose of the lever touches the wheels — the contact area — and when you're in it the dial feels different under your fingers. It doesn't click. People think it clicks. It goes soft. My father used to say you can feel it drop, and I spent years thinking that was a lie to keep me at the bench, and it's not a lie. It's just not a click. It's more like the floor giving a quarter inch. I found the contact area at eight and went back and set the first wheel. Then the second. I wasn't thinking about him. I want that on the record too. For about nine minutes he wasn't in the room, and the house wasn't anyone's, and I was a man with a job and my father's hands and nothing else, and it was the best I'd felt since Ray, and I'm not proud of that. I was reaching for the third wheel when I saw the photograph. It was on the desk, in a frame, the only thing left on the desk. The flashlight caught the edge of it. Two men at a lake, on a dock, both in swim trunks, both younger than anybody in that room. The big one was laughing at something off to the side. The thin one was looking at the big one. He had his hand on the big one's shoulder, and it was the hand — I knew it by the thumb, even then, even in that light. I stopped. I don't mean I paused. I mean I stopped, with my fingers on the dial, and looked at the picture, and some amount of time went by. I've tried to figure out how much. He said my name. I didn't hear it as my name. He said it again, "Tom," lower, and I came back into the room like a man coming up out of water and my hand was on the dial and I didn't know where the third wheel was anymore. "Sorry," I said. "Don't." I went around again to pick up the wheels. I was going fast now. I found the contact area and went back and I felt the third one go and my hand kept going, I don't know why, it just did, and the dial has a lip on it and my knuckle caught it wrong and opened up. Not a bad cut. A cut. I looked at it. Blood came out in the ordinary way and ran down the back of my hand and I pulled the hand back and it dripped, three or four drops, onto the desk, onto the green blotter, and made three or four dark places there and stayed. "Jesus," he said. "It's fine." "You're bleeding on the —" "I know what I'm bleeding on." I wrapped it in my shirttail and did the third wheel again and turned the handle and the door came open the way they do, heavy and quiet and all at once, like it had been waiting to. Letters. A stack the height of my hand, rubber bands gone soft, typed envelopes. Photographs in a shoebox. A ring box, blue, the hinge kind. Those were on the top shelf. The bottom shelf was money. It was banded. I'd never seen banded money outside a bank. Eleven stacks, I counted later, hundreds and fifties, in a canvas bag with the top folded back like somebody had wanted to be able to see it. I looked at it. Then I looked at him. I've gone over his face more than I've gone over anything. He wasn't surprised. That's all. He didn't do the thing people do when they see money — the intake of breath, the hand toward it. He looked at it like he was checking it was still there. Then he looked at me and saw me looking, and he didn't pretend. I'll give him that too. He could have. He just held the flashlight and let me see him not be surprised. Headlights came down Beechwood and slowed. We didn't talk. He put the letters in the coat, inside, against his chest. I looked at the door. I'd have to pick it again to go back. The headlights were in the driveway two houses down. We left it. Stood in the back, in a coat. I knew him, I'd seen him at the restaurant twice. He didn't say anything. He didn't have to." "Why didn't you tell me."
