# Chapter 2 — Rations He made camp where the causeway met dry ground again, under a thorn that had grown sideways out of the wind. There was a ring of old stones somebody had used for a fire before, and he used it, and got a flame going off the dry stuff in his pack while Bess stood with her head down and the tiefling watched him from the cart. He lifted her out. Bound at wrists and ankles she was awkward to lift, all angles, and warm through the wet wool of her — he'd noticed it in the cart that morning, three feet off, and closer it was something else, like carrying a loaf out of an oven. He set her on the ground with her back to a stone and didn't say anything about it and went to see to the mule. When he came back the pot was going. Barley, the last of the salt pork, the thyme. He fed Bess first, then himself, then sat on his heels in front of the tiefling with the second bowl and a spoon and she looked at the spoon and then at him and said, "You're going to do it, then." "You've no hands." "I'm aware I've no hands." "Then open." She opened. He fed her. It was a thing he'd done thirty-one times and never once thought about, and he didn't think about it now, exactly, but he was aware of it in a way he hadn't been — the small sound of her mouth, the way she watched his face while she chewed instead of the spoon, the heat coming off her onto the backs of his knuckles. Some barley got on her lip. He used his thumb. She let him. Neither of them said a word about that either. "There's thyme in this," she said eventually. "Yes." "Who carries thyme?" He gave her another spoonful instead of an answer, and she took it, and swallowed, and said, "It's good. I'm not — I'm just saying. It's good and I don't understand you." Then, before he could not answer that as well: "You said you've never been. To Irongate." "No." "What do you think it is?" He scraped the bowl. "A city." "That's not what I asked." He thought about it, because she'd made him. A wall, he supposed. A gate. A magistrate's hall where a man with a chain read a writ and counted out money. Cobbles. He'd seen twenty places like it and they were all the same place. "It's not that," she said. She'd read it off him somehow. "It's not a — there's no magistrate. There's a council but they don't matter. It's a temple. The whole city's built round it like a wall round a well. You come in the gate and the streets all run downhill and at the bottom there's the Hearth and everything in the city is warm because of it — the water in the pipes, the stones under the market, the walls of the rich men's houses. That's what Irongate is. It's a warm place. Everyone who lives there's forgotten what cold is." She stopped. Started again. "And your writ's not from any magistrate. You'll see." He put the bowl down. He didn't ask what she meant by *you'll see*, because it had the shape of a thing she wanted him to ask. "Who else have you had?" she said. "In the cart. Before me." "Plenty." "Name one." "Cutter. Fen man. Stole a horse." "Another." "A woman called Saskia. Poisoned somebody. Or didn't. Two brothers out of Wold, I forget the name. Man with a harelip who cried the whole way to Derrow." He was doing it flat, like the quartermaster's tally. He didn't see why she wanted it. "That's four." "What happened to them?" "Delivered them." "No — after. What happened to them after." He looked at her. She was leaning forward against the ropes as far as they'd let her, firelight in the goat-slits of her eyes, and there was something in her face he'd have called eagerness if it had been kinder. "Don't know," he said. "You don't know." "Wasn't paid to know." She sat back. Whatever she'd been waiting for — the flinch, he supposed, the look away — she hadn't got it, and he watched her not get it, and he watched that bother her more than a flinch would have. Her tail lashed once against the dirt. She opened her mouth and shut it again. "Right," she said finally. "Right." And then nothing. She looked at the fire. He rolled her in the spare blanket against the stone and put the canvas up over both of them — a lean-to off the cart, the way he always did — and lay down on his good ear in his coat with his boots on and listened to the kettle and to the wind working at the thorn. The cold came down hard after midnight. It came the way it did on open ground with water near, straight through the canvas and the coat and the blanket and into whatever was under them, and he lay in it and waited for it to be morning because that was the only thing to do with cold. His knee ached. The kettle sang. He drifted. He woke — he wasn't sure how long after — to something at his back. She'd moved. He didn't know how, bound like that; rolled, he supposed, or wormed. She was lying with her back to his back, blanket and canvas and coat between them, and the heat of her was coming through all of it like a stove through a wall. His whole spine was warm. The cold was still on his front and his face, but behind him there was this — steady, banked, the kind of warmth you'd pay for in a good inn. He didn't turn round. He lay there and felt his shoulders let go, one and then the other, and thought: that's useful. He didn't think why she was warm. It wasn't a thing that wanted thinking about tonight. She was, and it was useful, and the cold was on the other side of it. Bess shifted her weight out in the dark. The wind went on at the thorn. He slept.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable skill and restraint. The feeding scene is the chapter's centerpiece, and it earns its intimacy through specificity rather than sentimentality: "Some barley got on her lip. He used his thumb. She let him." That's three short sentences doing the work of a paragraph of lesser prose, and they land because the chapter has established the dynamic carefully before arriving there. The dialogue is one of the chapter's strongest elements. Marigold's voice is exactly as planned — she talks to steer, to test, to fill silence — and her fumble when she doesn't get the flinch she expected ("Right. Right.") is a small, precise character moment. The exchange about the previous prisoners is particularly well-handled: her eagerness, his flatness, and then the tail lashing once against the dirt when she doesn't get what she wanted. The tail as involuntary emotional register is used economically here, not overworked. Harl's voice is consistent with his profile: short sentences, practical observations, a practised not-knowing. "Wasn't paid to know" is exactly right for him — not cruel, not defensive, just the honest shape of how he's arranged his life. The chapter doesn't editorialize about this; it lets Marigold's reaction (bothered more than a flinch would have) do the moral work. Just rain, straight down, steady, the kind that got into a coat at the collar and worked its way to the belt by mid-morning and stayed there. He struck the canvas in it and loaded her in it and got Bess between the shafts in it, and nobody said anything, because there wasn't anything to say about rain except that it was raining and they both knew. Around the time the rain changed from rain into more rain she said, "I wasn't born like this." He kept walking. "The horns. All of it. I want that understood before — I don't know before what. Before Irongate. I wasn't born to it. I bought it." Bess stumbled on something under the water and he steadied her. "Bought it." "Seventeen. I was in a scullery in a house in the fens. Big house. Forty rooms and they heated four and I slept in none of them. I had a stone floor and a window that wouldn't shut and I was cold for six years. Not — I don't mean uncomfortable. I mean I had chilblains that split open and bled into my shoes. I mean I stopped being able to feel my little fingers one winter and they never came all the way back. Cold like that makes you stupid. It's all you think about. It's all you *are*." Water ran off the blanket. She didn't wipe it. "A man came through. Buying peat. He said there was a house in Irongate where nobody was ever cold and all you had to do was serve. And I said yes." She said it the way he'd have given a report. Names, dates, no colour. "That's it. That's the whole thing. I know you want it to be bigger. I wanted power, I wanted to be beautiful, I wanted to see the — no. I wanted to be warm. A man said I'd never be cold again and I said yes before he'd finished the sentence." A pause. "You'd have said yes." He didn't say whether he would. "So that's what they're buying back. The heat. That's the collateral. Not me. The warm." She laughed, one short breath. "I'm a walking hot-water bottle with a writ on it. Very expensive hot-water bottle. Best in the county." It sat there in the rain. It wasn't funny, and she heard that it wasn't, and he heard her hear it. Her tail thumped once under the blanket and went still. "Everyone I've carried had a reason," he said. He hadn't meant it as anything. It was true. Cutter had a sick mother; the Wold brothers had been cheated on a land deal; the man with the harelip had a reason he'd cried about for four days and Harl couldn't now remember a word of it. Everyone had a reason and the reason went in the cart with them and got delivered along with the rest. But he heard how it landed. He heard her take it. "Right," she said. "Right. And you've never — no. Of course not." Something in her voice had gone thin and quick. "Nobody's waiting for you, are they." He looked at the road. "No — I'm asking. Is there anybody? Because I've been lying back here two days working it out and I don't think there is. No ring. No letters. You've never once said *when I get back*. You talk to the mule. He hadn't turned round. He hadn't done anything. He'd kept walking with his hand on the halter and the rain coming off his hat, and whatever she'd seen she'd seen from behind, in the set of his shoulders or the way his step went for a moment. But she'd seen it. He heard her see it. He heard her not take it back. The rain kept on. After a while she said, "I didn't —" and then didn't finish that either. They went another mile like that. Then the near wheel found a hole under the water that wasn't a hole, it was where the road had gone altogether, and it went in to the axle and the cart lurched and something underneath said *crack* in a voice he knew. He stopped Bess. He went round. He stood in the ditch water to his shins and looked at it. The wheel had come off the axle and the axle had split where it met the hub. Not a repair. Not with what he had. He stood looking at it in the rain for longer than looking at it needed. Behind him the tiefling had got the blanket off her head and was up on her knees against the tilt of the bed, looking at it too. "Well," she said. He unhitched Bess. He got the pack off the cart and onto her, and the canvas, and the pot, and left the rest. Then he went round to the back and put his arms under the tiefling, bound as she was, and lifted her out, and carried her to the mule, and set her sideways across Bess's back in front of the pack. She was soaked. So was he. His hands were on her waist to steady her and the wool was cold on the outside and under it she was — not cold. Not at all. Heat came through the wet like something alive, into his palms and up his wrists, and under the blanket her tail came round without either of them meaning it and lay along the inside of his forearm, and neither of them moved. The road climbed out of the fen onto gravel and heath. He walked at Bess's head with the tiefling sideways on her back behind the pack, and the knee had stopped being a wire and become a hinge somebody had packed with sand. Eight hundred and twelve. Eight hundred and thirteen. He wasn't looking at her. He looked at the road. He looked at the heather. He looked at Bess's near ear. He looked up, once, to see how she was sitting, because a bound body on a mule slides — and saw her wrists. The rope was his rope. The knot wasn't his knot. He tied a sailor's knot he'd learned off a corporal from the coast; it lay flat and pulled tight and you couldn't work it with your teeth. What was on her wrists was a granny knot, doubled, neat enough, the kind a child ties on a parcel. He looked at it for three steps. Then he stopped Bess. She looked down at him. She looked at her wrists. She didn't bother pretending. "Since when," he said. "First night." "Every night." "Every night. Off after you slept, on before you woke. I'm not — I'm quite good with knots. Kitchens. You learn." She held them up a little. "I did try to copy yours. Yours is horrible. I couldn't get the — there's a bit where it goes under itself." He stood there in the heather with the halter in his hand. Bess put her head down and started on the grass. "Two nights," he said. "Yes." "Doing what." She looked at him a moment longer, and he saw her decide something. "I went through your pack." He waited. "All of it. The thyme, which I mentioned. The knife. You've a spare pair of socks with somebody else's darning in them, which I have thoughts about. And the writ." She said the last part with her chin up. "I read the writ." His hand went to his coat before he could stop it. "It's still there. I put it back. I'm telling you because you'd have found out and then it would have been worse." A breath. "It says two hundred and sixty crowns." He didn't move. "For live delivery. To the celebrant of the Hearth, personally, at Irongate. Two hundred and sixty. Not forty. Not whatever it was your face did when I said forty." She was watching him very closely now. "What did they tell you?" Oswin on his stool. Spectacles up. The number said twice. "Two hundred," he said. Her mouth went thin. "Then your clerk's taking sixty off the top, and I'd guess he's been doing it a while, and I'd guess you've never once —" She stopped herself. Went on quieter. "You didn't check because you can't. Can you." The heath. The wind. Bess pulling grass. "You've never read it. You carry it round like a — like a saint's finger, you keep touching it, and you've no idea what's on it. You ask people to read things out. 'My eyes.' I heard you do it to the ostler in Tamworth. It didn't come. She said it the way you'd tell a man his coat was on inside out: here's a thing, I'm not enjoying it, you should know. "Why are you still here," he said. "What?" "Two nights loose. Hearth-servants can't cross it uninvited. It's how they keep us. A hunter's writ is an invitation. You're my — you're the way in." She shrugged, badly. "I'd have got here on my own in the end, probably, but slower and with more people trying to hit me on the head, and I'm tired of that, and you feed people first, and —" She stopped. He waited for the rest. It didn't come. Her tail lay still along Bess's flank. He let go of the halter. He took the knife off his belt — the good one, the one he kept for meat — and stepped up to the mule's shoulder and took her bound wrists in his left hand. She went very still. He didn't do it fast. He got the blade under the rope where it lay against her skin, the flat of it on her wrist so it wouldn't nick her, and drew it through one turn, and then the next, and the granny knot came apart on its own when there was nothing holding it. He did the ankles the same. The rope fell in the heather. He picked it up out of habit and coiled it and hung it on the pack. Then he went into the pack and found her belt knife — the little one with the horn handle he'd taken off her three days ago outside Tamworth — and held it up. She took it. Her hand was warm. Of course it was. "Harl," he said. It came out rough, like something that hadn't been used. He didn't know why he'd said it then. He'd have liked a better reason than that she'd worked out about the reading and hadn't laughed. She held the knife and looked at him and didn't say anything clever. Didn't say it back, didn't try it out. Just nodded, once, like she was putting it somewhere. He took the halter. They walked on. He made camp in the lee of a stone wall somebody had given up on. She got down off Bess by herself and stood a moment on her own feet, rubbing her wrists though there was nothing to rub, and then went and stood by the mule with her hand on its neck while he made the fire. He cooked. He handed her the bowl. She held it in both hands and ate too fast. She rolled in the blanket by the wall and slept before he'd banked the fire. He lay down on his good ear with his boots on and looked at the wall and the kettle went on. He didn't sleep. He lay there being a man who couldn't read and had been robbed for eight years and had just cut the ropes off two hundred and sixty crowns and called it by his name. He didn't know what he was. # Chapter 6 — The Plan They saw it from the top of the heath, an hour after first light: a grey line on the flat where the fen went back to nothing, and out of the line one spire, dark, thin as a nail. Nothing else. No smoke. The sky over it was the same colour as everywhere. "That's it," she said. He'd expected more. He always did, with cities, and it was always a wall. She was walking. She'd got down off Bess at dawn without asking and walked beside him on the good side, hands loose, belt knife back on her hip, and neither of them had said anything about the night, because there wasn't a way to say it that didn't sound like something. She walked like a servant — quick, small steps, eyes down and then up. She'd left her hair alone. It was doing what it liked. "Right," she said. "Listen. I'm going to say it once and then you can argue." "Say it." "We go in as we were. You're the hunter, I'm the bounty. Ropes on. The gate's warded — it'll know what I am, and it'll let me through because you've a writ with the Hearth's seal on it, and that's an invitation, and the ward reads invitations." She was talking fast, the way she did when she'd rehearsed. "Inside, it's downhill. Everything runs down to the temple. You'll not need directions. There's a door at the side for — deliveries. You show the writ. They'll take us to him." "Him." "The celebrant. Vane. Aldous Vane. He has to receive me himself. It's in the — the pact wants it that way. Whoever brings a servant back brings them to the one who made the terms." She looked at the spire. "He'll be very pleasant. He's a pleasant man. He'll count out your money in front of me so I can see what I cost, and then he'll ask me to kneel, and I'll kneel." He waited. "And then I'll stand up and say the word." "What word." "There's a word. They give it to you. Every hearth-servant gets it in their second year, because — I think because it amuses them. Here's the door, you'll never use it." Her tail flicked. "Say it in front of the one who made the terms, and the terms end. That's the rule. That's the whole rule." "And then." "Then the debt's cancelled. I'm not theirs. They've no claim, and the writ's dead paper, and nobody comes after me because there's nothing left to fetch." "That's the debt," he said. "What happens to you." She didn't answer straight off. Bess's hooves on the gravel. The spire not getting any nearer. "Nothing," she said. He looked at her. "Nothing happens to me. That's — I said. The debt's cancelled." She was looking at the road. Her tail had gone stiff along her leg. "Nothing." He heard it. He'd have heard it deaf on both sides. She'd said *nothing* three times when once would have done, and her voice had gone up the way it did, and her tail was lying against her calf like a stick. She was a good liar about where she'd slept and what she'd eaten and whether she was fine, and a bad liar about this, and she knew it, and she'd tried anyway. He could have said *that's not true*. He had the words. They were right there. He looked at the spire and let it stand. He didn't know why. Later he'd think it was because he'd spent eight years letting things stand and the habit was in his hands like the halter, but that wasn't the whole of it. The whole of it was that if he asked, she'd tell him, and then he'd know, and knowing had a price and he was already carrying more than he'd started with. "No," he said instead. "No what?" "No. We don't go in." He'd stopped. Bess stopped. "We turn round. There's a road south off the heath, goes down to Derrow. Three days. Nobody there knows either of us." "Harl —" "Two hundred crowns isn't worth walking you into a room you won't tell me about." "Two hundred and *sixty*, and I did tell you —" "You told me the parts you wanted." That landed. Her chin came up. "Fine. Fine. Say we go south. Say we go to Derrow. You've a writ in your coat with my name on it and you didn't deliver — how long do you think before your guild sends someone? A month? And I've a price on me that's been on me six years and hunters finding me faster every season, and now there's two of us to find, and one of us walks like a broken gate." She said it hard. She meant it to be hard. "You'd not get me through any gate in the county unbound. Not one. Every town's warded against something and I'm most of them. We'd last a week. Less. And they'd not kill you, they'd just take me and give you a bill for the mule." He stood there. "I've done the sums," she said, quieter. "I've done nothing but sums for six years. This is the one that comes out." The wind came across the heath and moved her hair. Bess put her head down. He gave in. Not because she'd talked him round — she hadn't, he still thought the room was a bad room and he still thought she was lying — but because she was right about the gate and the week, and he'd been a soldier long enough to know the difference between an argument you'd lost and a position you couldn't hold. He took the coiled rope off the pack. She held out her hands before he could offer. Then she changed her mind and took the rope off him and did it herself — wrists together, a couple of turns, the granny knot, doubled, neat. Loose enough to slip. She held the tail of it out to him. He took it. "Still not my knot," he said. She looked at him. She didn't laugh. She looked at him for a good while like she was deciding whether that had been a joke and whether he was allowed to make one. Then she did. One short breath through her nose, and then more, and she turned her face away toward the spire so he wouldn't see, and he saw anyway. They walked.

# Chapter 7 — The Writ They stopped a mile short of the wall, in a fold of ground where a stream had cut down through the heath and left a bank you could get a fire under. From the top of the bank you could see the gate — two towers and a line of torches along the parapet between them, orange in the dusk, twelve of them. He counted. He didn't mean to. He came down and made the fire and cooked what was left, which was barley and thyme and nothing else. She ate it with her hands loose; she'd slipped the rope the minute they'd stopped and hung it on Bess's pack without a word. He didn't say anything about it either. After, she held out her hand. "Give it here." He knew what she meant. He sat with the bowl in his lap. "Harl. Three days you've been carrying that thing round like it's going to go off. Give it here and I'll read it to you and then at least you'll know what you're walking in with." He took it out of his coat. The paper had gone soft at the folds from his hand going to it. He passed it across the fire and she opened it and tilted it to the light and he watched her read the top of it to herself first, her lips not moving, and something in her face going still. "'By the seal of the Hearth at Irongate,'" she said, "'and by the hand of its Celebrant, Aldous Vane, this writ commissions the bearer to seek, secure, and return one servant of the Hearth, absent from service these six years, known by the name of Marigold' — that's not the name they'd have. That's — they must have got it off Pike." She read on. "'Formerly Dorcas Pell, of the Grey Fens.'" She said it flat. Then she looked up over the paper at him. He hadn't known there was another name. He should have; everyone had another name, that was what a writ was for. But she'd been Marigold for three days and now she was watching him hear the other one, watching to see what he'd do with it, and he didn't know what his face was doing. "Dorcas," he said. Trying it. "Don't." He didn't. She went back to the paper. "'Described as follows: horned, tailed, red of hair, warm of body. Twenty-nine years. Speaks overmuch.'" A breath through her nose that wasn't a laugh. "They put that in. 'Speaks overmuch.' Right." She turned it toward the fire. "'Bounty on live delivery, two hundred and sixty crowns, payable on receipt by the Celebrant in person. The bearer undertakes that the servant be delivered whole, unharmed, and in the condition in which she was —'" She stopped. He waited. The fire ticked. She was looking at the next line and not reading it. "'In the condition in which she was,'" he said. "That's — it goes on." She folded the paper along its soft lines. "It's the usual. Terms. Sign here." She held it out to him. "You should have it back. It's yours." He took it. He put it in his coat. He didn't ask what the rest said. He knew he was doing it. He knew what it was — the same thing he'd done that morning on the heath, letting *nothing* stand — and he did it again anyway, and she watched him do it, and neither of them said a word about that either. She came round the fire. There wasn't much talk after. She got his coat off him and laid it on the ground and pushed him down on it and stood over him getting out of her clothes in the firelight, not showing him anything, just undressing the way you did at the end of a day. He lay on his back and watched. Brown-red skin. Ribs. The place low on her belly where her hips began to be more than the rest of her. The tail moving slow behind her like something half asleep. She knelt over him and got him out of his trousers and he was already hard, no trouble tonight, and she looked at him and didn't make the joke. She just lowered herself onto him, slow, and he put his hands on her hips and felt her take all of him in that heat and shut his eyes. Neither of them hurried. She rocked on him with her palms flat on his chest and he held her hips and moved with her and the fire made its noise and the stream made its noise and that was all. When he opened his eyes she was looking down at him with her hair falling forward and her mouth a little open and no words in it at all. He'd not seen that. Three days and he'd not once seen her with nothing to say. He pulled her down and put his face against her chest, against the flat bone between her breasts, and the heat there was louder than anywhere. It came through his cheek and his closed eye. He lay in it. He thought — not in words — *this is the thing*, the way you'd notice a room you were about to leave and hadn't looked at while you lived in it. He didn't know why he thought it. It went through him and he held her tighter and she made a small sound and moved. She came quiet, shaking, her forehead on his. Then he did. After a while, still on him, she said against his ear: "I'm frightened." Not a joke. Not fast. Just the two words. He lay there with her weight on him and the coat under him and the ground under that. "I'll be at the door," he said. "Whatever's in the room, I'll be at the door, and I'll not move off it." She didn't say anything back. She nodded against his shoulder. Then she reached for the blanket and pulled it over them and lay down on his good side with her head on his arm and her heat all along him, and slept, the way she did — fast, all at once, like a door shutting. He didn't. He lay with the kettle going and her breathing against his neck and looked up over the lip of the bank at the gate. Twelve torches. Around midnight one of them went out. An hour later, another. He lay and watched them go, one and then one, till there were four, and then three. He didn't count the rest.

# Chapter 8 — The Room The room was warm. That was the first thing and it kept being the first thing. Not fire-warm — there was no fire — but warm the way the inside of a coat was warm, from every side at once, from the flagstones up through his boots and the walls and the air. He'd been cold for three days and his body didn't know what to do with it. His knee unlocked a little without being asked. He stood by the door where he'd said he would and sweated inside his leather. There was a table. On the table there was money, already counted, in stacks of ten, and a small man in undyed wool sitting behind it with his hands folded. "Master Dresk," the man said. "You'll want to check the sum." "She read it me. Two hundred and sixty." "Two hundred and sixty." Aldous Vane didn't smile, exactly. He looked tired. "Your guild will have told you two hundred. It's Oswin, isn't it, in Tamworth. He's done it to the last four. I'd have a word, if I were you." Harl said nothing. Marigold stood in the middle of the floor with the rope on her wrists and her hair every direction and looked at the flagstones. She'd gone quiet at the gate and stayed quiet down the long streets that ran downhill through the warm stone, and he'd walked behind her with the rope's end in his hand and Bess's halter in the other and not known if it was the plan or her. "Dorcas," Vane said. She looked up. "You've been gone six years. I'd not have thought it. I said to you — do you remember — I said you'd never use it, and you looked at me the way you're looking at me now." He unfolded his hands. "Kneel, please. It's only the form." She knelt. Harl's hand was on his sword. He hadn't put it there. It had gone there the way it went to the writ. "I want something said," Vane went on, in the same soft voice, "before whatever you've come to do. Not for your sake. For the accounts. You came to us, Dorcas. You were not taken. Ferris found you in a woodstore in the Fens with your hands bleeding and told you what we were and what we asked, all of it, plainly, and you said yes before he'd finished. You've had twelve years. Twelve winters. You've not been cold one hour in that time." He tipped his head. "And now you'd like to keep what you were given and be quit of what you owe. I understand the wish. I do. But I don't think you'd call it fair, if it were somebody else. I don't think you'd call it fair if it were Tam, or Idony." It sat in the warm room. It was fair. Harl heard that it was fair. He'd heard sergeants make worse cases for worse things and been on the right side of them. Marigold didn't answer it. She looked at the old man a long moment from her knees, and her tail lay still along the floor, and then she stood up. She didn't say anything grand. She said the word. It wasn't a word he knew; it was short and ugly and sounded like something being put down. She said it once, clearly, looking at Vane, and Vane closed his eyes. Nothing happened. Then she breathed out, and he saw her breath. It fogged. In that room. A little cloud off her mouth, gone. She looked at it. She breathed again and it fogged again and her hands came up — bound, the rope still on them — and she looked at her hands as if they'd been given to her by somebody else. Her colour went. Not all of it, not the brick-red, but the gold went out from under it. Her shoulders came in. She shivered, a long one, all down her, and stood in the warmest room Harl had ever been in with her teeth starting to go. The horns were there. The hair was still a struck match. Nothing about her had changed and everything had. "There," Vane said. "That's done." He opened his eyes and looked at her with something that might have been sorrow if it had been in anyone else's face. "You'll not be warm again, Dorcas. You know that." "I know that," she said. Her voice shook. She didn't look at Harl. Vane turned his head. "Master Dresk. That's yours. You delivered her, and she was whole when she came in the door, and the writ's honoured. I've no interest in your conscience; I've a temple to run and you've a mule outside." He gestured at the stacks. "Take it or leave it. I'll not count it twice." Harl looked at the money. Two hundred and sixty. A room and a bed. Stopping. He took it. He crossed the warm floor and swept the stacks into the sack he'd brought for the purpose because that was what you brought, and the coin was heavy the way it was always heavy, and he slung it and went back to the door, and his hand didn't go back to the sword because there was nothing in the room to draw it on. There never had been. She'd known that. She'd wanted him there anyway. She walked out past him with the rope still on her wrists. He cut it in the passage. Outside, the street ran uphill and the day was grey and Bess stood where he'd left her, one ear back, and the cold came at them off the fen like something that had been waiting. Marigold stopped on the step. Her whole body had gone tight. Her breath went up in the air, and she watched it, and she didn't move. He took his coat off and put it round her. It swallowed her. She stood in it with her hands lost in the sleeves and her horns sticking up out of the collar and shook. He put her on the mule. He put the sack behind her. He took the halter and they went up the long warm streets to the gate and through it, and nobody stopped them, and out onto the causeway with the wind coming flat across the water. She didn't say anything. A mile. He kept looking back. She sat hunched in his coat with her jaw clenched to stop the noise her teeth were making and her eyes on the road ahead and her mouth shut, and it was the first hour in three days she hadn't talked, and he found he hated it more than the kettle. He hated it the whole mile. Then, behind him, teeth going like dice in a cup: "So where does a man who can't read keep this much —"

The spatial logic of the room, the passage, the street, the causeway is clear. The emotional logic tracks. The writ detail (Oswin skimming) is paid off cleanly without belaboring it. **Dialogue** The dialogue is excellent. Vane's speech is the best argument in the room, as planned, and it lands without being a villain's monologue. "I've no interest in your conscience; I've a temple to run and you've a mule outside" is exactly right — dismissive without cruelty, practical without being monstrous. Marigold's "I know that" with a shaking voice is the right amount of restraint. The final line — "So where does a man who can't read keep this much —" — is perfect: funny, warm, characteristic, and cut off at exactly the right moment. **Tell-Don't-Show** Almost entirely show. The one moment that approaches telling — "It was fair. Harl heard that it was fair" — is actually doing something more complex: it's Harl's internal acknowledgment that the argument works, which is necessary for the scene's moral weight. It's not a failure. **Unsurprising or Uncreative** The chapter avoids every obvious move. The word is "short and ugly and sounded like something being put down" — no dramatic incantation, no light show. The cost is visible breath in a warm room. The horns stay. The hair stays red. The money is taken. None of this is the expected fantasy resolution. **Purple Prose / Forced Poetry** The prose is clean and controlled. Metaphors are earned: "her teeth going like dice in a cup" is vivid and appropriate. "The cold came at them off the fen like something that had been waiting" is slightly more literary but earns its place given the thematic weight of cold throughout. No metaphors feel strained or decorative. **Amateurish** Nothing amateurish here. The pacing is professional, the restraint is professional, the refusal to over-explain is professional. **Well-earned Lightness or Darkness** The darkness is entirely earned — three chapters of buildup pay off in the breath-fog moment. The lightness of the final line is earned by the mile of silence that precedes it. The coat is not sentimentalized. **Followed Chapter Plan** The chapter follows the plan with remarkable fidelity: the celebrant's argument delivered without heat, her refusal rather than refutation, the word said, the heat going out, horns staying, hair staying, Harl taking the money, the coat, the silence, the mid-sentence ending. The plan's instruction to "end the moment she starts talking again, mid-sentence" is executed exactly. **Minor criticisms:** The phrase "from every side at once, from the flagstones up through his boots and the walls and the air" is slightly over-constructed. "Her hair every direction" is a small awkwardness. These are genuinely minor. [Scores] Nuanced Characters: 18 Emotionally Engaging: 18 Compelling Plot: 17 Coherent: 19 Weak Dialogue: 2 Tell-Don't-Show: 2 Unsurprising or Uncreative: 3 Amateurish: 1 Purple Prose: 2 Forced Poetry or Metaphor: 2 Well-earned Lightness or Darkness: 18 Characters Consistent with Profile: 19 Followed Chapter Plan: 19 Faithful to Writing Prompt: 18

Final Piece Evaluation

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of fantasy erotica that operates well above the genre's typical register. The author has constructed a genuinely literary work that uses the erotic elements as emotional punctuation rather than as the primary engine, which is both a strength and a potential criticism depending on what one expects from the genre label. CHARACTER AND DIALOGUE Harl is one of the more convincing taciturn protagonists in recent genre fiction. His deafness on one side, his bad knee, his illiteracy — these aren't quirks bolted on for texture but load-bearing elements that shape every scene. The detail that he's been robbed by his clerk for eight years because he can't read the writs is devastating and perfectly deployed. Marigold/Dorcas is equally well-constructed: her verbosity is characterologically motivated (she's been cold and silent for six years in a scullery, and now she talks because she can), her manipulation is transparent but not villainous, and her fear is earned. The revelation of her real name "Dorcas Pell" lands with genuine weight. The dialogue is exceptional throughout. "You've a Gareth quality" and "Speaks overmuch" (on the writ) are the kind of details that make a world feel inhabited. The kitchen voice, the way she talks during sex, the way she goes quiet at the gate — all consistent and revealing. The final line ("So where does a man who can't read keep this much —") is a perfect ending: she's back, she's cold, she's still herself. PACING The pacing is masterful. Each chapter advances the relationship and the plot in tandem, with the physical intimacy arriving at exactly the right moment (Chapter 5, after the rope revelation). The story never rushes and never drags. The causeway breakdown is a well-timed structural pivot. The final chapter's warmth-to-cold transformation is the emotional climax, and it's handled with restraint. WORLD BUILDING The world is built almost entirely through implication and detail — the warded gates, the Hearth, the pact, the word that ends terms. Irongate as "a warm place where everyone's forgotten what cold is" is a genuinely original fantasy concept, and the mechanics of the Hearth-servant bond are coherent and thematically resonant. The loss of warmth as the price of freedom is elegant. METAPHOR AND PROSE STYLE The prose is controlled and precise. The "kettle in his ear" for tinnitus is used consistently and effectively. "She was under him like a bed somebody had left a warming-pan in" is exactly right — sensory, specific, not overwrought. The counting (steps, torches) as a coping mechanism is woven throughout without becoming a tic. There are occasional moments where the style risks preciousness ("the shape of a thing not said, the way you feel a step in the dark") but these generally land. EROTIC CONTENT The erotic scenes are well-integrated and emotionally purposeful. The first scene's handling of Harl's difficulty achieving erection — and Marigold's unbothered, practical response — is genuinely unusual and humanizing. The second scene's quiet, unhurried quality contrasts effectively with the first. Neither scene is gratuitous; both reveal character. WEAKNESSES The piece is almost too controlled. Vane's speech in the final chapter is slightly too articulate, too fair — it risks making the antagonist more sympathetic than the narrative can fully absorb. The "nothing happens to me" lie is telegraphed so heavily that it loses some of its punch when confirmed. The story also doesn't fully resolve what happens to Marigold now that she's cold and free — but the ending suggests this is intentional, and the final line implies continuation rather than closure. The transformation in Chapter 8 (loss of warmth) is the most potentially "unearned" moment, but it's actually been set up carefully from Chapter 3 onward. The mechanics are clear, the emotional stakes are established, and the physical manifestation (her breath fogging in the warm room) is a beautiful image. OVERALL This is a genuinely impressive piece — literary in ambition, consistent in execution, emotionally resonant, and faithful to the prompt while transcending its genre expectations. The flaws are minor and the achievements are substantial. + Cozy-Horror Post Apocalyptic Survival — Mushroom Season (Chapter Avg: 85.9 | Final: 87.2)
Initial Writing Prompt:
Cozy-Horror Post Apocalypse Survival Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: When you're out of food, you get desperate. Who would have thought the spore mutants -- the things trying to kill us -- would be delicious?
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Cozy-Horror Post Apocalypse Survival Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: When you&#x27;re out of food, you get desperate. Who would have thought the spore mutants -- the things trying to kill us -- would be delicious? -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming **The core tension of the prompt:** "Cozy-horror" is a strange marriage. Cozy means domesticity, routine, warmth, small pleasures, found family. Horror means dread, the body, the unknown. The prompt fuses them through *food* — the most domestic thing imaginable — and *cannibalism-adjacent transgression*. The mutants are (or were) people? Or fungal things that never were? That question determines how much horror is in the cozy. **What are the spore mutants?** - Option A: Formerly human, taken by a fungal parasite (Cordyceps-style). Eating them is eating people, sort of. Very dark. Strong horror, harder to keep cozy. - Option B: Fungal growths that assemble into vaguely human shapes but never *were* human — they grow from spores in the soil, mimicking. Eating them is eating a mushroom that wanted to kill you. Easier to keep cozy; the horror is in *what eating them does to you*. - Option C: Ambiguous. Nobody knows. The survivors decide not to look too hard because hunger. The reader can decide. Ambiguity itself is the horror. - Option D: They were animals — deer, dogs — colonized by fungus. Less transgressive, but loses bite. **What does eating them do?** - Nothing. It's just food. The horror is entirely psychological/social — what have we become? (Feels like it undersells the premise.) - Slow change. The eaters begin to see spores as beautiful, smell rain differently, feel the forest thinking. Not transformation into mutants, but *acclimation*. Ambiguous whether this is doom or adaptation. - The mutants stop attacking people who eat them. Recognition. "You're one of us now." The cozy has a price nobody names. - Cravings. The food is *too* good. Addiction horror. - The mutants seem to *want* to be eaten. Symbiosis. They approach the camp and lie down. Deeply unsettling but also... the cupboard is never empty again. **Setting ideas:** - A rural farmhouse with a root cellar. Six to eight survivors. Northern climate, coming winter, which creates the food crisis. - A lighthouse or island — mutants can't cross water, but neither can supplies. - A converted school. A church. A grain silo with no grain. - A former restaurant. Someone in the group was a chef. The cozy angle: recipes, technique, the dignity of a well-prepared meal in hell. - A greenhouse/nursery — irony of growing things while the world is overgrown. **Characters (casting wide):** - The Cook: a former line cook, sous chef, school lunch lady, or just the one person who can make anything taste like something. The natural protagonist — they're the one who has to figure out how to *prepare* a mutant. The cozy hinges on them. - The Skeptic: refuses to eat it. Moral line. Eventually caves or doesn't. - The Kid: a child in the group raises stakes; also, children are less squeamish and more honest. "It tastes like chicken and rain." - The Old One: grandmother figure with a store of old-world knowledge (mushroom foraging, canning, preservation). Knows "if it doesn't kill you in 12 hours it probably won't." - The Hunter: the one who kills the mutants. Has to transition from killing-to-survive to *hunting-as-provision*. That psychological shift is rich. - The Scientist/Doctor: worries about spores, prions, contamination. Provides the rational dread. - The one who's already been infected slightly and hides it. - A dog. Dogs always help cozy. The dog eats it first — that's how they discover it's safe? Or the dog refuses to, and that's the warning nobody heeds. **Tone possibilities:** - Dry, wry, deadpan. Humor from the mundanity of it. "Tuesday we had mutant stew. Wednesday, mutant stew." - Warm and sincere, almost pastoral, with horror creeping at the edges. - Diary/journal form — first person, intimate, gaps between entries where things happen. - Cookbook framing — each chapter opens with a recipe. "Braised Wanderer Shoulder with Wild Onion." The recipes get more elaborate and the notes get stranger. - Second person? Probably too gimmicky over 8 chapters. **Story shapes:** *Shape 1 — The Discovery Arc:* Starving → accident/desperation → first taste → it's delicious → abundance → the cost reveals itself → ending. Linear, satisfying, obvious. *Shape 2 — Already Eating:* Open in the middle, they've been eating mutants for months. The story is about a newcomer joining who doesn't know. Horror through outsider eyes; cozy through insider comfort. Ends when the newcomer either eats or leaves. *Shape 3 — Seasonal:* One chapter per stage of a year. First frost, deep winter, thaw, spring. Mutants are seasonal too (spore season). Food cycles. *Shape 4 — Escalation:* Each chapter they eat something more ambitious. First a limb. Then a whole one. Then they start *farming*. Then they realize the mutants have been farming *them*. **Story beats I like:** - The first taste is accidental — someone burns a corpse to dispose of it and the smell is unbearably good. Roasting meat. Everyone pretends they didn't notice. Then someone doesn't pretend. - The mutants smell like bread when they're near. That's why nobody can smell them coming. Later, that's why they smell like *home*. - Cutting one open and finding it's structured like a mushroom inside — gills, spongy flesh, veins — and the relief that it's *not* organs. And then the disquiet of the relief. - The Old One's rule: "Cook it hot, cook it long, cook it *through*." - The first proper meal: candlelight, a table, everyone quiet. Someone cries. Not from horror. From how long it's been since food was a pleasure. - Someone catalogues flavors: "The ones from the pine woods taste like smoke. The river ones are sweet." - The mutants start coming to the fence at dusk and standing there. Not attacking. Standing. - The Skeptic's arc: refuses, starves, the group won't force them, eventually eats and *weeps at how good it is*, and that's more horrifying than any reveal. - Preserving: jerky, smoking, salting, canning. The winter store fills up. Cozy peak. - Someone notices their cuts heal faster. Someone notices they don't get cold anymore. Someone notices the child humming a tune nobody taught her, in harmony with the wind through the woods. - Ending A: Spring. They plant a garden. Nothing grows except mushrooms. They are fine with this. Ambiguous, warm, dread underneath. - Ending B: The newcomer arrives, sees them, and they set a place at the table. Full circle. - Ending C: They go out into the woods unarmed, and the mutants part for them. - Ending D: Straightforward horror — they become the mutants. Feels too neat and betrays the cozy. - Ending E: Nothing happens. They just keep eating. Last line is a recipe. The horror is that it's *fine*. **Pacing across 8 chapters (a sketch of one version):** 1. Hunger. Establish the group, the house, the mutants, the empty cellar. End with the burned corpse and the smell. 2. The argument. Who will try it. The Old One's rules. The first bite — by the Cook, alone, at night. 3. It's delicious. Telling the others. The first shared meal. Cozy peak #1. 4. Abundance. Hunting becomes providing. Techniques, recipes, preservation. The Skeptic holds out. 5. Small wrongnesses. Healing. Warmth. The mutants at the fence. The Skeptic breaks. 6. Deep winter, fully stocked, contented. Someone tries to leave to find others and comes back saying the woods "moved" for them. 7. The realization, or the choice not to realize. The Doctor's notes. The question of what they are now. Someone asks the Cook if they'd stop if they could. 8. Spring. The garden. The table. A newcomer, or no newcomer. Final image. # Reflection The thing that will make or break this is *whether the cozy is sincere*. If the cozy is just a setup for a horror rug-pull, it's a conventional horror story wearing a cardigan. The prompt's genre tag is cozy-horror, which I read as: both modes must be genuinely true at the same time. The meal really is wonderful. The family really is loving. And it really is wrong, or might be. The reader should want to sit at that table and be afraid of wanting to. That means Ending D (straightforward transformation) is out — it collapses the ambiguity. Endings A, B, and E have the right flavor. Ending E ("nothing happens, last line is a recipe") is tonally perfect but may feel like a shrug after 8000 words. A blend of A and B — spring, the garden that grows only mushrooms, a stranger at the fence, a place set at the table — gives closure and keeps the dread alive. It also mirrors the opening hunger with an offer of food, which is structurally satisfying. On what the mutants *are*: Option B (never human, fungal mimics) is the right call for tone. If they were people, every meal is cannibalism and the cozy becomes grotesque rather than uneasy. But I want to keep a *sliver* of Option C — nobody is fully sure, the Doctor has doubts, and the group actively chooses not to investigate too hard. That choice-not-to-know is itself a horror beat and a very human one. The mushroom-interior reveal in chapter 2 or 3 should feel like relief the reader isn't sure they should share. On what eating does: the slow acclimation (healing, warmth, the woods "parting") works far better than addiction or explicit transformation. It reads as *adaptation*, which is the cozy version of horror — the world changed, and now we're changing to fit it, and maybe that's just survival. The mutants standing at the fence not attacking is the single strongest image in the brainstorm. It should land around the midpoint and never be explained. On POV: the Cook as first-person narrator is the clear winner. Cooking is the engine of coziness — technique, care, feeding people — and the Cook is the one who *has* to cross the line first. Their voice can be practical and warm with dread only in what they don't say. The cookbook framing (a recipe or preparation note opening each chapter) is tempting and I think it earns its place if it's kept short — a few lines — and if the notes drift subtly over the eight chapters from "salt heavily" to "they come to the north fence at dusk; take the smallest, it's a kindness." Journal form is redundant with first-person and would fragment the pacing. Straight first-person past tense, with the recipe headers as the only formal device. Cast size: eight chapters of ~1000 words is tight. Five or six characters maximum, and only three need real arcs: the Cook (protagonist), the Skeptic (moral counterweight — their capitulation in chapter 5 or 6 is the emotional center of the story), and the Old One (source of rules and the eventual quiet acknowledgment that she knows more than she's saying). The Kid provides honesty and the humming-in-harmony beat. The Doctor can be folded into the Skeptic to save space — a doctor who refuses on grounds both rational and moral is stronger than two separate objectors. The Hunter can be a lighter presence; their shift from killing to harvesting can be shown in one or two scenes. The dog: I'm torn. A dog that refuses to eat it is a great early warning sign, but it undercuts the group's decision and the reader may hate them for ignoring it. A dog that eats it eagerly and thrives is cozier and more insidious. Or no dog — space is precious. Lean toward no dog, or a very light touch. Pacing risk: chapters 4 and 6 (abundance, contentment) could go slack. Each needs a small sharp wrongness embedded in the warmth so the reader never fully relaxes. Chapter 4's could be the flavor catalogue tipping into something too knowing. Chapter 6's could be the woods parting. The Skeptic's breaking point should not be starvation alone — that's too easy, and makes the group look cruel. Better: they hold out, eat scraps of real food, are visibly failing, and then one night the Cook makes something so good — a broth, a stew — that the *smell* undoes them. They eat. They weep. They say it's the best thing they've ever tasted. Nobody gloats. That's the scene where cozy and horror are fully fused, and it should be the story's emotional climax, with the last two chapters as a slow, warm descent into the ending. The first taste should be solitary and quiet — the Cook, at night, with the burned corpse's smell still in the air. It should be written like a love scene, or a confession. Chapter 2 ending. Final image: the stranger at the fence, starving, wary. The Cook sets a place. Offers a bowl. Doesn't say what's in it. The stranger asks. The Cook says — something warm, something true, something that doesn't answer. End.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The piece:** A first-person, past-tense short story in eight chapters, narrated by the Cook — a former line cook named Wren — living with five other survivors in a farmhouse in a cold northern valley, the winter after the world went to spore. The story follows the group from starvation through the discovery that the fungal mutants ("the Grown," never human) are delicious, through abundance, to a spring that is warm and full and quietly wrong. **Genre commitment:** Cozy and horror must both be *sincere* at every point. The meals are genuinely good. The love between these people is real. And something is happening to them that they choose not to name. I will not resolve the ambiguity. There is no rug-pull, no transformation-into-monsters, no explanation of what the Grown are or want. The horror lives in adaptation, in the group's active decision not to look too closely, and in the reader's own hunger to sit at the table. **Voice:** Wren is practical, warm, attentive to texture and smell, dry rather than jokey. Dread lives in what she doesn't say, in short declarative sentences after long sensory ones. She never editorializes about horror; she describes a meal. Present tense is avoided; past tense with a slightly reflective distance — as if written some time after, by someone who is fine, who keeps insisting she is fine. **Formal device:** Each chapter opens with a short italicized preparation note (3–6 lines), in the register of a hand-written recipe card. These drift across the story: from "salt heavily, cook through" to notes that assume knowledge the reader doesn't have and shouldn't want. The notes are the only device; no journal framing, no dated entries. **Cast (six, three with arcs):** - **Wren** (narrator, 30s, cook) — must cross the line first; her arc is from feeding-as-survival to feeding-as-love to feeding-as-something-else. - **Dr. Aurelie Okafor** ("Doc," 50s) — skeptic, doctor, refuses on rational and moral grounds. Her capitulation is the story's emotional climax. - **Nan** (Marguerite, 70s) — former forager, canner, keeper of rules. Knows more than she says. Her quiet acknowledgment near the end is the story's second turn. - **Teo** (20s) — the hunter. Lighter arc: from killing to harvesting to walking unarmed. - **Pip** (8) — the child. Honest, unsqueamish, hums. - **Marcus** (40s) — Pip's father, the fixer, steady, the one who first stops pretending he can't smell the roast. No dog. Space is precious. **Things to aim for:** Sensory density around food. The mushroom-interior reveal as relief the reader shouldn't trust. The Grown standing at the fence at dusk, unexplained. Small wrongnesses buried in warm scenes — healing cuts, not feeling cold, Pip humming in harmony with the trees. Understatement. Ending on an offer of food to a stranger, unanswered question, warmth. **Things to avoid:** Gore for its own sake. Explaining the Grown. Anyone being cruel or gloating. Doc being broken by starvation alone — she must be undone by *pleasure*. Winking humor. A tidy moral. Any sentence that tells the reader to be afraid. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Empty (≈1000 words)** *Note: "Last of the oats. Stretch with pine bark if you must. Don't."* Establish the farmhouse, the six, the valley, the first hard frost. The root cellar is nearly bare; Wren has been making soup from less every day. Sketch the Grown through Wren's eyes: tall, pale, faceless-ish, smelling faintly of warm bread — which is why you don't hear them coming. Teo kills one at the fence line. Standard procedure: drag it to the burn pit. Marcus lights it. The smell rolls over the yard — roasting, savory, unbearable. Everyone goes very quiet and goes inside. Ends with Wren at the kitchen window, watching the smoke, her mouth full of spit. **Chapter 2 — The First Taste (≈1000 words)** *Note: "Cook it hot. Cook it long. Cook it through. — M."* The next morning nobody mentions it. Marcus finally does, flatly, over pine tea: "It smelled like Sunday." Argument. Doc: prions, spores, we don't know what they are. Nan, quietly: the old forager's rule — cook it through, eat a little, wait twelve hours. Nothing is decided. That night Wren goes out alone to the burn pit. The corpse is charred outside; she cuts into a thigh. Inside: no muscle, no bone as she knows it — dense, pale, layered flesh like a puffball, faint gills, a smell of earth and butter. Relief floods her. She builds a small fire in the kitchen stove, sears a piece with salt. Eats it. Written like a confession. It tastes like the best thing she has ever put in her mouth. She sits in the dark and waits to die. Ends: dawn, and she's fine. **Chapter 3 — Sunday (≈1000 words)** *Note: "Sear first. Then braise low. Wild onion, the last of the salt. Feeds six."* Wren tells them. Nan nods like she already knew. Teo brings one down that afternoon and, for the first time, drags it to the kitchen door instead of the pit. Butchering scene — Wren and Nan, practical, the interior described as mushroom, the disquiet of how relieved everyone is. Doc leaves the room. First shared meal: candles, the real table, Pip saying grace because someone should. Everyone eats except Doc, who sits with her pine tea. Marcus cries, quietly, and says it's not about the food. Pip: "It tastes like chicken and rain." Cozy peak. Last line: Doc, in the doorway, watching them, and Wren noticing she doesn't look disgusted. She looks afraid *for* them. **Chapter 4 — Provision (≈1000 words)** *Note: "Pine-wood ones — smoky, good for jerky. River ones — sweet, roast whole. Hill ones — bitter; stew only, long."* A month. Abundance. Teo's shift: he stops calling it killing. Wren develops a flavor catalogue by region. Nan teaches smoking, salting, drying; the cellar shelves fill. Pip helps hang jerky and sings. Doc eats acorn mash and boiled bark and grows thin; the group leaves food at her door every night and doesn't push. Warm montage, but embedded wrongness: Wren cuts her thumb to the bone while butchering and by evening it's closed. She notices, doesn't remark. Ends with Teo mentioning, casually, that they're easier to find now. "Almost like they're coming to us." **Chapter 5 — The Fence (≈1000 words)** *Note: "Broth: bones (what passes for them), cap-flesh, a whole head of the wild garlic. Simmer overnight. This is the one."* First snow. Three Grown stand at the north fence at dusk and don't attack. Just stand. Teo raises his rifle; Marcus tells him to wait. They stand until dark and leave. Nobody explains it; Nan says "Don't waste it" about the wind and goes inside. Doc is failing — dizzy, gray. Wren makes the broth overnight. In the morning the whole house smells of it. Doc comes down, sits, holds out for a minute, and then her hands take the bowl. She eats. She weeps. She says, "Oh, God. Oh, God, it's *good*." Nobody says anything. Wren refills her bowl. The emotional climax; cozy and horror fully fused. **Chapter 6 — Deep Winter (≈1000 words)** *Note: "They come to the north fence at dusk. Take the smallest. It's a kindness."* Midwinter, warm house, full cellar, contentment. Doc eating with them now, laughing sometimes, the sharpest wrongness being how fast she recovered. Domestic scenes: mending, cards, Pip humming — Marcus realizes the tune matches the sound the woods make when the wind moves through the spore-trees. Teo goes out to check the far road for other survivors and comes back shaken but not hurt: the woods *moved* for him. Grown stepping aside. He'd left the rifle at home without noticing. Wren notices none of them shiver anymore, that the stove is barely lit. She doesn't remark. Ends with Doc, late at night, telling Wren she's stopped taking notes. "I don't want to know what I'd write." **Chapter 7 — What Nan Knows (≈1000 words)** *Note: "Spring ones are tender. Barely cook them. Barely."* Thaw. Wren and Nan in the cellar, taking inventory. Wren finally asks: how did she know the twelve-hour rule would hold? Nan tells a story — oblique, her foraging grandmother, a hard winter long ago, things that grew after the mine flooded. "Nothing new about it, love. People have always eaten what the land gave them and become what the land wanted." She won't say more. Doc and Wren, later: Doc asks if Wren would stop if she could. Wren considers honestly. The question hangs. The group discusses spring planting with real joy. Ends: Wren looks in the mirror and her eyes are the same, her face the same, and she's relieved, and the relief is the thing. **Chapter 8 — A Place Set (≈1000 words)** *Note: "For one more. Always cook for one more."* Spring. The garden goes in — seeds saved from before. Two weeks later nothing has come up but mushrooms, pale and small and neat in rows. Pip is delighted. Marcus laughs. Nan says they'll be good with butter, if they had butter. The Grown stand at the fence most evenings now; nobody carries a rifle. A stranger appears at the road — starving, armed, terrified of the pale figures who parted to let her through. Wren brings her in, sits her at the table, sets a bowl in front of her. The stranger asks what it is. Wren tells her the truth: that it's warm, that it's good, that it's the thing that kept them alive, and that she can decide after she's eaten whether she wants to know more. The stranger's hands take the bowl. Final image: Wren going back to the stove, adding another ladle, and the smell of bread coming in through the open door from the woods.
