# Chapter 8 — Rows The thaw came in March and took the snow off in four days, and then it rained for a week, and then one morning the yard was mud and the fence posts stood in it dark and dripping and the ridge behind the house had gone from grey to something with green in it. Nan had seeds. I found them in a coffee can on the pantry shelf behind the jars, in envelopes she'd made from folded newspaper and labeled in that leaving hand — *beans, Kentucky wonder. Tomatoes, the good ones. Squash, don't crowd.* Some of the envelopes were from before I'd come. One said *2019*. We put them in on the first dry day. Marcus turned the beds with the spade that had dug her grave and didn't say anything about it and neither did anyone. Pip made the rows with a stick and a string, straight as a ruler, because Nan had said don't crowd and Pip had read it. Doc knelt in the mud in her trousers, which I'd never seen her do, and pushed beans in with her thumb one at a time to the knuckle. Teo carried water from the pump. I stood at the edge with my arms crossed and told people where things were supposed to go, which was what I was for. Pip wrote the names on stakes. Her B's went backwards. Two weeks. Nothing. Then something. I saw them from the kitchen window with the coffee that wasn't coffee — small pale caps along the bean row, a finger high, evenly spaced. Down the row exactly where Pip had put the string. I went out in my socks. They were in the tomatoes too, and the squash, in rows, neat as if they'd been planted, off-white going to cream, with the faint ridging underneath when I turned one over. No beans. Not one bean. Pip came out behind me in her cardigan and stopped at the edge of the bed and put her hands behind her back. "They came up," she said. "Something did." "They're in the *rows*." She was delighted. She looked up at me to make sure I'd seen it. "Wren. They're in the rows." Marcus came out and looked at the beds a long time, and then he laughed. Not much. But it was the first sound like that I'd heard out of him since January, and he stood there in the mud in his socks with his hand over his beard and shook his head and laughed at Nan's garden. Doc came and crouched and pinched one off at the base and smelled the cut. "They'll want butter," she said, and stood, and went in to put the pan on. We ate them that night. Barely cooked — Nan would have said something. They were tender, and they tasted like the river ones did, faintly sweet, and Pip ate hers off the fork one at a time and said they were the babies. Nobody told her not to say it. She'd been going to the corner of the yard past the pump. Every few days, alone, with her hands behind her back. I saw her from the window standing there looking down at the dirt where the ground was still a little higher than the ground around it. One evening she came in and hung up the cardigan and said, to the room, "Nan's coming up." Marcus put down his cards. "In the garden. In the corner. She's the little white ones." Pip climbed onto her chair and sat on her knees. "It's okay. She doesn't mind." I didn't go and look. I've thought about that. I could have gone out the next morning and walked to the corner and looked down and known, and I stood at the sink with the water going instead. Teo went. He came back and washed his hands and sat down and picked up his hand of cards and played the two of clubs, and nobody asked. They stood at the fence most evenings now. Two or three, at the north wire, in the blue before dark, the way they had in November. Nobody went to the step to watch anymore. You'd look up from the dishes and they'd be there, pale against the trees, and you'd go back to the dishes. The rifle was on the hook in the mudroom. Teo cleaned it Sundays. Nobody had carried it out the gate since the thaw and nobody had said so. The woman came on a Thursday, if it was Thursday. Teo saw her from the ridge and came down at a run, and by the time I got to the front step she was at the gate. She had a shotgun in both hands and a pack that had been full once and a face that had gone past thin into something else. She was shaking so hard the barrel of the gun went up and down. "They let me through," she said, before anyone had said anything. "They were — there were dozens, they were all through the woods, they just — they stood aside. They *let* me. Why did they let me." "Come in," I said. "Why did they—" "Come in and sit down." She sat at the table. Marcus took the shotgun out of her hands the way you'd take a thing from a child, gently, and stood it by the door next to the rifle. Doc looked at her hands and her eyes and said nothing. Pip stood in the front room doorway and stared, and the woman stared back, and Pip said "hi," and the woman started to cry. There was stew on the back of the stove. There always was. I filled a bowl and wiped the edge with my thumb and put it in front of her with a spoon. She looked at it for a long time. She picked up the spoon. She ate three mouthfuls fast, the way you do, and then she stopped and closed her eyes and sat there with her jaw working and I watched her chest go in and out. "Oh God," she said. She opened her eyes. She looked at the bowl and then at me. "What is it." "One of them." The spoon stopped halfway. It hung there. I watched it — I watched her hand, and she watched her hand, and behind me nobody at the table moved. Then it finished the trip. She ate. She ate the rest of the bowl without looking up, and when it was done she pushed it toward me an inch and I filled it. I went back to the sink. Tomorrow's was laid out on the board under a cloth, a pine one Teo had brought in that morning, and the last of the wild garlic from the sill in a jar with its roots in water. I turned the tap on and let it run over my hands and looked out the window at the fence, where there were two of them now, in the blue, standing a little apart. The garlic goes in last. If you put it in early it turns bitter. Nan told me that the first week I was here, and it's the one thing I've never once gotten wrong.

[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of writing that executes its plan with precision and restraint. Let me work through the key elements. VOICE AND CRAFT: The first-person voice is consistent and earned throughout. The cook's specificity is maintained without becoming a tic. The final line about garlic going in last is exactly the kind of plain kitchen detail the plan called for, and it lands because it's genuinely true (both as cooking advice and as a closing image that doesn't overreach). The plan explicitly called for "a plain kitchen detail, not an image that was planted" — and the garlic detail was seeded in the plan as something Nan told her, making it feel organic rather than manufactured. CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: Every character behaves exactly as profiled. Doc crouches in the mud in her trousers (a small physical detail that signals her transformation without announcing it), says "They'll want butter" and goes to put the pan on — efficient, clinical, but now participating. Marcus laughs for the first time since January, which is noted without sentimentality. Pip's "Nan's coming up" is perfectly in character — literal, direct, not precocious, and genuinely unsettling in the way the plan intended. Teo goes to look at the grave, comes back, washes his hands, plays the two of clubs. Nobody asks. That's exactly right. FOLLOWING THE PLAN: The chapter follows its plan closely. The garden mushrooms in the rows — check. Pip's delight — check. Marcus laughing — check. Doc wanting butter — check. Pip at Nan's grave saying she's "coming up" — check. Wren not going to look — check. The stranger, the letting-through, the bowl, the question, the answer, the spoon stopping and then continuing — all executed. The final image of the garlic going in last is the plain kitchen detail the plan specified. The rifle in the mudroom, nobody carrying it — check. DIALOGUE: The dialogue is spare and effective. "They came up." / "Something did." — this exchange is perfect. Pip's "They're in the rows" with the italics captures a child's specific delight. "What is it." / "One of them." — the period instead of a question mark on "What is it" is a nice touch, suggesting exhaustion rather than curiosity. "They'll want butter" is Doc in four words. The stranger's "Why did they let me" repeated is appropriately traumatized. None of the dialogue is expository or on-the-nose. HORROR AND COZY BALANCE: The horror is present but not foregrounded. The Grown at the fence in the blue before dark, the spoon stopping halfway, Pip at the grave, Teo washing his hands after looking — these are all handled with the restraint the plan demanded. The "cozy" elements (mud, socks, coffee that isn't coffee, stew always on the back of the stove) are genuinely warm without being saccharine. WEAKNESSES: A few small things. "A face that had gone past thin into something else" is slightly vague — the plan's voice would probably be more specific. The stranger's crying when Pip says "hi" is a little convenient emotionally, though not egregiously so. The line "the way they had in November" is a minor continuity note — it was actually October/November in chapter 1, so this tracks. The phrase "off-white going to cream, with the faint ridging underneath when I turned one over" is good sensory detail. The "blue before dark" is used twice in the chapter (once for the Grown at the fence, once at the end), which is a slight repetition that could have been varied. The Pip/Nan grave moment is handled with genuine restraint — Wren not going to look is a real character choice, and Teo going and washing his hands and playing the two of clubs without anyone asking is one of the best moments in the chapter. It trusts the reader completely. The ending doesn't bow. The garlic line is practical, true, and quietly devastating in context — Nan told her that, Nan is now possibly in the garden, and Wren is thinking about not getting it wrong. It earns its weight without announcing it. OVERALL: This is a high-quality execution of a demanding plan. The writing is controlled, the voice is consistent, the horror is earned, the lightness is earned, and the ending resists the temptation to be beautiful. Minor quibbles about one vague description and a slight repetition don't significantly diminish what is otherwise a near-masterclass in restrained, specific, character-driven prose. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of post-apocalyptic fiction that takes the prompt's darkly comic premise — eating the monsters — and transforms it into something genuinely literary. The narrator, Wren, is a former banquet chef, and this professional identity is deployed with remarkable consistency and intelligence throughout all eight chapters. The cooking knowledge is never decorative; it structures the narrator's perception of everything, from the way she assesses the "breadmen" as ingredients to how she reads people's emotional states through how they eat. CHARACTER WORK The ensemble is well-differentiated and consistently rendered. Marcus is the grieving father holding himself together through ritual and denial. Pip is one of the more convincing child characters in recent AI fiction — her "chicken and rain" line, her backwards B's on the stakes, her matter-of-fact announcement that "Nan's coming up" in the garden, all feel genuinely observed rather than constructed. Teo functions as the group's dark humor and its conscience simultaneously. Nan is rendered with tremendous economy — she's defined by what she doesn't say, by the paring knife in her apron pocket, by "I said long." Doc's arc from principled refusal to reluctant participation is the most carefully constructed transformation in the piece, and it earns its resolution. The narrator Wren herself is the most interesting character — self-aware, professionally competent, morally compromised in ways she acknowledges without excusing. The moment where she admits she didn't kick dirt on the fire, and knows why she didn't, is quietly devastating. PROSE QUALITY The prose is genuinely excellent. The voice is distinctive and consistent — clipped, observational, with a chef's precision about process and a survivor's precision about people. The sentences vary well between short declarative statements and longer accumulative ones. The metaphors are almost always earned: "a hand that slanted like it was leaving," "the way a house smells after that," "pulled the quilt over Nan's face the way you'd pull a sheet over a pan of dough to proof it." These are not decorative flourishes but functional images that carry meaning. There are occasional moments where the prose reaches slightly too hard — "the quiet of a kitchen at four in the morning when the bread's just come out and nobody wants to be the first to speak" is beautiful but perhaps slightly over-deployed as a comparison. The "long pig" moment is handled with appropriate restraint. PACING AND STRUCTURE The eight chapters move with excellent pacing. The story doesn't rush its transformations. The horror of the first chapter (the attack on Nan, the smell from the fire) gives way to the desperate pragmatism of chapter two (Pip eating from the pit), then to the communal meal of chapter three, then to the routinization of chapter four. This is exactly how human adaptation works, and the story honors that process. The January chapter (six) is a masterclass in cozy horror — the card games, the warmth, the rifle on the hook — while maintaining the underlying dread. WORLD BUILDING The world is built through implication rather than exposition. We never get a full explanation of the spore mutants, and we don't need one. The detail that they smell like bread, that they come apart in layers like puffballs, that they're warm, that they step aside for Teo in the woods — these accumulate into something genuinely unsettling and original. The ending, with the woman arriving and the breadmen having let her through, opens the world outward without resolving it, which is exactly right. WEAKNESSES The piece is not without flaws. Doc's transformation, while carefully prepared, still moves somewhat quickly from principled refusal to eating the broth. The "something Doc said to me that I won't write down" moment in chapter five is a slight cheat — it gestures at depth without providing it. The final chapter's arrival of the woman is a somewhat conventional "new arrival" device, though it's handled with restraint. Nan's death, while emotionally effective, is perhaps slightly too neat in its timing and execution. The "Nan's coming up" moment — the implication that Nan has become one of the breadmen — is the story's most daring idea, and it's handled with admirable restraint. Teo going to look and coming back and playing the two of clubs without speaking is perfect. But the story doesn't quite commit to exploring what this means, which is both a strength (restraint) and a weakness (missed depth). DIALOGUE The dialogue is generally excellent — spare, character-specific, and doing real work. "It tastes like chicken and rain" is a genuine achievement. "I said long" is perfect. The Doc/Marcus confrontation in chapter two is well-handled. The only slightly weak moment is Teo's "Long pig" line, which feels slightly too on-the-nose, though the story acknowledges this by having Marcus react to it. OVERALL This is a piece that takes its premise seriously, executes it with genuine craft, and earns its emotional moments. The cozy-horror balance is maintained throughout — the warmth of the card games and the full pantry exists in genuine tension with the horror of what they're eating and what's happening to Nan. The prompt is followed faithfully and creatively. Initial Writing Prompt:
Victorian Romance Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Victorian Romance Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming **The prompt itself:** "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows." The voice is wry, practiced, a little rueful—someone who has done this often enough to call it an art. Victorian Romance as genre. So: who climbs into manors through upper windows in the Victorian period, and why is it romantic? **Possible climbers:** 1. A lady's maid or governess conducting a secret affair with someone in the house—entering to avoid the servants' stair. 2. A cat burglar / gentleman thief who repeatedly targets the same manor and finds himself drawn to its inhabitant. 3. A physician making illicit night visits to a patient whose family forbids treatment (e.g., a woman being "kept" for hysteria, or a consumptive kept from a doctor of the wrong class/religion). 4. A suitor barred by a father—the classic Romeo mode. Too familiar unless twisted. 5. A woman climbing in—to see another woman? A fiancé she isn't permitted to see alone? A brother's friend? 6. A disgraced governess returning to retrieve letters. 7. A young clergyman. 8. A woman who is the *owner's estranged wife*, sneaking in to see her own children. 9. A naturalist/botanist assistant sneaking in to consult a library or a herbarium. 10. Reversal: the climber is a woman, the person inside is a man kept under a form of house arrest—an invalid heir, or a man his family has declared incompetent to control his fortune. **Idea 10 has legs.** Victorian period is full of stories of women locked away; inverting it—a man kept upstairs by a controlling mother/brother who manage the estate "on his behalf"—is fresh. The woman climbing is someone with a practical reason initially: she is a copying clerk, a legal amanuensis, a bookseller's daughter delivering books he's ordered, a naturalist's correspondent. She's plain-spoken, working-class or lower-middle, has climbed trees all her life. The romance grows through repeated visits. **Alternative strong idea—the thief:** A woman thief (Victorian female cracksman is delicious) who enters the same manor three times: first for jewels, second because she left something, third because she cannot stop thinking of the man who caught her and let her go. Fun, brisk, but could tip into caper rather than romance. **Another: the physician.** A young woman doctor (post-1876, when women could register) enters through the window to treat the daughter of the house whose father refuses "lady doctors." The romance is with... the brother? The daughter? The steward? It gets crowded. **Tone options:** - Wry, first-person, retrospective ("One quickly learns...") — narrator looking back with fondness. Allows humor about ivy, drainpipes, torn stockings, the geometry of sash windows. - Third-person close, more gothic. - Epistolary. The prompt's voice strongly suggests first-person wry retrospective. A narrator who has *learned* something, and the learning implies repetition, which implies an ongoing relationship. **Fleshing out Idea 10:** Narrator: Nell (Eleanor) Baxter, 24, daughter of a Cheltenham bookseller/stationer who also does copying and binding. Her father is ailing; she runs the shop. She can climb because she grew up climbing the shop's ladders and the elms behind the churchyard. The manor: Ashcombe, a decaying Gloucestershire house. The man inside: Julian Thorne (or Edmund Vance), 30s, heir to Ashcombe. Following a riding accident and a bout of "brain fever" seven years ago, his elder half-brother Godfrey and mother obtained a lunacy commission's finding of unsound mind, and he is confined to the upper east wing. He is, in fact, entirely sane—melancholic, lame in one leg, sharp, sardonic, a keen amateur entomologist or cartographer. Godfrey controls the money. How does Nell first get in? Julian has been ordering books through the shop for years by letter, smuggled out via a sympathetic old servant (Mrs. Pryce, the housekeeper). When the servant dies/is dismissed, the letters stop. Nell, owed money and curious, comes to the house, is turned away at the door by Godfrey's man. She sees a lamp in an upper window. She's stubborn. She climbs. That's Chapter 1. Then the "art" develops across chapters: the ivy, the leaded roof of the orangery, the loose bar on the nursery window, the particular window whose latch Julian learns to leave open. Each entry a variation, marking time and growing intimacy. **Plot beats:** - Ch1: First entrance. Nell arrives to collect a debt, is refused, climbs, meets Julian. He's astonished, dry, delighted. She learns he is "mad." - Ch2: Second visit—she brings the books he ordered. The rules of the house. Godfrey, the mother (Lady Thorne, cold, perhaps genuinely believes Julian is unwell). Nell notices the laudanum. Julian explains the lunacy finding. - Ch3: Visits become regular. The craft of climbing. Their conversations—his maps of a county he cannot walk, her shop. Growing affection, neither admits. - Ch4: A near-discovery. Nell hides in a wardrobe/on a ledge while Godfrey visits Julian. She hears something that suggests Godfrey's motive—debt, the estate mortgaged, the need to keep Julian declared incompetent before Julian turns 35 and inherits outright under the grandfather's will? Or simply that Godfrey has been selling off Julian's inheritance. - Ch5: Nell's own life—father worse, shop struggling. She meets a solicitor's clerk who explains that a lunacy finding can be challenged (a traverse). She resolves to help. Julian resists—pride, fear. - Ch6: The plan. Nell needs Julian's testimony/a physician's examination. She smuggles a doctor in through the window? Or she takes documents out. Confession of feeling—the first kiss, awkward, on the window ledge. - Ch7: Crisis. Caught. Godfrey finds the rope/ladder. Nell arrested for trespass or threatened. Julian, for the first time in seven years, goes *down* the stairs—or goes out the window himself. - Ch8: The hearing and aftermath. The inquisition traversed; Julian declared sane. Ending: Julian, now master of Ashcombe, insists on using the front door; Nell, out of habit, comes in the window anyway. Or reversed: he climbs to her window above the shop. The art passed on. **Other flavor notes:** Victorian detail—Lunacy Act 1845/1853, Commissioners in Lunacy, "traverse" of an inquisition. Sash windows, casements. Ivy tearing off in sheets. Nell's practical dress—she takes to wearing her dead brother's trousers under her skirts. Julian's cartography—he maps the room, then the view, then imaginary counties. Season progression: October to spring. **Alternative ending twist:** Julian is *not* fully sane—he has genuine episodes—and the romance is about Nell accepting that. Darker, truer, but 8k words may be too short to handle responsibly. # Reflection The thief idea is fun but gives me a caper; the physician is crowded. The inverted-confinement idea (Idea 10) fits the prompt best because the *repetition* implied by "one quickly learns the art" requires a sustained reason to keep climbing, and a confined beloved is exactly that. It also fits Victorian Romance squarely—the gothic house, the wicked brother, the lunacy commission—while letting the woman be the active party, which keeps it from feeling musty. The wry first-person retrospective voice is the right choice: the prompt line practically is Nell's voice. It also lets me handle 1000-word chapters efficiently—she can summarize the weeks between visits in a sentence and dwell on the moments that matter. Humor about the practical difficulties (ivy, skirts, a gutter that gives way) will keep the tone from getting too heavy and make the romance land by contrast. Concerns: eight chapters of 1000 words is tight. The plot must not sprawl—one villain (Godfrey), the mother can be ambiguous rather than a second villain, and the legal machinery should be sketched, not explained. The near-discovery in Ch4 and the actual discovery in Ch7 give structure; Ch5 is the dip into Nell's world so she isn't just an instrument of rescue. The romance needs its own beats independent of the plot: the first laugh, the maps, the kiss on the ledge, and above all Julian *leaving* the room for her—the reversal of who does the climbing. The "is he really sane" question—I'll keep it clean: he is sane, though the seven years have marked him with real melancholy and a dependence on laudanum he's been quietly weaning himself from. That gives him something to overcome without making the villainy ambiguous. The ending should return to the window: the art learned, now unnecessary, but kept out of affection. That's the emotional shape—entering by the window was necessity; choosing to, at the end, is love.

# Intention I'm writing an eight-chapter Victorian romance narrated in first person by Eleanor "Nell" Baxter, a Cheltenham bookseller's daughter who repeatedly enters Ashcombe, a decaying Gloucestershire manor, through its upper windows to reach Julian Thorne—a man declared of unsound mind by a lunacy commission seven years ago and confined by his half-brother Godfrey, who is quietly bleeding the estate. **Voice:** Wry, retrospective, practical. Nell tells this from some years' distance, with the fondness and dry humour of someone who knows how it ended. The prompt line is her voice, and I'll keep that register throughout: concrete about ivy, gutters, skirts and latches; sparing and unsentimental about feeling, so that when feeling breaks through it lands. She summarizes weeks in a sentence and lingers on moments. **Structure:** Each chapter is anchored by an entrance—a different window, a different method, a different season. The "art" develops literally (ivy, orangery roof, nursery bar, rope, the latch he leaves open) and stands in for the deepening of intimacy. The final chapter reverses it: he leaves the room; she enters by choice, not need. **Plot discipline:** One villain, Godfrey. Lady Thorne is cold but ambiguous—a mother who found it easier to believe her son ill. Legal machinery (a traverse of the inquisition, a physician's independent examination) is sketched, never lectured. Julian is sane; the seven years have left him lame, melancholic, and weaning himself from laudanum—real damage without moral ambiguity about the villainy. **Romance beats independent of plot:** the first laugh, his maps of a county he cannot walk, her stubbornness matched to his dryness, a kiss on a window ledge, his going down the stairs for the first time in seven years. **Aim for:** specificity of period texture, humour from physical difficulty, restraint, a satisfying reversal at the close. **Avoid:** melodrama, exposition dumps, a second villain, a saccharine ending, making Nell merely a rescuer—she has her own failing shop and dying father and must be a person with stakes. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 – The Ivy (October).** Nell arrives at Ashcombe to collect eleven pounds owed for books ordered by "J. Thorne" over five years, letters having ceased three months ago. Godfrey's man refuses her at the door: Mr. Julian Thorne sees no one; he is unwell. She sees a lamp in an upper east window. Stubborn and owed money, she goes round by the kitchen garden, finds the ivy, and climbs badly—torn cuff, a fright on a rotten trellis. She comes through a casement into a room lined with books and hand-drawn maps. Julian, thirty-four, in a dressing gown with a stick beside him, regards her without alarm and says something dry about tradesmen's persistence. She learns he is "mad." He pays her from a hoard in a hollowed atlas. She learns Mrs. Pryce, who carried his letters, has died. **Chapter 2 – The Orangery Roof (November).** Nell tells herself she is returning only to deliver the books he'd ordered and never received. She learns the ivy has been cut back—Godfrey noticed—and finds a new route across the leaded orangery roof to a nursery window with a loose bar. Julian explains the accident, the fever, the commission of inquisition, Godfrey's stewardship. She notices the laudanum bottle and that he measures it out reluctantly. She meets, from a hiding place behind the door, Lady Thorne's voice: solicitous, distant, calling him "poor boy." Nell's own life sketched: her father coughing, the shop's ledgers. **Chapter 3 – The Art (Winter).** Visits become weekly. Nell takes to wearing her dead brother's trousers under her skirts; she learns which stones are sound, how to move on frost. Julian leaves the nursery latch open. Their conversations: his maps, first of the room, then the view, then the whole county from memory, with corrections from her. He asks about Cheltenham streets like a man starving. The first real laugh. Neither names what is growing. Nell, riding home on the carrier's cart, realizes she is looking forward to the climb more than the collection of any debt. **Chapter 4 – The Wardrobe (January).** Godfrey comes up unexpectedly; Nell hides in the wardrobe among Julian's old riding coats. She hears Godfrey press Julian to sign something—a lease of the Lower Farm—and hears Julian refuse, and Godfrey's cold reply that a lunatic's signature is not needed anyway; he wanted it only to be "tidy." She hears that the grandfather's will settles the estate outright on Julian at thirty-five, unless the finding stands. Julian's birthday is in June. After Godfrey leaves, Julian is shaking. Nell holds his hand for the first time. She resolves something, silently. **Chapter 5 – The Ground Floor (February).** Nell's chapter at home: her father worsening; a solicitor's clerk named Hobbs who takes his newspapers from the shop and courts her mildly. She asks him, hypothetically, about lunacy findings; he explains a traverse, the need for a petition and an independent physician's certificate. Her father dies. Nell does not go to Ashcombe for three weeks. When she returns she finds Julian gaunt—he had thought she'd stopped. She tells him what Hobbs said. He refuses: pride, fear of failing the examination, the laudanum. She tells him, plainly, that she has just buried one man who would not be helped and does not intend to do it again. **Chapter 6 – The Rope (March).** Julian agrees. Nell brings a rope-ladder for a heavier climber: Dr. Ansell, a Cheltenham physician of radical sympathies, sixty and stout, who is hoisted through the nursery window swearing under his breath. The examination scene—Julian answering questions about the date, the Prime Minister, his own affairs, with a precision sharpened by terror. Ansell signs. Nell and Julian alone afterward on the window ledge, legs over the leads, in the first mild night; the kiss, awkward, his hand on her cheek. She takes the papers out in her bodice. **Chapter 7 – The Stairs (April).** The petition lodged; Hobbs's principal acts. Godfrey learns of it and finds the rope-ladder. Nell arrives to find the nursery window nailed shut and Godfrey waiting below in the garden with a constable, threatening prosecution for trespass and worse—her reputation, her shop. Above, Julian sees her held. For the first time in seven years he opens his door, goes down the stairs on his bad leg, and walks out the front door of his own house to stand beside her and say, to the constable, that Miss Baxter is his guest and always has been. Lady Thorne, in the doorway, says nothing—and does not contradict him. **Chapter 8 – The Front Door (June).** The hearing sketched briskly: Ansell's certificate, Julian's own testimony, Godfrey's debts exposed. Finding traversed; Julian declared of sound mind; the estate his on his birthday. Godfrey removed to a cousin's in Ireland; Lady Thorne to Bath. Julian insists everyone use the front door and has the ivy replanted anyway. Nell refuses, at first, his proposal—she has a shop—until he answers that Ashcombe has a library that wants a bookseller. The closing image: some years on, a summer evening, Nell coming home late from Cheltenham, the front door standing open, and choosing, out of habit and love, the ivy. He is at the window, waiting, having left the latch open.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This A human writer given "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows" would probably start by hearing the sentence out loud a few times and asking who says a thing like that. Not what plot it implies—who. The sentence has a specific music: the impersonal "one," the "quickly," the faintly self-mocking "art." It's the voice of someone who has been embarrassed by the activity and has decided to be funny about it rather than ashamed. A human writer would likely spend the first chapter *earning* that sentence—getting the narrator's voice so particular that the reader believes this person would phrase it exactly so. A human would also probably resist the immediate pull toward a Big Victorian Plot. The prompt is small and comic. The first instinct of a working writer might be to ask: what if the climbing is the whole story? What if nothing much happens except the climbing, and the relationship is revealed through what she notices about the house on the way up—the state of the gutters, whose window is lit, which servants are lazy? A human might write a version that is far more interior and far less eventful than mine, and trust the reader to find that sufficient. Human writers also tend to write from something. Not autobiography necessarily, but a real texture they know—an actual house they've climbed into as a child, the specific feel of a rotten sash cord, the way a wool skirt behaves on a slope. They'd let one or two of these details carry disproportionate weight rather than distributing period detail evenly like seasoning. They would also, crucially, allow the story to be uneven. Some chapters would be nearly all conversation. One might be two pages of Nell walking home and thinking about her father, with the manor barely mentioned. A human doesn't feel obliged to hit the manor in every chapter because the prompt mentions it. # Telltale LLM Approaches and Why They Fail Here **Symmetry and completeness.** LLMs love a structure where every chapter has an "anchor image," every setup is paid off, every character gets a resolution line. Real short fiction is lopsided. My plan gives every chapter a window-title and an entrance. That's a pleasing scaffold but it risks feeling like a template rather than a life. Readers sense when a story is *arranged* rather than *told*. **The tidy ending.** The bow. The villain removed to Ireland, the mother to Bath, the ivy replanted, the latch left open. Everything settled, everyone accounted for, a final image that rhymes with the opening. LLMs do this because ambiguity feels like failure. Humans know that the most affecting endings often leave one thread frayed—a mother who never does apologize, a shop sold with real grief, a leg that never gets better. **Explaining the metaphor.** The plan literally states: "the 'art' develops literally and stands in for the deepening of intimacy." An LLM will then *write that*—will have Nell observe, near the end, that learning the windows was learning him. A human writer trusts the reader to notice and would be embarrassed to say it. **Emotional labeling.** "Nell resolves something, silently." "Neither names what is growing." These are stage directions for feeling. In prose, LLMs tend to render them as "something shifted in me" or "I did not yet have a word for it." Humans render feeling through misdirected action—she cleans the grate, she's rude to the carrier, she buys him a book she can't afford and tells herself it's stock. **Competence porn.** Every character in my plan is good at something. Nell is a good climber, a good bookseller, has the practical mind to think of lawyers. Julian is a good cartographer with sharp wit. Ansell is the exact right doctor. Hobbs conveniently knows about traverses. LLM characters are furnished with skills like a well-stocked kitchen. Humans write people who are bad at the thing the plot needs them to do and have to bumble through anyway. **Villains with motives.** Godfrey has debts, a will, a deadline. That's a mechanism. Real family cruelty is usually lazier and less coherent—Godfrey may genuinely half-believe Julian is odd; he may simply have got used to the arrangement; he may resent that Julian was always the loved one. Mechanism makes for plot; incoherence makes for people. **Wit as default register.** LLMs, asked for "wry," produce a relentless drizzle of dryness—every line a little turned, every observation a little arch. This exhausts the reader and, worse, makes the moments of real feeling indistinguishable from the jokes. Human wry narrators go flat and plain when it matters. The wit is a coping mechanism the reader watches fail. **Over-sensory prose.** The "specificity of period texture" I promised myself often becomes, in LLM hands, an unbroken surface of ivy and leaded roofs and laudanum bottles and the smell of beeswax. A human picks three things and lets the rest of the house be dark. **Dialogue that advances plot.** LLM dialogue is efficient—everyone says what needs saying. Julian would explain the lunacy commission cleanly. Real people, and especially damaged, proud people, don't explain. Nell would have to piece it together from what he *won't* say, from a slip of Lady Thorne's, from something in a ledger. **The active heroine as compensation.** I flagged wanting to "keep it from feeling musty" by making the woman active. But the LLM version of an active Victorian heroine is a modern person in a bonnet—practical, unsentimental, trousers under the skirt, quietly feminist. A human would make Nell a genuine product of 1880s Cheltenham: she'd have real shame about the climbing, real anxiety about being seen, opinions about class that aren't ours, possibly some piety, possibly some snobbery toward the servants who won't let her in. # Deep Dive on the Plan **The chapter titles are a tell.** *The Ivy, The Orangery Roof, The Art, The Wardrobe, The Ground Floor, The Rope, The Stairs, The Front Door.* It's elegant. It's also exactly what an algorithm would produce: a progression from outside to inside, low to high to low, illicit to licit, with the reversal telegraphed by Chapter 5's title. A reader who spots the pattern will wait for it to complete rather than reading the story. Possibly fine as an internal scaffold, but the writing should not honor it too faithfully. **Chapter 1 is too efficient.** Nell arrives, is refused, sees a lamp, climbs, meets Julian, learns he's "mad," gets paid, learns Mrs. Pryce died. That's six plot beats in a thousand words. There's no room for her to be frightened, or to nearly go home, or to sit in the kitchen garden for twenty minutes talking herself into it. The climb itself—the actual physical difficulty the prompt is about—gets a sentence or two. A human might spend four hundred words on the climb and have her meet nobody at all, the room empty, Julian asleep, and she leaves the bill on his desk and goes. He finds it in the morning. The meeting is Chapter 2. **The debt as pretext is good but under-used.** Eleven pounds is a lot of money to a failing shop. In the plan, he pays her in Chapter 1 and the pretext evaporates. Then she goes back for "the books he ordered." Then it's just visits. A human would keep the money live longer—she needs it, he has a hoard, she is uncomfortably aware she's befriending a man who's paying her. That discomfort is more interesting than clean affection. **Julian's dryness is the LLM default charming-invalid.** Sardonic, sharp, self-mocking, secretly vulnerable. He's a type: the Rochester-lite. What if he's less charming? Seven years alone with laudanum and a mother who calls you "poor boy" does not typically produce wit. It produces someone who talks too much when finally given an audience, who repeats himself, who has odd fixations, who is frightening in his gratitude. Nell might not like him at first. She might find him tiresome and a little pathetic and go back anyway because of the money, and only slowly discover the person under the damage. **The maps.** Nice image, slightly writerly. "His maps of a county he cannot walk" is a metaphor that announces itself. Could be made stranger and more particular—he maps the *sounds* of the house, or he's mapping the estate for the purpose of working out exactly what Godfrey has sold, which is both sadder and more plot-useful. Or drop the cartography and give him something less picturesque: he's cataloguing beetles from the windowsill, or he's been teaching himself Portuguese from a grammar for no reason. **The wardrobe scene is stock.** Hiding while the villain monologues his scheme. Godfrey conveniently states the will's terms. This is a Victorian trope, so arguably fair game, but it's the plan's weakest joint. Alternatives: Nell never overhears anything; she works it out from the fact that the Lower Farm's tenant is now a man she knows from Cheltenham who won't meet her eye. Or the overheard conversation is about nothing—Godfrey being ordinarily unkind about Julian's untidiness, his smell—and that banal contempt is what decides her, not a scheme. **Chapter 5 kills the father off-page to motivate her.** The dead-father-as-fuel is a machine part. Either give the death real weight—it needs its own chapter, or Nell's grief needs to be allowed to be ugly and inconvenient rather than clarifying—or don't kill him. A living, querulous father who disapproves of her absences and whom she has to lie to is a more continuous pressure and less of a device. **Hobbs.** A convenient legal clerk who courts her mildly and explains the law. He exists to deliver information and to be the safe alternative she rejects. Pure furniture. Either cut him and have Nell go to a solicitor herself and be humiliated by the fee, or make Hobbs real: perhaps she's already half-promised to him, perhaps he's decent and it costs her something. **Dr. Ansell hoisted through the window swearing.** Comic set-piece. Genuinely fun. But it's the kind of fun that resolves too easily—stout radical doctor, examination, signature, done. What if Ansell isn't sure? What if Julian does badly under examination—freezes, can't remember the year, weeps—and Ansell signs anyway, doubtfully, and Nell has to live with the fact that she may have coerced a certificate? That's a much more human moral knot. **The kiss on the ledge, legs over the leads.** Exactly the image an LLM would choose—picturesque, slightly dangerous, spring night. Fine. But it's the *only* physical beat before the proposal, and it's positioned exactly where structure demands it. Humans put the kiss in the wrong place. In the wardrobe, badly, in Chapter 4, and then don't speak of it for two chapters. Or never on the page at all. **Chapter 7 is the big set-piece and it's a movie scene.** Constable in the garden, villain gloating, hero descends stairs on bad leg, emerges from front door, declares her his guest, mother silent in doorway. It's satisfying and completely predictable from the title of the chapter. It also makes Julian's recovery a single heroic act. Seven years of not going downstairs doesn't end because a plot requires it. What would it actually cost? He might not make it—might fall on the stairs, be found by servants, be carried back up, and the humiliation *is* the turning point because Lady Thorne sees him try. Or he doesn't come down at all, and Nell is prosecuted, and he has to give evidence at the trespass hearing, and that's how he leaves the house—in a closed carriage to a magistrate's court, not in glory. **Chapter 8 tidies everything.** Hearing summarized, villain exiled, mother exiled, ivy replanted, proposal refused-then-accepted with a quip about the library, and a closing image of the latch left open. Every strand tied. The proposal refusal is a fake beat—she refuses so she can accept a page later. The "library that wants a bookseller" line is the sort of clever button an LLM produces and a human editor cuts. And the final image, while pretty, is the metaphor explaining itself: she *chooses* the window now. Yes, we understood. **Class is absent.** A bookseller's daughter marrying into the gentry in 1880s Gloucestershire is a scandal. Lady Thorne would not merely go to Bath; the county would talk; Nell's Cheltenham acquaintances would have opinions. The plan treats class as a barrier for the plot (she's refused at the door) but not as a texture of the romance. A human would feel the awkwardness of Nell in Ashcombe's dining room, of Julian in her shop. **Godfrey has no interiority.** He's the bar on the window. What does he think of Nell? Does he know about her earlier than Chapter 7 and let it go on because he assumes she's Julian's whore and it keeps him quiet? That's nastier and more plausible than a brother who somehow doesn't notice for six months. **Lady Thorne's silence in the doorway is the plan's one genuine ambiguity, and it should be protected**—but the plan then sends her to Bath in the epilogue, which resolves her. Better she stays. Better Nell has to live with her. # Brainstorming Toward the Human - **Start slower.** Chapter 1 is only the approach and the climb. The physical comedy and terror of it—the point at which she realizes she can't get down. Meet him at the very end or not at all. - **Let Nell be embarrassed.** She thinks she's absurd. She doesn't tell anyone. She invents lies for the carrier. She is a respectable woman doing an unrespectable thing and never quite gets over it. - **Let Julian be difficult.** Talks too much, or too little. Smells of the room. Has been alone so long he's forgotten how to have a conversation and interrupts, or lectures, or goes silent for ten minutes. She's not charmed. She's paid. - **Keep the money live.** He keeps paying her. She keeps taking it. This is uncomfortable and they don't discuss it until late. - **Uneven chapters.** One chapter entirely in the shop. One chapter that's almost entirely one conversation in the dark because the candle went out and she can't light it without being seen from the garden. - **Break the window-title scheme,** or keep the titles but let one chapter's title be a lie—"The Front Door" is Chapter 4, when she tries to be admitted properly with a letter and is turned away again. - **Make Godfrey's cruelty lazy** rather than plotted. He's not scheming; he's comfortable. The estate's ruin is drift, not design. This is harder to fight than a villain. - **Let the examination go badly.** Julian fails, or nearly. Ansell hesitates. Nell pushes. Ambiguity about whether she's done right. - **Move the kiss to the wrong place.** Or cut it. - **Don't let Julian come down the stairs heroically.** Let it be a failure, or off-page, or a carriage to court. - **Let the ending cost.** The shop is sold and she minds. Lady Thorne stays and is never warm. Julian's leg is what it is. The county doesn't come to dinner. - **Cut the "library wants a bookseller" line** and any equivalent. The proposal, if there is one, should be unlovely and plain. - **Resist the closing rhyme.** Or if the final image is the window, don't let Nell tell us why. Just the ivy, the latch, the fact of it. Two sentences. - **Let the wit fail.** Somewhere around Chapter 5, the voice goes flat—the retrospective narrator stops being funny for a page because the thing she's telling wasn't funny. Then the wit comes back, and we hear it differently. - **Let her have opinions we don't share.** About servants, about Godfrey's Irish cousin, about what a woman ought to do. Not to make her unlikeable but to make her from *then*. - **One detail carried too far.** The trousers under the skirt, say—she keeps wearing them after she's mistress of the house, and no one mentions it, and she never explains. - **Something unexplained.** Where does Julian's hoard of money come from? Never say. What did Mrs. Pryce actually think of him? Nell never finds out and always wonders.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention Eight chapters, roughly a thousand words each, narrated in first person by Nell Baxter—a Cheltenham bookseller's daughter—looking back from some years' distance on the winter and spring she spent climbing into Ashcombe to reach Julian Thorne, a man his family had declared of unsound mind. The prompt sentence is hers and I will spend Chapter 1 earning it: a woman who has done something absurd and dangerous and has decided to be funny about it rather than ashamed, and who is not always able to keep that up. **The climbing is the story.** Every chapter contains at least one entrance, described with real physical attention—ivy that sheets away, lead that sweats in frost, a bar that bends, a moment where she cannot get down. The "art" is learned honestly: badly first, then better, never comfortably. I will not have Nell explain that learning the windows was learning him. The reader can do that. **Voice.** Wry and plain, and the wit is allowed to fail. Around the middle the narrator goes flat because the thing she is telling was not funny. Feeling is shown by misdirected action—she snaps at the carrier, she overcharges a customer, she buys a book she can't afford and calls it stock—not by "something shifted in me." **Nell** is from 1881. She is respectable, has real shame about what she's doing, lies to her father and the carrier, has snobbish opinions about the Ashcombe servants and a suspicion of gentry. She takes Julian's money for months and is uncomfortable about it. She is a competent climber only because she is stubborn; she is not competent at law, doctors, or gentlemen. **Julian** is not a charming invalid. Seven years upstairs with laudanum and a mother who calls him "poor boy" have made him a man who talks too much when given an audience, repeats himself, goes silent for long stretches, and is frightening in his gratitude. Nell doesn't like him at first. She goes back for the money. His project is not picturesque maps but a ledger: he is trying to reconstruct, from the view and from what servants let slip, exactly what has been sold off the estate—which is sad, useful, and slightly mad-looking. **Godfrey** is lazy, not scheming. He half-believes his brother is odd, has got comfortable, and has let the estate drift. He knows about Nell earlier than she realizes and permits it because he assumes she's Julian's woman and it keeps Julian quiet. That is nastier than a plot and harder to fight. **Lady Thorne** is the one ambiguity I protect. She is never explained, never exiled, never warm. Nell has to live with her. **Plot discipline.** No wardrobe monologue, no convenient clerk. Nell goes to a solicitor herself and is humiliated by the fee. The doctor's examination goes badly and he signs anyway, and Nell is not sure she has done right. Julian's leaving the room is not a heroic descent; it is a failure on the stairs that is nonetheless the turning point, because his mother sees him try. The hearing happens off-page. The ending costs: the shop is sold and she minds; his leg is what it is; the county does not come to dinner; the money's origin is never explained; the kiss happens in the wrong place and is not discussed. **Avoid:** chapter titles that telegraph structure; evenly distributed period texture (three details, the rest dark); a proposal with a clever button; a closing line that explains the metaphor; a bow. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — October.** Nell tells us she came to Ashcombe for eleven pounds four shillings owed on books ordered by letter for five years by "J. Thorne," the letters having stopped in July. She is refused at the door by a footman who says Mr. Julian is unwell and sees no one. Most of the chapter is her sitting in the kitchen garden in the drizzle talking herself out of it and then not, and the climb itself: the ivy, which comes away in a sheet; the trellis, which is rotten; the moment forty feet up when she understands she cannot go down and must go on. She gets a casement open with a hatpin and falls into a room that smells of a man who hasn't opened a window. He is asleep in a chair. She leaves the bill on the desk, weighted with his own inkwell, and gets out the way she came in, which is worse. She does not meet him. The prompt sentence closes the chapter. **Chapter 2 — Late October.** A letter arrives at the shop in a hand she knows, enclosing eleven pounds four shillings in notes and the words: *Come Thursday. The nursery window, east end, the middle bar is loose. Bring the Lyell.* She goes, angry at being commanded and needing the money. The nursery bar, the orangery leads. Julian awake: thirty-four, unshaven, lame, talking before she has both feet on the floor and not stopping—about Lyell, about the footman, about a hedge that was there in June. She finds him tiresome and a little frightening. He pays her for the Lyell and for the next order and for her trouble, and she takes it. On the way down she sees a lamp move behind another window and thinks she has been seen. She has. **Chapter 3 — November into December.** The visits become fortnightly because the money is good and her father's chest is bad. The art: she learns the leads sweat in frost, that the loose bar bends if you push at the base, that a wool skirt on a slope is a sail. She starts wearing her dead brother's trousers under her dress and tells no one. Julian's ledger—columns of fields, tenants, guesses at what Godfrey has sold—laid out on the nursery floor; she corrects one entry because she knows the new tenant of the Lower Farm from Cheltenham and he won't meet her eye. Julian goes silent for ten minutes and she nearly leaves. Then he asks her to describe the Promenade, shop by shop, and she does, and it is the first time she sees him as someone who was once outside. **Chapter 4 — January.** Nell tries the front door with a letter of introduction from the vicar, having decided this is ridiculous and she is a respectable woman. Lady Thorne receives her in a cold room, says Julian is not well enough for visitors and has not been for years, poor boy, and asks—mildly, with no expression—how Nell knows he wanted books. Nell lies badly and is shown out. That night, shaken, she climbs anyway. The candle is out and she can't light it without being seen from the garden, so the whole conversation is in the dark. He tells her his brother knows about her and has said so, and what his brother assumes she is. He apologizes for it. She says nothing for a long time. Then she kisses him, badly, because she is furious, and leaves without a word, and they do not speak of it for two chapters. **Chapter 5 — February.** No manor. Her father is dying by inches and knows she is going somewhere. The shop's ledger; the customers who don't pay. She goes to a solicitor in Regent Street with the word "traverse" she found in a legal dictionary in her own stock and is told what it would cost and, in effect, who she is. Her father dies. The wit goes out of the narration for this chapter. She doesn't go to Ashcombe for four weeks, and when she does, in the last paragraph, she finds Julian has not eaten properly and has been measuring his laudanum with a steadier hand, and he says he thought she had stopped, and she says she has buried one man who would not be helped. **Chapter 6 — March.** Dr. Ansell, a Cheltenham physician of radical sympathies who buys pamphlets from her, is sixty and stout and has to be got up a rope she has knotted herself; the first time it goes very badly and he has to come down. The second time he is in the nursery swearing. The examination is worse than she imagined: Julian knows the year and the Prime Minister and then cannot remember the name of the field outside his own window, and weeps, and Ansell looks at Nell over his spectacles for a long moment before he signs. She takes the certificate out in her bodice. She is not sure what she has done. Julian, at the window as she goes, says her name for the first time, and nothing else. **Chapter 7 — April.** The petition is lodged. Godfrey has the nursery window nailed and the ivy cut to the root, and when Nell comes anyway and finds no way up, he is waiting in the kitchen garden with the footman, not a constable—he doesn't need one. He is almost pleasant. He explains what she is, what will be said, what will happen to a shop when a town knows. Above them a door opens for the first time in seven years and Julian comes down the main stairs on his bad leg and falls on the landing, hard, in front of the housemaid and his mother. He does not make it to the door. He is carried back up. But Lady Thorne saw him try, and when Godfrey turns to her for the word that will finish Nell, she says: "Miss Baxter is Julian's guest, I believe," and goes upstairs to her son. **Chapter 8 — June and after.** The hearing in three sentences: Ansell's certificate, Julian's evidence given seated, Godfrey's accounts. The finding traversed. Godfrey goes to the Irish cousin. Lady Thorne stays. Julian's leg is what it is; he goes downstairs once a day and it costs him. Nell sells the shop in September and minds more than she expected. The proposal is unlovely and plain and made in the shop among the packing cases; she says she will think about it, and does, for a month. They marry quietly. The county does not come. Where the money in the hollow atlas came from she never learns. Last page, some years on: a summer evening, home late from Cheltenham, the front door standing open. The ivy has grown back because nobody thought to stop it. She goes round by the kitchen garden. He has left the bar loose.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. # Eleanor "Nell" Baxter **Background.** Born 1857 above the shop at 14 Winchcombe Street, Cheltenham—Baxter & Son, Booksellers, Stationers, Binders. The "Son" was her brother Tom, who died of a fall from a hayrick at Prestbury when he was fourteen and she was eleven; the sign was never changed because repainting costs money and because her father couldn't bear to. Her mother died the year after. Nell has kept the ledgers since she was fifteen and can bind a quarto in cloth boards in an afternoon. She reads what comes into stock but has no system and no pretensions; she has read *Middlemarch* twice and half of *Bleak House* and all of a manual on beekeeping because it was on the counter. She left the Church of England Girls' School at thirteen. She has never been further than Gloucester. **Personality.** Stubborn in the specific way of someone who has been left to run things and knows nobody is coming. She is not brave; she is unable to leave a thing undone once she has started it, which looks the same from outside. She is respectable and knows exactly what respectable costs and has paid it for years—the plain bonnet, the accounts kept to the penny, the vicar's wife's approval. She is faintly snobbish downward (she thinks the Ashcombe footman is jumped-up and says so) and suspicious upward (gentry don't pay their bills; she has the ledger to prove it). She lies badly and knows it, so she lies rarely and then over-elaborately. She is funny mostly in her own head and only later out loud. **Idiosyncrasies and anchors.** - Keeps her brother's things in a tea chest under her bed: a knife, a school slate, two pairs of moleskin trousers that she lets out at the waist in December and wears under her skirts to Ashcombe. She never explains this to Julian and he never asks. Years later she still wears them to garden. - Counts stairs. Any stairs. Has done since Tom died, without knowing why. - Bites the inside of her cheek when doing sums, so the left side is often sore. - Cannot abide a book shelved spine-in and will right it in other people's houses. - Talks to the carrier's horse rather than the carrier. **Flaws.** She takes Julian's money for five months and does not stop taking it after she has stopped needing the excuse, and she does not examine this. She is ashamed of him at first—of the smell of the room, the talking, the wet eyes—and is later ashamed of having been ashamed. She is unkind to her father in his last weeks because he is dying inconveniently. She pushes Ansell to sign. She has a bookseller's instinct to price everything, including people, and it takes her a long time to see Julian as anything but a debtor. **Physicality.** Middling height, strong forearms from the press and the ladders, a long plain face, brown hair scraped back. Hands red in winter. Moves with a shopkeeper's economy—no gesture wasted, everything put back where it goes. Climbs like someone who has never been taught: too much arm, not enough leg, until the leads teach her otherwise. When frightened she goes very still and her voice drops rather than rises. **Motives and relationships.** Wants, at first, eleven pounds four shillings. Then wants to keep the shop open through her father's illness. Then wants—without naming it—somewhere she is not the one holding everything up. Her father she loves and resents in equal proportion. The vicar's wife is her nearest thing to a friend and is not one. She has been walked home from church three Sundays running by a corn-factor's clerk called Purdy and has let it happen because it is expected. She is the last Baxter and feels it as a debt. **Voice.** > "Eleven pounds four is not a sum one forgives. It is a sum one climbs for." > "I should say here that I did not like him. I mention this because a great deal of the story turns on things holding that had no business to." # Julian Thorne **Background.** Born 1847, second son of Sir Edmund Thorne of Ashcombe by his second wife; Godfrey is the son of the first. Harrow, then a year at Christ Church he didn't finish. At twenty-seven, in the spring of 1874, he went over a hedge at the Ashcombe hunt, broke his left femur badly, and lay six weeks with a fever during which he said and did things—struck a nurse, tore up his father's letters, wept for days. His father died that autumn. Godfrey, as executor, petitioned for a commission of inquisition in lunacy; two physicians who had seen Julian in the fever's worst week gave evidence; the jury found him of unsound mind and incapable. Godfrey was made committee of his person and estate. The grandfather's settlement, which passes the entailed land to the second son outright at thirty-five, was mentioned by nobody. Julian has been in the east wing since. He has not been down the main stairs since 1875. **Personality.** Not charming. Seven years alone with a lame leg, a laudanum bottle, and a mother who visits on Sundays have made him a man who has forgotten the shape of a conversation. He lectures. He repeats himself. He goes quiet for ten minutes at a time, looking at the window, and does not know he's done it. His gratitude for company is frightening—he will thank Nell four times for a book. Underneath is the man he was: dry, precise, once good at estate business, with a horseman's patience and a real love of the land he can see and cannot walk. That man surfaces in flashes and is gone. **Idiosyncrasies and anchors.** - The ledger: a folio account book in which, by observation from three windows and what housemaids let fall, he is reconstructing what Godfrey has sold—fields, timber, the Lower Farm, the rectory living. Some entries are shrewd. Some are wrong. One column is headed "Things I Cannot Account For" and includes a hedge. - Measures his laudanum drops into a wine glass with a marked strip of paper pasted to it; has been cutting the dose by one drop a fortnight since 1879 and is at eleven. - Keeps his money—perhaps two hundred pounds—in a hollowed Cary's *Atlas*. Where it came from he never says. Nell suspects Mrs. Pryce. Nell may be wrong. - Has kept every one of Nell's shop invoices and reads them. - Cannot bear to have the door of a room shut behind another person; will ask her to leave it ajar even when it's dangerous. **Flaws.** Pride, of the humiliated kind—he would rather stay upstairs than fail at the stairs in front of anyone. He does not tell Nell that Godfrey knows about her for three weeks after he learns it. He is a coward about his mother. Under the examination he lets terror make him stupid. He is capable of self-pity and knows it and hates it and does it anyway. **Physicality.** Tall, gone thin, with the softness of a body that doesn't move. Unshaven more often than not; dark hair too long. The left leg is a half-inch short and won't bear weight without a stick and won't bend fully at the knee. He holds himself as if the room were a horse he's not sure of. Long hands that were good on reins and now fold and refold paper. Eyes the color of tea and usually wet, which Nell at first takes for weeping and later understands is laudanum. **Motives and relationships.** Wants to know what has happened to Ashcombe—not to get it back, at first; just to *know*. Wants someone to talk to so badly that he'd take anyone, which he knows is not a compliment to Nell and says so. Godfrey he does not hate; he's frightened of him and ashamed of the fear. Nell begins as the bookseller and becomes, without his consent, the whole of the outside. **Voice.** > "You'll want to leave that door. No—open. Yes. Thank you. I know it's absurd. He has a wife in Bath he sees quarterly and no children. **Personality.** Lazy, not wicked; the distinction matters to nobody but him. He believed Julian was mad in 1874 because the doctors said so and it was convenient, and has never revisited the question because revisiting things is effort. He is pleasant in company and has real, easy county manners. He does not think of himself as having done anything. He thinks of Julian's confinement as a sad arrangement that suits everyone, including Julian, who after all doesn't come down. He noticed the bookseller's girl in November and let it go on because a man in Julian's position needs *something* and it kept the letters to solicitors from starting. He finds it, if anything, a relief. **Idiosyncrasies and anchors.** - Rides every morning and is a good horseman; the one thing he does well and knows it. - Calls Julian "the boy" to servants, "my brother" to guests, "Julian" to nobody. - Keeps his own accounts in a locked drawer and has never once added them up. - Has a habit of agreeing with people warmly and then doing nothing whatever. - Will not go up to the east wing. Sends the footman. **Flaws.** Indolence as a moral condition. Contempt worn as kindness. When threatened he is not cruel but *precise*—he knows exactly what a town does to a woman's name and will say it aloud with regret. **Physicality.** Heavier than Julian, florid, handsome in a way that is going. Good coats. Stands with his weight back on his heels like a man leaning on a gate. Smiles with his whole face and it means nothing. Smells of horse and bay rum. **Motives and relationships.** Wants nothing to change. Wants, specifically, for June 1882 to pass without incident, though he has not put this to himself in words. Resents Julian for having been their father's favorite and would deny it. Is fond of Lady Thorne in the way one is fond of a housekeeper. Regards Nell as a problem of the same order as a leaking roof. **Voice.** > "Miss Baxter. I'd hoped we might avoid this. You'll understand I've known for some months—one does, in a house—and I'd rather thought it a kindness to say nothing. He's had so little." > "A shop, isn't it? In Winchcombe Street. I know the sort. Very much depends on goodwill." # Lady Thorne (Honoria) **Background.** Born 1826, a clergyman's daughter from Wiltshire; married Sir Edmund at twenty as his second wife and gave him one son. Never quite accepted by the county and stopped trying in about 1860. Was in the room during the worst of Julian's fever; he struck her. She has never said so. She signed nothing—as a woman she couldn't—but she told the commission's physicians what she had seen, truthfully, and has lived since on the belief that she was truthful and the suspicion that truth was not the same as right. **Personality.** Composed to the point of absence.
