+ Classic Sci-Fi — The Azra Gambit (Chapter Avg: 86.1 | Final: 87.1)
Initial Writing Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Task: write a short story over several chapters. Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Begin the story as an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. Arthur meets with this unknown party, who makes an offer. This early scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The first chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. The remainder of the story is open to your choices & direction.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Task: write a short story over several chapters. Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra&#x27;s secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Begin the story as an armed retinue descends on Arthur&#x27;s home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. Arthur meets with this unknown party, who makes an offer. This early scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description &amp; scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes &amp; dangers. Include Asimov&#x27;s trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The first chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he&#x27;s gotten involved in. The remainder of the story is open to your choices &amp; direction. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. Model Output:
# Brainstorming **Core premise and Asimovian flavor** Asimov's hallmarks: ideas over action, dialogue-driven scenes where clever people reason toward a twist; the "big picture" (galactic politics, economics, the physics of a MacGuffin treated rigorously) sitting alongside the "small picture" (a lone engineer, a domestic detail, a cigar, a pocket computer). Retrofuturism: slide-rule-adjacent instruments, "positronic"-style jargon, vacuum-tube glow, transfer vessels with ferro-glass ports, men in grey suits smoking in pressurized cabins. Cool, slightly dry narration. The protagonist is usually an ordinary, rational person who wins by out-thinking rather than out-fighting. Endings often flip an assumption. **Azra — how does it work, and what are its secrets?** - A metal that catalytically accelerates radioactive decay in nearby unstable isotopes. Field effect scales with mass and purity. Small quantities: superb drive catalysts (burn fissiles hot and fast). Large quantities: a lump of uranium next to a large Azra mass becomes a bomb without any need for critical geometry. Hence the arms race. - Secret #1: the acceleration effect is proportional to the *total* Azra mass in proximity — meaning a large enough vein is itself a strategic weapon/danger. Arthur's vein is so large that its field is measurable at the surface — which is how the various parties found it (their neutron detectors flagged an anomaly). - Secret #2: Azra itself is slowly decaying into something inert. It's not a permanent resource; the galaxy is fighting over a candle. Or: Azra is *produced* by decay of something else — Mars's core, or an ancient artifact. - Secret #3: In very large masses, Azra accelerates its *own* decay — a runaway. Mining the vein by the corporations' brute methods (concentrating it) would set off a self-accelerating burn that could sterilize the region. The small-holder's slow, dispersed method is the only safe one. This makes Arthur's engineering knowledge, not just his deed, the real prize. - Secret #4 (twist option): Azra weakly accelerates *all* decay including the potassium-40 in living bodies — long-term Azra miners die early. The indenture system is built on this: labourers are leased because they're disposable. Arthur, first-gen settler who's lived on his plot for years, may already be affected. **Factions** - Antares Diplomatic Corps: outer-system power bloc (Antares = a colony cluster/star system rival to Earth). Polished, dangerous, wants the vein for drives to reach beyond. - Terran Combine / Earth Ministry: the old power, holds Mars nominally as colonial territory, licenses corporations. - The Corporations: Meridian Extraction, Tharsis Consolidated — lease indentured labourers, care about tonnage. - The Martian settlers/indentured labourers — no power, but they're the ones who do the work; Arthur straddles first-gen settler (free) and the indentured (he employs two? or he refuses to?). - A scientist faction — someone who actually understands Azra's physics. **Characters** - Arthur Neegan: 40s, mining engineer, first-generation settler, taciturn, methodical, doesn't want to be important. Widower? Or has a daughter/partner back on Mars who becomes leverage. Perhaps he keeps a hand-drawn geological log — the small detail that matters. - The Antares envoy: an urbane woman or man, Cordelia Vasht / Envoy Halloran. Offers Arthur a fortune plus citizenship; the "or else" is implied by the armed retinue. - Her opposite number: a Terran ministry man — Commissioner Ostrow — who meets Arthur later, offers "protection." - A physicist: Dr. Idris Palo, an Azra researcher, maybe an indentured scientist owned by a corporation, who knows the runaway secret. - Marguerite — Arthur's neighbour or foreman, indentured labourer whose lease Arthur bought out, providing the human stake in the labour system. - A minor retrofuturist touch: the ship's steward, an aged robot or a man with a brass carafe. **Plot shapes** 1. *Bidding war → Arthur plays factions against each other → wins independence for Mars.* Clean but maybe too heroic. 2. *Arthur discovers the vein is dangerous → must prevent anyone from mining it → ends with him convincing all factions that the vein is worthless/lethal (true or bluff).* Very Asimov: the solution is an idea. 3. *Arthur is a pawn; the meeting is a kidnapping; he escapes.* Too action-y. 4. *The twist: the vein isn't Azra at all but the decayed remnant; the real Azra is somewhere else; Arthur's knowledge misdirects everyone.* 5. *Arthur trades the vein for the abolition of indenture leases on Mars — the "gambit" of the title. He can do it because he's the only one who knows how to mine it without triggering runaway.* **The "gambit"** — should be Arthur's, a chess-like sacrifice. He gives up the thing they all want (the deed) in exchange for something they think worthless (the labourers, or a survey-rights clause, or independence for a small plot). Then it turns out the thing he kept is the real value. E.g., he sells the vein but keeps the method — or he sells the vein knowing it's a self-limiting deposit, and keeps the tailings/adjacent claim where the real thing is. **Chapter beat sketch (8 × ~1000 words)** 1. Aboard the transfer vessel. Arthur reflects: the retinue's arrival, the Antares insignia, his plot, his readings. Establish Azra basics and Mars economy. Ends with docking at an orbital station or cruiser. 2. The meeting. Envoy Vasht. Dialogue-heavy. Offer: buy the plot for a fortune plus Antares citizenship. Hints: they know exactly how big the vein is; they mention Terran cruisers already in transit; she asks an oddly specific question about his decay-rate logs. Arthur asks for time. She grants 72 hours — "the Terrans will make you an offer too; hear it, then choose us." 3. Return to Mars; Terran Commissioner Ostrow arrives — different style, bureaucratic menace. Reveal that Earth can simply void his claim under colonial law. Marguerite (indentured) and the labour system given a human face. Arthur notices his own instruments: the vein's field has grown since the Antares ship arrived? Or since the corporations started drilling next door. 4. Arthur seeks Dr. Palo, a leased scientist at Meridian's camp. Learn Azra physics: field scales with mass; corporations concentrating ore nearby are pushing toward a threshold. Palo's hint about runaway. Palo is being recalled — his lease sold to Antares. 5. Arthur does the arithmetic (Asimov loves this). Realizes: whoever mines the vein fast will trigger a runaway that vaporizes the Tharsis settlements. He also realizes no one will believe a settler. The gambit forms. 6. Arthur summons both envoys to his plot (neutral ground, or the only place both will come). Sets the board. Dialogue scene: he offers to sell to the highest bidder — but stipulates terms about labour and method. Both refuse the terms. 7. The demonstration: Arthur shows them the runaway in miniature — a sample chamber; the Geiger screaming; or the data. Reveal that Meridian's adjacent drilling has already begun the climb. Standoff resolved by mutual terror: neither side can let the other mine fast; both need slow extraction; slow extraction needs skilled free workers, not disposable indentured ones. 8. Resolution. The deed goes into a joint trust; indenture leases on Tharsis dissolved as the price of Arthur's cooperation; Arthur remains an engineer on his own plot, now the most watched man on Mars. Closing Asimovian coda: he lights his pipe, checks his counter, notes the reading has dropped a hair. Or a darker note: he knows the vein is a candle and says nothing. **Tone options**: wry and cool (classic Asimov), or grim. Probably wry with steel underneath. # Reflection The runaway-decay idea (Secret #3) is the strongest engine: it's rigorous-feeling, it makes Arthur's specific expertise the actual prize, and it converts a political tug-of-war into a problem solved by reasoning and demonstration rather than by a gun. That's exactly the Asimov register. It also gives the title its meaning — Arthur's gambit sacrifices the deed to secure the terms, and the terms (method + free skilled labour) are the true value. Plot shape 5 fused with 2 works. Secret #4 (Azra harms miners) is tempting for the indenture theme but risks overloading 8,000 words; better as a single grim line from Palo rather than a subplot. Secret #2 (candle) makes a good final ambiguous note in chapter 8 — Arthur knows the vein won't last forever, and that's fine, because the labour reforms will. Keep it to a paragraph. Chapter 1 needs care: the prompt demands it open aboard the vessel and be reflective, yet it must also convey the retinue's arrival (in memory) and lay down the world. Asimov handled exposition through calm narration; a bit of back-and-forth with a steward or an Antares officer would break the monotony and let the "diplomatic in name only" observation land. Chapter 2 must be the showpiece dialogue — the envoy should be genuinely clever and almost likeable, and the hints (Terran cruisers, the interest in his decay logs, a mention of "the Meridian incident") should pay off later. Avoid making her a cartoon. Risks: too many factions for the length. Trim to three real voices — Vasht (Antares), Ostrow (Terra), Palo (science) — with Meridian as an offstage force and Marguerite as the human stake. Also avoid action set-pieces; the "demonstration" in chapter 7 should be tense through instruments and numbers, not explosions. The middle (chapters 3–5) risks sag; giving each a concrete revelation (claim can be voided; the physics; the arithmetic) keeps momentum. The ending should feel earned but not triumphant — Arthur wins a narrow, precarious peace, very much in the mode of Asimov's pragmatic, unheroic resolutions.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention I'll write an idea-driven, dialogue-forward short story in the classic Asimov register: cool, wry third-person narration close on Arthur Neegan; scenes built from clever people reasoning at each other; a MacGuffin (Azra) treated with pseudo-rigorous physics; and a resolution achieved by an argument and a demonstration rather than a firefight. The retrofuturist texture will be consistent and unfussy — ferro-glass ports, hand-plotted decay logs, Geiger counters with needle dials, men in grey suits smoking in pressurized cabins, a steward with a brass carafe — never winking at itself. **Plot spine:** Arthur's plot sits on a vein so large that its decay-acceleration field is measurable at the surface. Two powers (Antares, Terra) and a corporation (Meridian, offstage but active) want it. Arthur learns from a leased physicist that Azra's effect scales with concentrated mass and that above a threshold it accelerates its *own* decay — a runaway that would sterilize the Tharsis basin. Fast, brute-force corporate extraction with disposable indentured labour is therefore lethal; only slow, dispersed, skilled mining is safe. Arthur's gambit: he gives up the deed (the thing everyone wants) into a joint trust, in exchange for the terms nobody values — the extraction method, and the dissolution of indenture leases on Tharsis, since safe mining needs free, skilled, permanent workers. He wins a narrow, precarious peace, not a triumph. **Choices made:** Three real voices only — Envoy Cordelia Vasht (Antares, urbane, genuinely clever, almost likeable), Commissioner Ostrow (Terra, bureaucratic menace, law as a weapon), Dr. Idris Palo (leased physicist, the science). Marguerite Okonkwo, an indentured foreman whose lease Arthur bought out, gives the labour system a face and a stake. Meridian Extraction stays offstage — its drilling next door is the ticking clock. **Aim for:** exposition through calm narration and dialogue; each middle chapter delivering one concrete revelation; hints in chapter 2 (Terran cruisers, interest in Arthur's logs, "the Meridian incident") that pay off; tension through instruments and numbers; an ending flip — the deed was never the real prize. A closing coda that's quiet and slightly ambiguous: Arthur knows the vein is a candle that will burn out, and that's fine. **Avoid:** action set-pieces, cartoon villains, more than three factions with speaking parts, the "Azra kills miners" subplot (reduce to one grim line from Palo), heroic speechifying, and a tidy utopian ending. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The Transfer Vessel.** Arthur aboard an Antares shuttle rising off Mars, in a narrow cabin with a ferro-glass port. In memory: the retinue's landing at his plot at dawn, the polished politeness of Lieutenant Serrat, the Antares insignia (a red star and olive branch — "diplomatic in name only"). Calm narration establishes Azra (accelerates decay; drives and weapons; the gold rush), Mars's indenture-lease economy, and Arthur's own modest history — first-gen settler, engineer, his hand-plotted decay logs showing anomalous readings he'd thought were instrument drift. A brief exchange with the steward (brass carafe, real coffee — a luxury and a message). Ends with docking at the Antares cruiser *Concordance*, its hull bristling with things not diplomatic. **Chapter 2 — The Envoy.** The showpiece dialogue. Envoy Cordelia Vasht in a wardroom with a real wooden table, offering Arthur cigars and a staggering sum plus Antares citizenship for his deed. She knows the vein's size to the tonne; she asks pointedly about his decay logs — "your neighbours' instruments don't show what yours show." Hints: Terran cruisers already inbound; "the Meridian incident" mentioned and deflected; she wants the vein for drives to reach beyond the outer colonies. Arthur asks for time; she grants seventy-two hours — "Hear the Terrans out. Then choose us." Menace stays velvet. **Chapter 3 — The Commissioner.** Back on Mars. Marguerite meets Arthur at the plot; her history as leased labour, his buying out her lease, the way Meridian's camp next door treats its people. Commissioner Ostrow arrives with paper rather than guns: under Colonial Charter, Terra can void his claim outright and lease the vein to Meridian; his "protection" is the alternative to being erased. Arthur, checking his instruments after they leave, finds the field reading has risen since Meridian began concentrating ore at their adjacent site. **Chapter 4 — The Physicist.** Arthur bribes his way into Meridian's camp to see Dr. Idris Palo, a leased scientist who understands Azra. Palo explains the physics: field strength scales with concentrated mass; above a threshold Azra catalyzes its own decay — a runaway. One grim aside about what long exposure does to a miner's potassium. Palo's lease has just been sold to Antares; he leaves Arthur his notes and a figure for the threshold. Meridian's stockpile is closer to it than anyone at Meridian knows. **Chapter 5 — The Arithmetic.** Arthur alone with logs, slide rule, and Palo's notes. He works it out: fast extraction by any faction pushes the concentrated mass past threshold within months; the runaway would sterilize Tharsis. No one will believe a settler with a hand-drawn graph. He realizes the deed is worthless as a lever but the method is not — and safe mining requires skilled, free, permanent workers. The gambit forms. Marguerite: "They'll never agree to that." Arthur: "They'll agree to anything if the alternative is nothing." **Chapter 6 — Setting the Board.** Arthur invites Vasht and Ostrow to his plot — the only ground both will come to. Dialogue: he announces he'll place the deed in a trust open to the highest bidder, with binding conditions on extraction rate and the abolition of indenture leases in the basin. Both dismiss the terms; Ostrow reaches for the Charter, Vasht for her fortune. Arthur says nothing yet about the runaway. He proposes they look at his instruments before deciding. **Chapter 7 — The Demonstration.** In Arthur's sample shed: a shielded chamber, a small Azra mass, a Geiger with a needle. He adds Azra stepwise; the needle climbs faster than mass should predict, then jumps — the curve turns upward. He shows Palo's threshold figure beside Meridian's current stockpile. The tension is all instruments and silence. Vasht sees it first; Ostrow argues, then does the arithmetic himself. Mutual terror does the work: neither can let the other mine fast, and Meridian must stop tonight. Ostrow radios the halt order. **Chapter 8 — The Trust.** Weeks later. The deed sits in a joint Antares–Terran trust; extraction limits are law; indenture leases in Tharsis dissolved as the price of Arthur's method. Marguerite runs a crew of free miners. Vasht visits to say goodbye — she knows he outplayed them and half admires it; she notes he's now the most watched man on Mars. Coda: Arthur alone, checking his counter. The reading has dropped a hair. Azra decays into something inert; the vein is a candle. He doesn't tell anyone. The candle will outlast the treaties, and the freed workers will outlast the candle. He lights his pipe.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human writer might approach this A human who loved Asimov enough to imitate him would probably not start from a system of factions and a physics chart. They'd start from a voice and an itch. Maybe they've always wanted to write the scene where the polite men with guns come to the door, and everything else is scaffolding to get there. Maybe they're a lapsed engineer and the thing they actually care about is what Martian dust does to pump bearings, and the geopolitics is the excuse. Their story would be lopsided in the direction of what interested them. Some chapters would run long on a conversation they enjoyed; others would be dispatched in a page because they were bored. They'd also know Asimov in a way that's partly misremembered, which is good. What people remember: dialogue, puzzles, the twist that reframes the puzzle, the cheerful bureaucrat, the man who wins by being less stupid than everyone else. What people forget: Asimov's prose is *thin*. There is very little sensory description. Rooms are "a room." People "said" things. The retrofuturism isn't decorated brass and ferro-glass — it's just that nobody questions a slide rule, and a computer prints its answer on a tape. The texture comes from the assumptions, not the set dressing. A human imitator who has actually reread *The Caves of Steel* recently would write leaner than an LLM guessing at "retrofuturistic vibe." A human would also give Arthur a body and a temper. He'd have a bad hip from a rover accident. He'd be irritated that the retinue tracked dust into the airlock. He'd want the money, at least for a night. He'd have opinions about his neighbours that aren't flattering to him. The "small picture" in Asimov isn't a tasteful brass carafe; it's a character being petty about something. # General LLM tendencies and why they'd hurt this piece **Symmetry and payoff hygiene.** Every planted hint returns; every character has a function and a moment; the ending rhymes with the opening. Real stories have loose threads and lopsided emphasis. In an Asimov puzzle-story specifically, *some* misdirection should be genuinely dead: a red herring that turns out to be a red herring, not a secret second clue. **Wrapping with a bow.** The final image that closes the thematic loop (the pipe, the candle, "the freed workers will outlast the candle"). Asimov's endings are often a last line of dialogue — a joke, a shrug, a bureaucrat filing a form. The reader supplies the resonance. **Everyone is competent and articulate.** Envoys are "urbane and genuinely clever," commissioners are "bureaucratic menace," scientists are lucid. Nobody is tired, wrong, distracted, petty, or bad at their job. Asimov's people are often *somewhat* stupid; the pleasure is watching the one non-stupid person navigate them. **Characters who say the theme.** "They'll agree to anything if the alternative is nothing." Aphorism-as-dialogue. Once per story is a treat; a plan that pencils these in per chapter is a tell. **Moral congeniality.** The reward for cleverness is a progressive outcome delivered cleanly (indenture abolished). This is the safe ending. It flatters the reader and requires no cost. Asimov's resolutions were pragmatic and often grubby — the Foundation wins by trade and manipulation, not by justice. **"Impressive" prose.** Metaphor stacking, adjective triplets, "the weight of the silence," "something shifted in her expression." It fights the Asimov register directly, which is plain to the point of flatness. **Names as flavour.** Cordelia Vasht, Idris Palo, Okonkwo — the faux-cosmopolitan salad that signals "future" without being anyone's actual name. Asimov's names were odd but plain: Hardin, Baley, Mallow, Seldon, Darell. **Even pacing.** One revelation per chapter, each ~1000 words. Mechanical. A human lets one chapter be a single long argument and another be two pages of a man staring at a graph. **Sanitized stakes.** Menace is always "velvet." Nobody is hurt. Nobody is humiliated. The gun in the first scene is a prop. # Critique of the intention and plan **The ending is the biggest problem.** Chapter 8 as planned is nearly a checklist of LLM closure: the villain who "half admires" the hero; the phrase "most watched man on Mars"; the secret the hero keeps for the greater good; the candle metaphor stated outright; the pipe. It's four bows on one package. It also makes Arthur *too* right — he wins the argument, the reform, and a private wisdom the others lack. Asimov's heroes usually win the argument and *lose* something incidental, or discover the win was arranged by someone else. **The indenture abolition is too clean and too convenient.** Two galactic powers dissolve a labour system because an engineer put it in a contract? Realistically Terra reclassifies indenture as "term employment" and nothing changes; or the leases are bought out by Antares and the same people are now leased to the trust. A human writer with a cynical streak would let Arthur win something smaller and stranger — a wage floor, a rotation limit, the right to quit — and let him notice it's not enough. Or let the labourers themselves be lukewarm about what he's "won" for them. **Arthur is stock.** "Taciturn, methodical, doesn't want to be important." The reluctant, quietly wise engineer is the default protagonist of this genre as an LLM imagines it. He has no vanity, no appetite, no complicity. But he *bought a lease*. He participated in the system before he bought Marguerite out of it. Did he buy her out on principle or because she was a good foreman and it was cheaper long-term? A human writer would make that ambiguous and let Marguerite know it. **Marguerite is a function.** "Gives the labour system a face and a stake." She exists to be the moral stakes and to say "they'll never agree." She should want things that aren't Arthur's things. Maybe she'd rather take Meridian's contract — guaranteed work — than Arthur's precarious freedom. Maybe she's the one who wanted him to sell. **Palo is a plot dispenser.** He appears, explains the physics, hands over notes, and is conveniently removed. Also: why is Arthur the only one who figures this out? Meridian has physicists. Antares has physicists. The plan implies everyone else is negligent. More human and more Asimovian: they *know*, or suspect, and have decided the risk is acceptable because it's Martians who'd die. That makes Arthur's demonstration not a revelation but a forcing move — he makes the private knowledge public between two rivals who now can't unknow it in front of each other. **The physics of the demonstration doesn't hold.** If the runaway threshold requires Meridian-stockpile masses, a shed sample cannot show "the curve turning upward." At best it shows nonlinearity. This matters, because it opens a better possibility: Arthur *can't* prove the runaway. He has a curve, Palo's extrapolation with wide error bars, and a bluff. The "gambit" becomes real — he's betting that two frightened men won't check his arithmetic. Asimov would have loved that; the plan as written has Arthur simply being correct. **Every ch. 2 hint pays off.** "Terran cruisers," "the Meridian incident," "your logs" — all threads to be tied. "The Meridian incident" in particular is a placeholder-shaped mystery. Either make it concrete and slightly banal (a shaft collapse that killed leased men and was ruled an accident) or let it be a thing Vasht says to unsettle him that turns out to mean nothing much. **Vasht is written to be liked.** "Almost likeable," "genuinely clever." Planning likeability is a tell. Let her be good at her job and *dull* in places — reading from a brief, checking the time, getting a detail about Mars wrong and not caring. **Ostrow is a type.** "Bureaucratic menace, law as a weapon." Fine as a starting point, but give him a human tic that doesn't serve menace — he's carsick in the rover, he's genuinely interested in Arthur's pump design, he complains about the food. **The prose plan invites decoration.** "Ferro-glass ports, brass carafe, real coffee as luxury and message." This is cosplay retrofuturism. Asimov would have said "the port" and "coffee." The steward scene is planned as a texture beat, which means it will read as one. **Structural evenness.** Eight chapters, eight revelations, each 1000 words. The middle (3–5) is three consecutive "Arthur learns a thing" chapters. Chapter 5 — the lone man with the slide rule — is the LLM's favourite montage. # Brainstorm: making it more human **Let Arthur want the money.** For at least a chapter he intends to sell to Antares. He does the sums on what the fortune buys. He tells Marguerite he's selling and she has to hear it. His change of mind comes not from conscience but from Palo's number frightening him about his own plot — where he lives. **Make him complicit and a little vain.** He's proud of his logs in a way that's slightly ridiculous. He bought Marguerite's lease partly because it flattered him to be the good employer. She knows. **Give Marguerite her own agenda that conflicts with his.** She wants the Meridian contract or she wants off Mars entirely; freedom to keep mining on a poisoned plot isn't a prize to her. Her last scene shouldn't be gratitude. **Make the powers already know.** Vasht's pointed question about his logs isn't detective work — she's checking whether *he* knows. The runaway is an open secret in two admiralties and one boardroom, judged acceptable. Arthur's move is to make it unacceptable by making it mutual. **Make the demonstration partly a bluff.** The shed shows a bend, not a runaway. Palo's threshold has a factor-of-three uncertainty. Arthur presents the low end as fact. Neither Vasht nor Ostrow can check it that night, and neither can afford to be the one who was wrong. Leave the reader unsure whether Tharsis was ever in real danger. **Let the win be small and grubby.** Not abolition. A rate cap that Meridian will lobby to raise. A conversion of leases to fixed-term contracts that look a lot like leases. Arthur's plot placed under a trust in which he's an employee. He gets a title, a salary, and a supervisor. **Kill the coda.** No pipe, no candle speech. End on dialogue or a mundane action: Arthur signing a delivery manifest; Marguerite telling him the number two pump is down again; Ostrow's aide asking him to spell his name for the form. If the "Azra decays" note survives, it should be one dry clause Arthur thinks and then sets aside because there's work. **Let one hint be dead.** The Terran cruisers never arrive; they were a Antares invention. Or "the Meridian incident" is exactly what it sounds like and everyone already knows. **Uneven chapters.** Make chapter 2 run long — it's the piece. Make chapter 5 short and unglamorous: Arthur can't sleep, does the arithmetic badly the first time, gets a decimal wrong, has to redo it. **Plain names.** Envoy Prell. Commissioner Deems. Dr. Sabin. Keep Marguerite. Ordinary surnames age better than Vasht. **Thin the texture.** Cut the brass carafe. Keep the slide rule because Arthur uses it, not because it's period. One retrofuturist detail that's *wrong* in an interesting way — the ship has a smoking lounge and a pressurized ashtray. **Let people be bad at things.** Vasht mispronounces Tharsis. Ostrow can't read Arthur's graph and says so. Palo is condescending and rushed. Arthur loses his temper once, unproductively. **Humor that's actually funny.** Asimov's humor is deadpan and situational. A running bit — everyone offers Arthur coffee and it's always terrible — is better than wry narration. **Dialogue that doesn't answer.** People talk past each other. Arthur asks a direct question and Vasht answers a different one. Ostrow interrupts himself to check a form. **Consider dropping Palo as a person.** Arthur gets the physics from a paper Palo wrote that Meridian had him retract. Then Arthur is working from a document, not a wise mentor, and the "convenient exit" problem disappears. Alternatively keep Palo but make him unhelpful — he tells Arthur nothing directly because his contract forbids it, and Arthur has to infer from what he refuses to answer. That's a good Asimov scene.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention An Asimov pastiche done properly: thin prose, dialogue that carries the ideas, a protagonist who wins by being marginally less stupid than everyone else, and an ending that is a shrug rather than a bow. Third person close on Arthur Neegan, past tense, plain declarative sentences. Rooms are rooms. People say things. The retrofuturism lives in unquestioned assumptions — slide rule, printed tape, a smoking lounge on a warship — not in decorated nouns. One or two odd period details, never a catalogue. **Plot spine.** Arthur's plot sits on a very large Azra vein. Antares and Terra both want it; Meridian Extraction is already stockpiling concentrated ore next door. The runaway property of Azra above a concentration threshold is not a secret Arthur uncovers — it is an open question in two admiralties and one boardroom, judged an acceptable risk because the people at risk are Martians. Arthur cannot prove the runaway; he has a bent curve, a retracted paper with a factor-of-three uncertainty on the threshold, and a shed. His gambit is to present the low bound as fact to both rivals in the same room, so that neither can afford to be the one who was wrong in front of the other. It works. The win is small and grubby: a rate cap, the plot placed in a trust where Arthur is a salaried employee, indenture leases in the basin converted to "fixed-term contracts" that look much like leases. Whether Tharsis was ever in real danger, the reader never learns. **Characters.** Arthur: forties, engineer, first-generation settler, a bad knee, proud of his logs to a slightly ridiculous degree, and for most of a chapter fully intending to take the money. He bought out Marguerite's lease years ago partly on principle and partly because good foremen are hard to find; she knows the proportions better than he does. Marguerite Hale: indentured foreman, now free, would rather have a Meridian contract than Arthur's precarious independence, and says so. Envoy Prell (Antares): efficient, reads from a brief, mispronounces Tharsis, checks the time. Commissioner Deems (Terra): carries paper not guns, gets rover-sick, cannot read a graph and admits it. Dr. Sabin (Meridian's leased physicist): appears once, contractually forbidden to say anything, and is useful entirely through what he declines to answer. **Aim for.** Chapter 2 as the long showpiece. Uneven chapters elsewhere. One hint that is dead (the Terran cruisers never come). One aphorism in the whole piece, at most. People talking past each other. Arthur losing his temper once, uselessly. A running bit about bad coffee. Ending on a mundane line of dialogue. **Avoid.** Action, velvet menace, metaphor stacking, characters stating the theme, everyone being competent, likeable villains by design, the pipe, the candle, abolition, gratitude. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The Shuttle.** Arthur in a bolted seat on an Antares transfer shuttle, knee aching, watching Mars shrink in the port. Memory, delivered flatly: the retinue arriving at dawn, Lieutenant Serrat wiping his boots before stepping into the airlock and then tracking dust anyway, the red-star-and-olive-branch insignia, the invitation phrased as a request. Narration establishes Azra (accelerates decay; small quantities catalyse drive fissiles, large quantities make bombs of anything unstable nearby), the lease-labour economy, and Arthur's history in a paragraph each. His logs: readings he'd filed as instrument drift, which he's now fairly sure were not. A steward offers coffee; it is bad. The shuttle docks with the *Concordance*, which has a diplomatic pennant and torpedo tubes. Short chapter. **Chapter 2 — Prell.** Long chapter, nearly all dialogue. A wardroom; a table; a pressurized ashtray. Envoy Prell offers a sum Arthur has to ask her to repeat, plus Antares citizenship, and reads the tonnage estimate off a sheet. She asks whether he keeps his own decay logs and whether anyone else has seen them — checking, though Arthur doesn't yet know it, whether he has noticed the curve. She mentions Terran cruisers three weeks out and "the business at Meridian's number four shaft" and moves on before he can ask. She mispronounces Tharsis; he corrects her; she doesn't care. Arthur asks for time. She gives him seventy-two hours and says the Terrans will offer less and threaten more. He leaves wanting the money. **Chapter 3 — Marguerite, then Deems.** Back at the plot. Arthur tells Marguerite he's selling. She's neither surprised nor grateful for anything; she asks whether Antares will keep the crew on and points out that Meridian pays more. The old ambiguity about why he bought her lease surfaces and neither of them resolves it. Commissioner Deems arrives green from the rover, carrying the Colonial Charter: Terra can void the claim and lease it to Meridian tomorrow; his offer is a management stipend and Terran protection. He asks, genuinely interested, about the pump design. After he leaves, Arthur checks his counter; the surface reading has risen since Meridian began stockpiling next door. He does not yet sleep on it. He intends to sell anyway. **Chapter 4 — Sabin.** Arthur drives to Meridian's camp with a bottle for the gate guard and asks for the physicist. Dr. Sabin is rushed, condescending, and contractually forbidden to discuss Azra. Arthur asks a series of direct questions; Sabin answers none of them and, in declining, tells him nearly everything — including that the retracted paper exists and where a copy might be. The one grim line about long-exposure miners is Sabin's, said as an aside about his own hands. Arthur leaves with the paper. The number-four shaft "business" turns out to be a collapse that killed nine leased men and was ruled a collapse; everyone at the camp already knows, and nobody thinks it means anything. **Chapter 5 — The Arithmetic.** Short, unglamorous. Arthur at his table at two in the morning with the paper, his logs, and a slide rule. He gets a decimal wrong and has to redo it. The paper gives a threshold with a spread of a factor of three; Meridian's stockpile sits comfortably below the high estimate and uncomfortably near the low one. His own plot is inside the radius. He realizes nobody who matters will believe a settler with a hand-drawn graph — and then that they don't have to believe him, only be unable to disbelieve him in front of each other. The gambit forms as a bet, not a certainty. He rings Prell and Deems and invites them to the plot. Marguerite, awake: "You were going to sell." "I still might." **Chapter 6 — The Shed.** Prell and Deems in Arthur's sample shed, both irritated to be there. Arthur announces the deed will go into a trust with binding conditions: an extraction rate ceiling and conversion of basin leases to contracts. Deems reaches for the Charter; Prell for the sum. They talk past him and each other. Arthur loses his temper, unproductively, and then runs the demonstration: a shielded chamber, a counter with a needle, Azra added in steps. The needle climbs faster than mass predicts. It bends. It does not run away — it cannot at this scale — but he lays Sabin's low threshold beside Meridian's stockpile figure and does not mention the high one. **Chapter 7 — The Bet.** The room is quiet in the way of instruments. Prell sees it first, or says she does; Arthur cannot tell whether she is frightened or has always known and is now watching Deems. Deems cannot read the graph and says so, then makes Arthur walk him through it on the tape. Neither asks about error bars. The turn is not terror but mutual exposure: each now knows the other has seen it. Deems radios Meridian to halt stockpiling pending review. Prell says Antares will match the rate cap and adjusts the sum downward on her sheet. The Terran cruisers are mentioned once more; Deems has never heard of them. **Chapter 8 — Terms.** Six weeks on. The plot is in a joint trust. Arthur is Chief Engineer, salaried, with a supervisor on the *Concordance* he has never met. The rate cap is law and Meridian has filed to raise it. Basin leases have become "fixed-term contracts"; Marguerite's crew signs the same forms with a different heading. She has taken the Meridian foreman job, which pays more, and says goodbye without sentiment. Arthur checks his counter: the surface reading has dropped a hair, which could be the halt or could be something the retracted paper hinted at about Azra's own half-life. He notes it in the log and does not pursue it. The last exchange is with Deems's aide, on the telephone, asking him to spell his name for the trust registry. He spells it.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Arthur Neegan **Background.** Born on Earth, Manitoba, to a family of grain-elevator mechanics. Trained as a mining engineer at a second-tier polytechnic and emigrated to Mars at twenty-six on the first wave of settler grants, before Azra was found and when Tharsis was a place you went to be left alone. Took a quarter-section plot on the basin's edge because it was cheap and the survey said "trace radiologicals, no commercial interest." Spent eleven years mining low-grade iron oxide for the Terran road-metal contracts, which paid enough to eat and not much more. Bought Marguerite Hale's lease from Tharsis Consolidated in his sixth year, after her previous crew boss was killed in a hoist accident and she ran the shift for three weeks without pay because nobody told her to stop. He tells himself it was principle. It was also that Consolidated was selling her cheap because she'd been written up for insubordination, and he'd spent two years going through foremen. **Personality.** Methodical to the point of self-parody. Keeps a decay log in a hardbound ledger in fountain pen, one line per day for fourteen years, and is quietly convinced it's the best continuous radiological record on the planet. It probably is, which does not make him less vain about it. Dislikes being interrupted mid-calculation and will finish the line before looking up even when armed men are in his airlock. Has never quite learned to want things in proportion — spent a month's income on a Swiss slide rule and eats tinned beans. Not brave; stubborn, which he has learned to present as the same thing. His temper is slow and stupid: when it goes, he says the true thing at the worst moment and then has to apologize for the timing rather than the content. **Flaws.** Believes that being right ought to be sufficient. Condescends to people who can't follow arithmetic and then is surprised they don't like him. Has a settler's contempt for Earth and a Terran's reflexive distrust of the outer colonies, and hasn't noticed the contradiction. Wants the Antares money badly and would be ashamed to admit how badly — he has already, on the shuttle, mentally spent some of it on a house with a real window. **Trivial anchors.** Corrects people's pronunciation of Tharsis (THAR-sis, not thar-SEES). Takes his coffee black because milk is a luxury and he'd rather not learn to miss it. Keeps a rover fuel log he doesn't need. Has read *Great Expectations* four times because it was the only novel in the plot when he bought it. **Physicality.** Forty-four. Tall and gone slightly stooped from low-ceilinged workings. Left knee ruined by a rover rollover eight years ago; he limps when tired and refuses a stick. Big hands with a tremor he hides by keeping them busy. Face weathered pink from UV; pale blue eyes that make people think he's calmer than he is. Wears the same brown work coverall to meet an envoy that he wears to fix a pump, not as a statement, because it didn't occur to him. **Motives.** Wants to keep his plot, then wants the money, then wants not to die, then wants — dimly, late — not to have been complicit in something. In roughly that order and never quite resolving. Allegiance to nobody; a grudging loyalty to Marguerite that he mistakes for something simpler. Trusts his ledger above any person. **Voice.** > "I'm not refusing, Envoy. I'm asking you to say the number again slowly, because I want to be sure I heard it before I do anything I'll regret." > *Fourteen years. Fourteen years of one line a day, and the drift was never drift. He felt, along with the cold, a small and shameful pleasure at having been right about the instrument all along.* > "You can't read it? Fine. Then you'll have to decide whether to believe the man who can." --- # Marguerite Hale **Background.** Born in the Lagos arcology, indentured at nineteen to Tharsis Consolidated to cover her mother's medical debt under a fifteen-year lease. Shipped to Mars in a bay with sixty others. Worked four Consolidated sites in six years, twice as shift lead without the title. Her lease was bought by Arthur Neegan in her seventh year, and she has run his crew — four to nine people depending on the road-metal contracts — for the eight years since. Technically free for five of those. Has never been off Tharsis basin. **Personality.** Practical in a way that reads as cold and isn't. Assesses every situation by who gets paid and who gets hurt, in that order, because that is the order in which the answers have mattered. Doesn't do gratitude — considers it a form of debt and has had enough of debt. Funnier than Arthur, drier, and uses it mostly on him. Has a very exact memory for figures, contracts, and who said what; has never once let Arthur misremember the terms of her buyout in her hearing. **Flaws.** Mistrusts principle in others because she's seen it spend itself. Reads Arthur's motives less charitably than they deserve and knows it, and has decided the error is the safer one. Cannot tolerate being managed by someone less competent, which has cost her three jobs. Has a habit of settling arguments by walking away to fix something. **Trivial anchors.** Keeps her Consolidated lease tag on a cord around her neck; says it's so she doesn't lose it, which is not the reason. Chews cardamom seeds, which cost a fortune and she buys anyway. Reads Arthur's ledger upside down across the table and is faster at it than he is. **Physicality.** Thirty-four. Short, broad-shouldered, heavy through the forearms. Hair cropped for the suit helmet. A pale burn scar across the back of the left hand from a heater coil. Moves economically — doesn't gesture, doesn't fidget, stands with her weight even. Looks at people slightly too long before answering. **Motives.** Wants steady work at a wage that goes up, for a crew that doesn't get killed, and eventually a berth off Mars. Arthur's independence is his dream, not hers. Meridian's contract pays forty percent more and comes with a pension clause, and she is not sentimental about a quarter-section of oxide she doesn't own. Owes Arthur nothing she hasn't repaid in labour and intends to keep it that way. Likes him, which she considers irrelevant. **Voice.** > "You bought me because Consolidated marked me down and you were sick of training foremen. That's fine. It was a good deal. Don't make it a story." > "They'll halt the stockpile, cap the rate, and rename the lease. That's not nothing. It's also not what you're going to tell yourself it is." --- # Envoy Prell **Background.** Antares Diplomatic Corps, second grade, nineteen years in. Career mostly in resource acquisition on the outer colonies — mineral rights, water concessions, one plebiscite she helped lose on purpose. Not a scientist; has been briefed on Azra by scientists and retains what fits on one sheet. Was told about the runaway question in a room with the door closed and told, in the same breath, that it was a Terran problem. Has accepted this. **Personality.** Efficient and unembarrassed about it. Reads from her brief because the brief is correct and improvisation is where mistakes live. Doesn't perform warmth; doesn't perform menace either, which is more unsettling. Checks the time with a small wristpiece at intervals that have nothing to do with the conversation. Regards Mars as a place with a mispronounced name and a good deposit. Genuinely does not care whether Arthur likes her, which he finds harder to handle than hostility. **Flaws.** Incurious past the edge of the brief. Mistakes settlers for simple because she's met simple settlers. Underestimates how quickly a frightened Terran commissioner can become a witness. Her competence is real and narrow; outside it she is merely a person who wants to go home. **Trivial anchors.** Says "thar-SEES" and, corrected, says it again the same way. Smokes thin black cigarettes and uses the pressurized ashtray with practiced disdain for the design. Writes sums on the margin of her sheet in pencil and revises them downward without comment. **Physicality.** Fifties. Grey hair cut close; grey suit that fits. Sits very upright. Small precise hands, one always near the sheet. Doesn't lean in; makes people come to her. Has a slight cough from ship air that she ignores. **Motives.** Secure the deed for Antares at the lowest defensible price and get back to a system with proper gravity. The runaway is a line item under "known risks, external." Her allegiance is to the Corps and beyond that to the record, which will show she did the job. She would not have hurt Arthur; she would have let the Charter do it and filed the paperwork. **Voice.** > "The sum is as I said it. I'll write it down if that helps. It's not a negotiating figure, Mr. Neegan; we know what's under you to the tonne, and so, by now, does everyone else." > "You'll be offered less by the Terrans and told it's protection. You'll notice the two things aren't different." --- # Commissioner Deems **Background.** Terran Colonial Ministry, Mars Desk, twenty-two years. Came up through claims registry — a filing clerk who learned the Charter by typing it. Posted to Mars three times and hated it each time; gets sick in rovers and never adjusted to the gravity. Sent this time because he knows the voiding statutes cold and because someone more senior didn't want the trip. Was briefed on Azra in an afternoon. The runaway came up as a footnote; he asked if it was serious and was told Meridian's people were satisfied, and he wrote that down. **Personality.** Fussy, literal, and honest in the way of a man who has never been in a position to be anything else. Believes in the Charter the way other men believe in weather — not as a value but as a fact. Interested in machines he doesn't understand and asks about them at inappropriate moments. Uncomfortable with silence and fills it. Not stupid; slow, and knows it, and has built a career on never signing what he hasn't read. **Flaws.** Cannot read a graph and is old enough to have stopped pretending. Confuses procedure with safety. Frightens easily and then digs in rather than backs down. Has never once considered that the Ministry might have been wrong about something that mattered. **Trivial anchors.** Carries the Charter in a green cloth binder with tabs. Takes his coffee with powdered milk and finds Arthur's undrinkable. Asks about the pump's impeller design while Arthur is trying to tell him something else. Has decided that since he can't stop anything, nothing is his responsibility, and has stopped examining that. # Chapter 1 — The Shuttle The seat was bolted to the deck and the straps were too short for him, so Arthur Neegan sat with his knee bent at an angle it did not like and watched Mars go small in the port. It went small slowly. Antares shuttles were built for cargo, and the burn was long and gentle and made the whole hull hum at a pitch he could feel in his teeth. The port was a hand's width across and scratched. Through it the basin was a brown smear with the Tharsis rise at one edge, and somewhere in the brown, invisible at this altitude, was a quarter-section of iron oxide with a pump house, a sample shed, and a ledger he had not been allowed to bring. He had asked. The lieutenant had said the ledger would be safer where it was. The lieutenant's name was Serrat. He had arrived at dawn with eleven men in two rovers and had wiped his boots on the airlock mat before stepping through, which Arthur had noticed because nobody wiped their boots on Mars — there was no point — and then Serrat had tracked red dust across the floor anyway. He had a young, clean face and a sidearm he did not touch. On his shoulder was a red star with an olive branch laid across it, and under the star, in small letters, the words *Antares Diplomatic Corps*. "Mr. Neegan," he had said. "The Envoy would be grateful for an hour of your time. There's a shuttle waiting." Arthur had been at the table with the ledger open and the day's line half written. He had finished the line before he looked up. Then he had said that he had a shift starting and a pump down, and Serrat had said the shift could wait and that his men would see to the pump, and Arthur had understood that he was going. It had all been very polite. Nobody had raised a voice. Eleven men with sidearms had stood in his yard and Marguerite had come out of the pump house with a wrench and looked at them and looked at Arthur and gone back in. *Diplomatic*, he thought, watching the brown smear tilt. He had known for years what the word meant when Antares used it. Everyone on Mars did. The Corps had come to Ceres as diplomats and stayed as administrators. They had come to the Jovian moons the same way. Nobody had ever been shot, so far as anyone knew. Nobody had needed to be. He shifted his knee and it complained. The thing they wanted was Azra, of course. There was nothing else on Mars worth two rovers and a shuttle. Nine years ago a Consolidated survey crew at Arsia had found a grey, heavy, faintly warm metal in a fault seam, and within a year the physics people had worked out what it did, and within two the basin had filled up with men on leases and the company camps had gone up like mushrooms. Azra sped up decay. Put a gram of it near a fissile pellet and the pellet burned hot and fast and clean, which was why every drive yard between here and Antares wanted it. Put a tonne of it near anything unstable and you did not need clever geometry; you had a bomb. That was why the admiralties wanted it, and why the price had gone from a curiosity to a number that made men do strange things. Arthur's plot had been surveyed before any of that. *Trace radiologicals, no commercial interest*. He had bought it for the price of a good rover because it was on the edge of the basin and far from anyone. He had mined oxide for the road contracts for eleven years. He had kept his ledger. The ledger was the trouble. One line a day, fourteen years, background count and pressure and temperature and a note. He had bought the counter used and had never quite trusted it, and when the count had started creeping up — a fraction of a percent a year, then more — he had written *drift* in the note column and gone on writing it. He had written *drift* for six years. He had recalibrated the instrument twice and it had come back the same and he had written *drift* anyway, because the alternative was that a quarter-section of nothing on the edge of the basin was sitting on something, and that was not the kind of thing that happened to him. Last month Meridian had begun stockpiling concentrate on the plot to his east. The count had jumped. He had stopped writing *drift*. He had not yet written anything else. Somebody at Antares had a counter too. That much was obvious. A steward came aft along the rail, an old man in a grey jacket, carrying a flask and two cups on a tray. He braced against the seat back and poured without asking. "Coffee, sir." Arthur took it. It was hot and it was terrible — burnt, thin, with something in it that was not coffee. He drank it anyway. "How long to the ship?" "Forty minutes, sir. The *Concordance*. She's holding at eight hundred." "That's a cruiser hull." The steward looked at him without expression. "It's a diplomatic vessel, sir." "With torpedo tubes." "I couldn't say, sir. I'm the steward." He topped the cup Arthur hadn't finished and went forward. Arthur turned back to the port. Mars had stopped being a place and become a disc. He found himself, against his intention, thinking about what a very large sum of money would buy. A house with a real window. A knee that had been looked at by someone who knew what a knee was. He put the thought away and it came back. The hum changed pitch. Something went past the port, grey and long and close, and kept going past — a hull, plated, with the red star painted large on it and beneath the star a row of recessed doors that were exactly the size and spacing of torpedo tubes. There was a pennant at the bow. It said *Diplomatic*. The shuttle turned toward the open bay and the disc of Mars slid out of the port and was gone.

"It's oak," said the woman across from him. "Or so I'm told. Sit down, Mr. Neegan." He sat. The chair was bolted. Everything on the ship was bolted, but the ashtray in the middle of the table was a squat steel thing with a hinged lid and a suction line running down through the wood, and she had a thin black cigarette going in it already. "I'm Envoy Prell. You've had a long morning. Would you like coffee?" "I've had some." "Then you'll not want more." She did not smile. She had a sheet of paper in front of her, one sheet, and a pencil laid across it, and a small wristpiece she looked at now and did not look at again for several minutes. "I'll be direct, because I'm told you prefer it and because I do. Antares would like to buy your plot. The quarter-section at grid Tharsees eleven-forty." "Tharsis." "As you like. We would pay—" and she read the figure off the sheet without emphasis, the way a clerk reads a docket number. Arthur heard it. He sat with it. Then he said, "Say that again. Slowly." She said it again, slowly. "That's not a plot price." "No. It's a deposit price. We know what's under you to the tonne, Mr. Neegan, or near enough, and so by now does everyone else with a neutron detector and a reason to point it at Mars." She tapped the sheet. "Eleven hundred tonnes at minimum, in a single fault body, at a purity that makes the Arsia seam look like slag. The figure is not a negotiating figure. I'm not authorized to go above it and I've no intention of going below." "You could just take it." "We could not. Mars is Terran territory under the Charter, and Antares is a signatory. We can buy from a title holder. We cannot annex a quarter-section." She drew on the cigarette and put it in the ashtray and closed the lid on it, and the suction hissed. "Which is why I'd like you to sign before the title holder becomes someone else." "Who?" "Terra can void a settler claim for cause. Cause is a flexible word. There are two Ministry cruisers three weeks out from Earth orbit. I don't know what they're for. I doubt they're for you personally." She let that sit. "There would also be citizenship. Antares, full grade, transferable to dependents. You've no dependents." "No." "Then it's simpler." She made a small mark on the sheet. He looked at the table. He was aware that he wanted to say yes and that the wanting was a physical thing, like hunger. He said instead, "Why me? You could buy Meridian's plot next door. They've a hundred men on it." "Meridian's plot is over the tail of the body. Yours is over the head. And Meridian is a company; it has shareholders and a board and a Terran registration. You're a man with a deed." She looked at him. "You keep a record. Counts, dates. A ledger." "Yes." "For how long?" "Fourteen years." "Has anyone else seen it?" He hesitated, which was a mistake, and she noted it. "My foreman. Nobody else." "And the readings have gone up." "Instrument drift," he said, and heard how it sounded. "Of course." She turned the pencil over. "Your neighbours don't keep ledgers. Meridian keeps tonnage. Consolidated keeps hours. Your record is the only continuous surface count in the basin, Mr. Neegan, and I'd take it as a courtesy if you kept it where it is and showed it to no one until this is settled. There was a business at Meridian's number four shaft last quarter. I'd rather not have that sort of thing muddy the sale." "What business?" "A shaft collapsed. Men were killed. It happens." She looked at the wristpiece. "I've told you the offer. I'd like an answer, but I'm not fool enough to expect one in an hour. You'll want to go home and look at your pump." "How do you know about the pump?" "Lieutenant Serrat has been fixing it since eight this morning. He tells me the impeller's shot." She stood, which meant he stood. "Seventy-two hours. In that time a Terran commissioner will land at your plot, because they've a shuttle in orbit as well and they've been watching us as we've been watching them. He'll offer you a stipend and call it protection. You'll notice, if you're paying attention, that the two aren't different things. Then you'll come to us." "You're very sure." "I'm not sure. I'm briefed." She picked up the sheet and folded it once. "Thar-sees eleven-forty. The shuttle's waiting." "Tharsis," he said again. She had already turned toward the hatch. --- On the shuttle down the steward brought the flask again without being asked. Arthur took the cup and held it and did not drink. Eleven hundred tonnes. He had mined oxide for the road contracts for eleven years and had cleared, in the best of them, enough to replace one rover. He did the sum she had read him against the price of a house on Earth with a window that opened, and then against a knee, and then, because he could not stop, against a small berth on a liner to nowhere in particular, and the sum was still not used up. He had never in his life had a number he could not use up. The coffee had gone cold in his hand. He drank it anyway. It was not better cold. Below the port the disc became a place again, and then a basin, and then a brown smear with a fault-line running across it that he had walked a thousand times and never once thought to wonder about. Somewhere along it eleven men in red-starred jackets were fixing his pump. He was going to sell. He knew it the way he knew the count in his ledger was not drift. # Chapter 3 — Marguerite, then Deems The pump was fixed. Serrat's men had left the old impeller on the bench in the pump house with a tag on it, and the yard swept, and a set of tracks running out east toward the Meridian road that the wind had not yet had time to take. Marguerite was in the pump house with the ledger. She had it open on the bench and was reading it upside down across the room, which she did faster than he read it the right way up. "They didn't touch it," she said. "I sat on it." "I know." "Impeller was shot. Their man knew what he was doing." She closed the ledger and pushed it toward him. "So. What do they want?" He told her. He told her the number and she didn't ask him to repeat it, which he noticed. She chewed one of her cardamom seeds and looked at the wall for a while. "You're selling." "Yes." "Good." He had been ready for a number of things and that was not one of them. "Good?" "It's a good number." She shrugged. "It's not my number. Will they keep the crew on?" "I didn't ask." "Ask. Meridian's paying a foreman two-forty a month and a pension clause. If Antares wants the head of a fault they'll want people who know the ground. If they don't, I want to know before Meridian fills the post." She picked up the old impeller and turned it over, looking at the pitting. "You've got a face on. Don't." "I haven't a face." "You've the face you had when you told Consolidated you were buying my paper. Like you were doing something." She put the impeller down. "You were sick of foremen and they'd marked me down for mouth. It was a good deal. I've said this." "You have." "Then don't make me say it again because a woman with a red star gave you a number." She wiped her hands on her coverall. "Rover on the road. Not theirs." He went to the door. There was a rover, a Terran government model, grey, coming slowly along the Meridian road with its lights on in daylight, which nobody did on Mars either. --- Commissioner Deems came out of the rover the colour of the underside of a leaf. He stood with one hand on the door for a moment and breathed, and then he straightened his jacket, which had been cut for a heavier man on a heavier planet, and came across the yard with a green cloth binder under his arm. "Mr. Neegan. Deems, Colonial Ministry, Mars Desk. Forgive me. I don't travel well." He wiped his forehead with a folded handkerchief and refolded it along the same creases. "Might we go in? I've been in that thing since orbit." Inside he sat at the table where the ledger had been that morning and put the binder down and did not open it. Arthur made coffee. Deems tipped powdered milk into his from a tin he carried in his pocket, tasted it, and set it aside. "You've had the Antares people." "This morning." "I know. We watched their shuttle go up. They watched ours." He hummed a little under his breath and stopped. "I'll not pretend to match their figure. I'm not here with a figure. I'm here with this." He put a hand flat on the binder. "The Colonial Charter, Mars Schedule. Section eleven. "For oxide. The assessed potential is now somewhat higher." He said it without relish, like a man reading a weather report. "I could void it tomorrow. "From what?" Deems looked at him from under his brows. "From being a man alone on a quarter-section that two admiralties would like to own. I'd have thought that was plain." He picked up the coffee, tasted it again, and put it down. "May I ask — that pump outside. Serrat's people replaced the impeller. What's the design? It's not a Terran pattern." "It's mine. I'll not give you a different number, because it'd be a lie; I can void it in twenty-four if I'm told to. I'm not telling you that to be clever." # Chapter 4 — Sabin The Meridian camp had a gate, which was a joke on Mars, and a man in it, which was not. Arthur stopped the rover and passed a bottle of rye across the sill. It was real rye, Terran, the last of three he had brought out fourteen years ago and had been saving for a reason he had never found. "Physicist," he said. "The one with the paper." The gate man looked at the bottle and then at him. "Sabin. Hut nine. He won't talk to you." "I know." "Then what's the bottle for?" "For you not asking that." The gate man put the bottle under his coat and waved him through. The camp was two hundred men on Meridian leases and a hundred tonnes of grey concentrate in a fenced yard at the east end, under tarpaulin, with a Geiger on a post that nobody was looking at. Arthur did not look at it either. He drove past it with his eyes on the road. Hut nine had a radiochemistry sign on it and a door that stuck. Inside it was one room, benches along the walls, and a thin stooped man in glasses sorting sample trays with hands that shook. "I'm not permitted to speak to you," Sabin said, without turning round. "Contractually. If you want to stand there, stand there." "Neegan. From the west plot." "I know who you are. The whole camp knows who you are. You're the man the red stars came for." He wiped his glasses on his sleeve, looked at one of two wristwatches, and went on sorting. "Whatever you're going to ask, I can't answer. That's not obstruction. That's a six-year penalty clause." "Then I'll ask and you won't answer." Sabin looked at him for the first time — at the space just left of his head. Something in his face moved and settled. "You've a ledger, I'm told." "Yes." "Fourteen years?" "Yes." "Then ask." Arthur sat on a stool. "Azra speeds up decay in anything unstable near it. Does it speed up its own?" "I can't tell you that." "Does the effect scale with mass? Straight, or faster?" "I can't tell you that either." Sabin picked up a tray, put it down. "I can tell you that if a man leased to Meridian had fitted a curve to Meridian's stockpile counts, and found it bent upward, and written that down, and put the word *self-catalytic* in the title, he'd have been asked to un-write it within the month. And he'd have done it, because he has six years left and a lease that can be sold to Antares tomorrow, which — " he checked the other watch — "I'm told it has been. I ship at noon." "And the paper?" "Retracted. Doesn't exist. Meridian was very clear." He wiped the glasses again. "The copy he wasn't supposed to keep would be in the third drawer of that bench, under the calibration sheets. That's not information. That's furniture. You can look at furniture." Arthur went to the bench. The drawer stuck like the door. Under a stack of calibration sheets was a typescript, eleven pages, with a title he did not read yet and a number circled on the last page in pencil, with a second number beside it and a third, and a bracket round all three. "There's a spread on this." "There's always a spread. It's one stockpile and eight months of counts. Factor of three, high to low. The tonnage people took the high number and were satisfied. They're satisfied men." Sabin came and stood beside him, not close. "You'll want to know where the yard sits against those. I can't tell you. You drove past it. There's a counter on the post." "Nobody's watching it." "Nobody's paid to." He went back to his trays. "You're looking at my hands. Everyone does. Fourteen years of the potassium in me going where it oughtn't, a little faster than God meant. It's not in the safety literature because there isn't any. Meridian says it's the gravity." He put a tray in a rack. "Take the furniture and go. I've a shuttle." "What happened at number four?" Sabin didn't stop sorting. "A shaft collapsed. Nine leased men. Ruled a collapse." "Was it?" "It collapsed. Whether the ground under it had been sitting next to eighty tonnes of concentrate for a year and had got — brittle — that wasn't in the ruling. I wasn't asked. Ask the gate man. Ask anyone. They'll tell you it was a collapse." He looked at the Lunar watch. "Everyone here knows about it, Mr. Neegan. Nobody thinks it means anything. That's the thing about knowing." --- At the gate the man with the rye leaned on the sill. "Get what you came for?" "Some of it. Number four shaft." "Collapse. Bad ground." He shrugged. "Nine of ours. They flew in nine more." "Anyone say it was anything else?" "Sabin, maybe. Sabin says a lot." He straightened. "Mind the yard on your way out. Counter's high today. They've stacked another twelve tonnes since Tuesday." Arthur drove out slowly past the fenced yard. This time he looked at the Geiger on its post. It was an old Consolidated model with a needle dial, the same as his, and the needle was standing at a mark he had never seen his own reach, and it was not moving, because nobody had told it to. He drove home with the typescript on the seat beside him, face down, and did not turn it over until he was in his own yard with the rover engine off. Then he read the title. Then he read the last page, with its three numbers and its bracket, and looked at the middle one for a long time, and then at the low one, and then out through the windscreen at the east horizon, where the Meridian tarpaulins were a grey line against a brown one, four kilometres off, which was inside every radius on the page.
