# Chapter 5 — The Arithmetic He got the decimal wrong the first time. It was two in the morning and the table lamp was the only light in the plot, and he had the typescript open at the last page and the ledger open at the last month and the slide rule between them, and he had run the sum from Sabin's low figure against the Meridian yard's tonnage as the gate man had given it, and the answer came out so bad that he did not believe it. So he ran it again and it came out an order of magnitude better, and he sat back, and then he saw where he had slipped the cursor and ran it a third time and it came out the way it had the first. He wrote it down. Then he made coffee, because there was nothing else to do with his hands. The paper was eleven pages and Sabin had written it the way Sabin talked — fast, contemptuous of the reader, and correct in a way that did not care whether you followed. The counts from the Meridian yard over eight months, fitted. A straight line through the first four months. A bend in the fifth. By the eighth the curve was pulling away from the line the way a rocket pulls away from its own smoke. Sabin had extrapolated. He had drawn three curves through the bend, one steep, one shallow, one between, and each one crossed a horizontal at a different tonnage, and the horizontal was labelled in Sabin's small cramped hand *self-sustaining regime (est.)*. Low figure, one hundred and thirty tonnes. High figure, three hundred and ninety. Meridian's yard, as of Tuesday, one hundred and twelve. Arthur looked at that for a while. Then he did the other sum, the one he had not wanted to do, which was the radius. Sabin had done it for him on page nine and he checked it anyway. If the yard went — if *self-sustaining regime* meant what the plain words meant, if a hundred and thirty tonnes of Azra began accelerating its own decay and the decay produced heat and the heat did what heat did to rock — then the basin within some tens of kilometres was not a place with people in it any more. The paper did not say *sterilize*. It said *thermal excursion* and gave a number with a lot of zeros after it and left the reader to translate. Arthur translated. His plot was four kilometres from the yard. The Consolidated camp was six. The Meridian camp was sitting on it. Eleven hundred tonnes under his own feet, Prell had said. In one fault body. He looked at that thought and put it down, because it was a different problem and he could only carry one. The thing was, nobody would believe him. He knew this without having to think about it. He was a settler with a bad knee and a hand-drawn ledger, and the paper was retracted, and the man who wrote it was on a shuttle to Antares, and the tonnage people had taken the high number and were satisfied. Deems would ask him what the picture meant. Prell would ask him whether anyone else had seen the ledger. Neither would look at the low figure, because the low figure was not the one on their sheet. He turned that over for a long time, and somewhere in turning it, it went upside down. They did not have to believe him. That was the thing. Prell had been told about this in a room with the door closed — he was sure of it now; her question about the ledger had been a check, not a discovery — and had filed it under *Terran problem*. Deems had it as a footnote somewhere in the green binder, initialled by a man at Meridian who was satisfied. Each of them knew, and each of them had decided the risk was acceptable, and each of them had made that decision alone. Put them in a room together. Show them the bend. Let each one see the other see it. Then it was not a risk that could be quietly filed, because the other side had watched you file it, and would remember, and would say so, later, in front of somebody with a longer table. He did not have to be right. He had to be impossible to disbelieve in company. It was a bet. He knew it was a bet. The low figure was the low figure and the high one was three times it and Sabin himself had said it was one stockpile and eight months. If the truth was the high figure, Meridian could stack for another year and nothing would happen and he would have thrown away a sum he could not use up on a curve that bent and then, quietly, straightened. If the truth was the low figure he had about eighteen tonnes of margin and Meridian was stacking twelve a week. He looked at his hands. They were doing the thing. He put them flat on the table until they stopped. Then he went to the radio and raised the *Concordance*, and asked for the Envoy, and was told the Envoy was asleep, and said he would wait, and waited. When she came on she sounded exactly as she had sounded across the oak table. He said he would like her at the plot at noon, with the Terran commissioner, and that he would explain then, and that he would not sign anything before. She said *Thar-sees eleven-forty, noon*, and rang off. Deems he got on the second try. Deems said *noon* and then said, "Is it about the pump?" and Arthur said no, and Deems said, "Pity," and rang off too. Marguerite was in the doorway. She had been there for some part of it. She had the lease tag on its cord in one hand and was turning it. "You were going to sell." "I still might." She looked at the paper, upside down, and then at him. "That's Sabin's." "Yes." "Sabin's shipping out." "At noon." She chewed her seed. "Then whatever you're doing, you've got the one copy and a bad knee. That's all." "That's all I've ever had," he said, and it came out sounding like something, and he was too tired to take it back.

Joint. Antares and Terra, equal seats, with a third seat held by the basin — the crews. Whoever the trust leases the ground to mines it, and I don't mind who. But there are conditions. Extraction is rate-capped, and the cap is written into the instrument, not a schedule that can be revised. And every labour lease in the basin converts to a fixed-term wage contract with the right to quit." There was a pause of about two seconds. "No," said Prell. "Mr. Neegan," Deems said, "the Ministry doesn't recognize a trust with a labour seat. There's no schedule for it. I'd have to write one, and I'd have to get it read, and by then—" "By then you'd have voided the claim." "Well. Yes." "I know what the Charter says, Commissioner, I've read it, I read it on the shuttle out, it's very clear on cause and very quiet on what happens when the ground under Meridian's yard gets brittle—" He stopped. He had not meant to say it yet. It had come out of him the way things did when the temper went, at the wrong moment and the true thing, and he stood in his own shed with his hands shaking and two people who did not want to be there looking at him, and felt the argument slide out of his grip and go somewhere he could not follow. "Brittle," said Prell. "Number four shaft," said Deems, slowly. "That was ruled—" "A collapse. I know. Everyone knows." Arthur got his hands under his arms and then made himself take them out. "I'm sorry. That's not how I meant to— Sit down, Commissioner. Take the crate. Marguerite, give him the crate." Marguerite got up without a word and Deems sat. "Right." Arthur went to the chamber and opened it. Inside, on a lead tray, was a grey pellet the size of a fingernail. "This is Azra. The needle stood where it stood. "Now four." He opened it, set a second pellet beside the first, closed it. The needle climbed and settled. "That's twice the mass. The needle climbed, and this time it did not settle quite where a straight line would have put it; it went past, and hung there, and the sound the counter made changed pitch in a way that had nothing to do with volume and everything to do with rate. "That's eight grams. I've one more step and it's the last I've got." He set four pellets in. Closed it. The needle went up and kept going up for a count of three, and stopped high, and the counter's clicking had run together into a tone. Nobody said anything. Deems had stopped breathing through his mouth. Prell had come two steps in from the door. "It's not straight," Arthur said. "It bends. # Chapter 7 — The Bet Deems did the sum longhand on the back of a calibration sheet, humming. It took him eleven minutes. Arthur read the counts off the counter's tape in order — two grams, four, eight, twelve — and Deems wrote them in a column and drew lines under them and did the ratios one at a time, and each time a ratio came out he stopped humming, looked at it, and started again. Nobody spoke. The counter sang its one note. Marguerite stood against the wall with the lease tag in her fist. Prell had lit nothing and touched nothing and had not looked at her wristpiece since the needle went up. "Twelve over eight," Deems said at last, "should be one and a half. It's two and a quarter." "Yes." "And the — the yard figure. A hundred and twelve, you said. Against—" he put his finger on the page where Arthur's had been, "—a hundred and thirty." "Yes." "Eighteen tonnes." He wiped his forehead and refolded the handkerchief on its creases and did not put it away. "How fast are they stacking?" "Twelve a week, the gate man said. Might be more. They've had a good month." Deems sat on the crate and looked at his column of figures and then at the shed door, as if the Meridian yard might be visible through it. "This paper. Who saw it?" "Meridian. They retracted it." "Did they send it to the Ministry?" "I don't know. Did they?" Deems opened the green binder for the first time since he had come to Mars. He turned tabs. He found a page and read it with his lips moving and then closed the binder and put both hands on it. "There's a footnote," he said. "Under *known risks*. Self-catalysis — theoretical — Meridian's assessment: not credible at planned yard volumes. Initialled." He looked up. "I initialled it too. I asked if it was serious and I was told the operator was satisfied, and I wrote that down. That was in March." "They took the high figure," Arthur said. "There's a high figure?" Arthur did not answer quickly enough, and Prell said, from the door, "There's always a spread, Commissioner. It's one stockpile." Her voice had no weight in it at all. "The paper was circulated to Antares as well, in draft. Under the same heading." Deems turned on the crate to look at her. "You knew." "I was briefed. It was characterized as external. Mars is Terran soil; a Terran operator's yard is a Terran matter. That was the position." She said it exactly the way she had read the tonnage off the sheet. "It remains the position, formally." "Formally." "Yes." They looked at each other across three metres of shed, and Arthur watched the thing he had been betting on arrive, which was not fear — he could not tell, then or afterwards, whether Prell was frightened, whether she had ever been — but exposure. Deems had seen the graph he could not read and had done the sum himself, in front of a foreign envoy, and had found his own initials on the footnote. Prell had stood in a shed and heard a Terran commissioner say *you knew* and had not denied it, in front of a Terran commissioner. Neither of them could now go back to a table with a longer sheet and say the risk was acceptable, because the other had watched them learn it was not, and would say so, and be believed. "I need your radio," Deems said. "Pump house." He went. Arthur heard him through the wall raising the Meridian camp, and then the Ministry shuttle, and then Meridian again, and the words *pending review* and *by authority of* and *tonight, not tomorrow, tonight*, and then a long pause while someone at Meridian said something, and then Deems's voice saying, quite mildly, "Then have your operator put it in writing to the Ministry that he declines a Charter halt, and I'll have it on file by the time the Envoy's dispatch reaches Antares," and then nothing, and then, "Thank you." He came back grey and sat on the crate. "They're stopping. Concentrate's to be dispersed to three lots below thirty tonnes each by morning. He wanted to argue. I mentioned the Envoy." He looked at Prell. "I hope that's all right." "It's what I'd have done," Prell said. She had her sheet out. She uncapped her pencil and wrote a figure in the margin, looked at it, crossed it out, and wrote another, smaller, and said without looking up, "Antares will match a rate cap written into the instrument, provided the cap is symmetrical and Terra's operators sit under the same number. The labour seat I'll refer. I'll not promise it. The sum I've adjusted, since you've made the ground worth less by insisting it be mined slowly." She turned the sheet toward him. "That is what a settler gets for being right, Mr. Neegan. I said I wasn't unkind. I didn't say I was generous." He looked at the figure. It was still a figure he could not use up. It was smaller than the one before by an amount that would have bought his plot eleven times over, and he found he did not mind, and did not trust that. "The cruisers," he said. "The Ministry cruisers. Three weeks out." Prell put the pencil down. Deems looked up. "What cruisers?" "Two. From Earth orbit. The Envoy mentioned them." "There are no cruisers." Deems frowned. "The Ministry hasn't a cruiser to spare for Mars; it's had two in refit since spring. I'd know. It's my desk." Arthur looked at Prell. She had picked the pencil up again and was making a small tidy mark on the sheet, and did not look back, and did not say anything, and the mark, as far as he could see, was not a number. Marguerite, from the wall, said quietly, "Told you. Rename the lease." The counter was still singing. Arthur went to the chamber and opened it and took the pellets out one at a time, and the needle came down in steps, and by the last one it was clicking again like an ordinary instrument in an ordinary shed, and he found that his hands, for the first time all week, were not doing anything at all.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of writing that executes its plan with unusual precision and discipline. Let me examine it across the relevant dimensions. **Craft and Prose Style** The prose is genuinely Asimovian in the best sense: declarative, unadorned, trusting the situation to carry the weight. "Deems did the sum longhand on the back of a calibration sheet, humming" is a perfect opening sentence — it establishes character, stakes, and atmosphere without a wasted syllable. The chapter avoids the trap of decorating its tension with adjectives. When the needle goes up, we're told Prell "had not looked at her wristpiece since the needle went up" — this is showing character through omission, which is sophisticated. The central mechanism — mutual exposure rather than fear — is articulated with real clarity: "Neither of them could now go back to a table with a longer sheet and say the risk was acceptable, because the other had watched them learn it was not, and would say so, and be believed." This is the kind of sentence that earns its length. It's analytical rather than poetic, which is exactly right for the genre and character. **Dialogue** The dialogue is exceptional. Deems's "There's a high figure?" lands perfectly — it's the question of a man who has just understood he was given a managed briefing. Prell's "It remains the position, formally" followed by Deems's flat "Formally" and her "Yes" is a masterclass in saying everything through what isn't said. The exchange about the cruisers at the end — Deems's genuine puzzlement, Prell's non-answer with the pencil mark — is the chapter's best moment. It retroactively recontextualizes Prell's earlier gambit without explaining it, which is exactly the right choice. Marguerite's single line from the wall — "Told you. Rename the lease." — is perfectly placed and perfectly voiced. It's dry, it's right, it doesn't editorialize, and it closes the chapter's emotional arc without sentimentality. **Character Consistency** Every character behaves exactly as their profile demands. Deems does the sum himself, longhand, humming — then finds his own initials on the footnote, which is a devastating detail. His radio call to Meridian, with the mild threat about putting the refusal in writing, shows the competence-within-limits the profile describes. Prell's adjustment of the sum downward without apology, her "I said I wasn't unkind. I didn't say I was generous," is pitch-perfect. Arthur's observation that the reduced figure "was still a figure he could not use up" and his distrust of his own equanimity is psychologically precise. **The Gambit's Resolution** The plan called for the turn to be "not terror but mutual exposure" and that's exactly what's delivered. The chapter doesn't cheat by making anyone heroic or villainous. Prell's admission that Antares was briefed and characterized it as "external" is chilling precisely because it's bureaucratic rather than malevolent. The cruiser reveal — that they never existed, that it was a pressure tactic — is handled with beautiful economy. Prell's non-response (the pencil mark that "was not a number") is the chapter's most elegant moment. **The Ending** The final paragraph — Arthur removing the pellets one at a time, the needle coming down in steps, his hands "not doing anything at all" — is earned. It's not triumphant, not elegiac, just the cessation of a particular kind of tension. The counter "clicking again like an ordinary instrument in an ordinary shed" is the right note: the world has not changed, the danger hasn't been eliminated, but this particular moment is over. **Minor Criticisms** The sentence "and Arthur watched the thing he had been betting on arrive" is slightly overworked — the long subordinate clause that follows it is doing a lot of analytical heavy lifting that might have been better distributed. It's the one moment where the prose tells us what to think rather than letting us arrive there. The chapter is also very short on physical grounding after the opening; we lose the shed somewhat as the dialogue takes over, though this is a minor complaint given the genre's priorities. The footnote detail — Deems finding his own initials — is perhaps slightly too convenient as a dramatic beat, but it's earned by the character work and the chapter plan, so it lands. **Overall** This is a chapter that does exactly what it sets out to do, does it with discipline and intelligence, and resists every temptation toward melodrama or false resolution. The writing is clean, the characters are consistent, the gambit lands as a bet rather than a certainty, and the ending is appropriately mundane. It's not flashy, but it's very good. Six weeks. The deed to grid Tharsis eleven-forty was held by the Tharsis Basin Extraction Trust, two seats, Antares and Terra. The third seat did not exist. It had been referred, Prell's dispatch said, and was under consideration by the appropriate directorate, which Arthur understood to mean it had been put in a drawer with the calibration sheets. He drew a salary that was not a Terran pension and not an Antares fortune and was, month for month, about what he had cleared in a good year on the road contracts, and he had a supervisor on the *Concordance* named Halvard whom he had spoken to twice by radio and never seen. Halvard wanted the pump replaced with a Terran pattern. Arthur had written a memorandum explaining why not, in language he thought Deems would have approved of, and had heard nothing back. The basin leases had converted. Every one of them. Consolidated's men and Meridian's men had signed new forms in the fourth week, and the forms said *Fixed-Term Wage Contract, Tharsis Schedule* across the top, and underneath they said much what the old ones had said, except that a man could now quit on ninety days' notice provided he repaid his transit costs and any training advanced, at a rate of interest the schedule set. Marguerite had read hers upside down across the pump house bench and had laughed once, not loudly, and signed it. She was leaving Tuesday. --- He found her in the pump house with her kit already bagged, checking the new impeller, which was his old design cast again, because Serrat's men had done it right the first time and he saw no reason to change. "Meridian's foreman," he said. "Two-forty a month, pension clause, and a berth allowance after five years." She wiped her hands. "They've thirty tonnes in three lots and a Terran on the gate who reads the counter now. It's the safest yard in the basin. You made it that." "You could stay." "I could. You'd pay me what the Trust pays, which is what you paid me, which was fine when it was yours." She shouldered the bag. "It's not yours." "No." "Then don't." She stopped in the door and turned the lease tag over once on its cord and looked at it and let it drop back against her coverall. "The crew's good. Petrov can run them. He's slow with the ledger but he doesn't lie to it." She looked at him for slightly too long. "You did a thing. It was a bet and it came in and you didn't sell. That's not nothing. It's also not what you'll tell yourself it was, in a year, so I'm saying it now, once. All right?" "All right." "Good." She went out. He heard the rover start, and heard it go east along the Meridian road, and did not go to the door to watch it, and then did, and it was already a smear. --- At five he went to the shed and wrote the line. Background, pressure, temperature. The count was down. Not by much — a hair, less than the day-to-day scatter, and he would have filed it as drift fourteen years ago without a thought. But he had the month behind it now, and the month behind that, and the hair had been there since the yard was dispersed, small and steady, one direction. The halt would do it. Thirty tonnes in three lots four kilometres off was not a hundred and twelve in one, and the field fell off with distance the way fields did, and the plain reading was that Deems had made a radio call and the needle had heard him. There was another reading. Sabin's page seven had a paragraph he had not needed for the arithmetic and had gone back to since, once, at two in the morning. It concerned the daughter product. Azra decayed. Slowly — slowly enough that the tonnage people had never put it on a sheet — into something grey and heavy and inert that did nothing to anything. Sabin had estimated a half-life with his usual contempt and his usual bracket, and the bracket was wide, and the low end was not geological. It was the sort of number a man could live to see the far side of, if he kept a ledger. Eleven hundred tonnes under his feet. A trust with forty-one pages and a petition to amend clause nine. Two admiralties who had watched each other learn something in a shed. He wrote the count. In the note column he wrote *down 0.3, cf. dispersal*, and then he sat with the pen over the page, and then he closed the ledger, because it was a different problem and he could only carry one, and because Petrov would need showing the ledger tomorrow and he had not decided yet how much of it to show. The telephone in the pump house rang. It was a new telephone; the Trust had put it in. He limped across the yard to it. "Neegan." "Mr. Neegan, this is Osei, Commissioner Deems's office. "Two E's." "Thank you. And the first name is Arthur, with a U?" "Yes." "Good. That's all. Good evening."
